You can do stuff that’s kind of, ‘1 don’t know how long this is going to last, but this is where I’m at right now.’” One jokingly suggests that, if Stanley pur- sues his sometimes-mentioned notion of dip- ping his toe into the waters of classical music, he’ll need yet another label — he may have to be lent out to Angel. “Well I’ve been talking to Angel about doing some things,” he says quite seriously, “but my feeling is that 1 don’t want to do that right now. Actually, I’d be more inter- ested in getting acceptance as a composer than as a guitar player in that world.” Some things on Stanley Jordan’s agenda for the not-too-distant future: the formation of a band (Stanley’s tired of the solo thing, he says he prefers to play in a band), the completion of a book detailing his tap-the- strings technique, further exploration of the stick (Emmett Chapman’s fret-only instru- ment), the possible design of a guitar with two extra bass strings, the eventual comple- tion of the Manhattan album, and a “Stan- dards Volume 2” for Blue Note. Stanley becomes slightly defensive when it’s pointed out to him that some people might not agree with his categorizing, oh, “One Less Bell to Answer” or “The Sounds of Silence” as a “standard,” in the tradition- al sense. “Look,” he says, “when Art Tatum played ‘You Took Advantage of Me,’ or something, he knew that song when he was younger. So, in a way. I’m just doing the same thing that he did then. To a lot of people of my generation, these songs are standards. “I hope people get the point of what the album is about, beyond just the songs. It’s not a real flashy technique album, I wasn’t trying to show off everything I could do, but 1 was trying to make the most out of what 1 have to bring out the most in the songs. And, in a way, 1 guess 1 was trying to make the guitar sing, to make it dance. “It’s real easy to take a song and cover it up with a lot of complex changes and every- thing you learned in theory class. Every- thing you learned in theory class you can apply to every song. But 1 found that when 1 was playing the standards that I grew up with, I knew when I was getting away from the song. Whereas the older standards, 1 might play the song without having ever heard the original version, and so 1 don’t really appreciate what it is I’m doing to the song. The songs that I put on the album, because I’d heard other versions before, I have a much better sense of when I’m losing a song — and I feel the responsibility to re- spect a song — no one has to explain that to me. And then the next time I hear some- body say, ‘You’re losing a song,’ I’m not going to say, ‘Oh, they don’t know anything about jazz.’ I’m going to say, ‘Oh, let me check it out, maybe it’s true.’” Don’t expect Stanley Jordan to be a flash in the jazz pan — he’s far too talented, far too committed, for that. Plus, for somebody who won’t be seeing his 30th birthday this decade, he has an unusually long view. When Stanley Jordan was at Princeton — he studied music, specifically computer music, at Princeton for four years — he had the op- portunity to meet one of jazz’s eminences grise, the great Benny Carter, who was teaching there at the time. “I’d signed up for his course,” says Stan- ley, “and I kind of timidly went up and said, ‘I’d like to play with you in your concert.’ And 1 brought my guitar over, and we jammed on ‘My Old Flame,’ and he said, ‘Sure, you can be in the show.’ “He was tremendously supportive and it was really good to know him and be in- spired by somebody who’s been in the mu- sic so long, who is such a survivor. 1 saw myself some day as a grand old man who people could look up to, and I’d know it all and they’d want to learn it from me.” Beatles CD Sales (continued from page 5) preorders for all four titles at $49.99. Chronis said the first day totals edged out the first day of the Bruce Springsteen pack- age last fall by only $400. “That shows you how close it was,” says Chronis. “There were no big lines the first day, be we have found a very consistent stream of customers coming in every day.” “1 think when the other titles come out, these titles will become a deep catalog kind of sales very quickly,” says Evan Lasky, president of Danjay Music & Video, a an 85- store franchise based in the Western half of the country. Lasky says the fact the first four Beatles disc are in mono may have an effect on the sales of the future stereo re- leases. “I don’t know how people feel about that.” Lasky says there wasn’t as much hoopla at their stores over the discs as there had been for Springsteen. “There was hype, but it wasn’t a frenzied kind of hype like with Springsteen.” Lasky had hoped their stores wouldn’t lowball the prices of the discs as many dealers had with the Spring- steen release. “I had basically told our fran- chisees that they would be nuts to give it away. Hopefully most of them stuck by that.” When told that some stores around the country had sold them for as little as $11.99 he said, “They could have put them out at $19.99 and the people who wanted them would have bought them.” “We sold, give or take a few, domestical- ly, 33,254 as of March 2,” says Tower Re- cords’ senior vice president Stan Goman. “It wasn’t Bruce Springsteen, but boy, we sure sold a lot more that 1 thought we would and people are buying ail four at a time.” Goman said they had been receiving reor- ders that they had placed the day the discs came out. “It’ll help Capitol’s year for sure and that’s great. They’re a great company and we’ve always been close with them. It couldn’t happen to a nicer bunch.” “We’re selling them like hotcakes,” says Harmony House spokeswoman Susan Thom. At press time, the 20-store chain, based in the metropolitan Detroit area, had nearly sold out their initial order. “We or- dered 1,200 on each title and probably about 10 minutes after our stores opened on Thursday, we reordered a thousand of each title and I’m understanding now that Capitol may not be able to fill our entire order. Harmony House buyer, Roy Burk- hert says that they had received 500 copies of only two of the four titles but that Capitol had promised more in a week. “They made either 200 or 300 thousand of each title. 1 don’t know if that’s the Jacksonville plant or the whole country.” The chain sold the discs at $13.99 on sale and has planned to sell them at the regular price of $15.99. Record Bar vice president Steve Bennett says his 130-store chain, with stores located mostly in the South and Southeast, had de- cided not to even advertise because of all the media attention the discs had been giv- en. “In terms of sales impact and overall impact, it’s certainly not as big as Spring- steen, but that’s a different situation — right before Christmas and with Springsteen at a popularity peak. It’s the next biggest thing, no doubt about that.” Record Bar sold the four disc set promotionally for $50. “We didn’t discount them individually. We were one of the highest price people when Springsteen came out and if you bought one Beatle CD from us, $15 is not exactly a lowball price, but in terms of a package deal, we’re as low as anybody.” He said many of their stores had sold out with just their preorder reservations. Bennett also feels that once the entire catalog of the Fab Four has been released, it will revert to a catalog type item. “I’m expecting it to be a fairly intense short lived phenomenon as far as the real strong sales levels go. We had five or six real strong days right out of the box. People who want them all have started now and of course 1 expect the next batch of releases, as everybody else does, to be huge.” STARLIGHTERS—Carole Bayer Sager and Burt Bacharach recently received the Starlight Foundation 's Humanitarian Award at a gala in their honor in Los Angeles. POINTS WEST r 1 ' NEWFACES TO WATCH TINSEL TOWN TRIBUTE—Seems Hollywood is getting aggressive in the doling out of stars on its tourist-laden Walk of Fame. As the town approaches its 100th anniversary this summer, fe- verish star-bestowing has occurred - but not undeservingly. Maybe space is get- ting scarce or maybe the city has gotten wise, but these nifty little pedestrian CEMENTED—Bob Seger and The Silver Bullet Band recently joined the legions of sidewalk celebrities with a star on Holly- wood’s Walk Of Fame. engravings finally seem to be going to more of the folks who’ve earned ‘em rather than to the latest movie studio hype, as was common in decades past. Tina Turner was a recent inductee (does any woman in the music business work harder?), so was Billy Holiday. The latest is Capitol’s Bob Seger and The Silver Bullet Band, an en- during little rock'n’roll outfit if there ever was one. The ceremony took place last Friday, and the band’s star, which is located, conveniently enough, outside the Capitol Tower on Vine St (as is Tina Turner’s - another Capitol artist), marks the Walk of Fame’s 1,844th star. MUCHA MADONNA— Reliable sources out here on the West Coast tell us that “True Blue,” Madonna’s latest outrageously successful Sire LP, is gonna’ keep birthin’ singles until the al- bum is plum singled-out. If so, “True Blue” will become the first album we can think of to have all its cuts released as singles (the most-singles record is held, to our knowledge, by Michael Jackson’s “Thriller,” which spawned a total of seven). The album’s latest re- lease, “La Isla Bonita,” is single no. 5 (“Jimmy Jimmy” and “Where’s The Party,” two popular album tracks, have yet to be released as singles). JOINING THE PIPELINE—Son oma, CA-based Global Pacific Re- cords (the indie jazz/new age/multi- cultural label) has signed on for manufacturing and U.S. distribution with CBS Records. Now, along with hitting all those health food and book stores it always has, the label will be able to funnel its product to a much broader market via the CBS pipeline. A package of five first releases under the deal will appear in April, including Paul Horn’s “Traveller,” David Friesen’s “Inner Voices,” Steve Kindler and Teja Bell’s “Dolphin Smiles,” the Paul Greaver re-issue “Joy,” plus a double album sampler “The Fruits Of Our Labor.” Quarterly releases will fol- low. The once tiny label is also expand- ing its staff, opening offices in New York and Los Angeles. Promo and mar- keting, which the company retains un- der the new deal, are being beefed up to include listening parties and video pro- jects (long and short form). And while we’re on the subject. Global Pacific also has a nice little showcase coming up at the opening bash for Music Business Symposium 3 at the Beverly The- atre in L.A. April 2. As part of the evening’s entertainment (which in- cludes an as yet unscheduled rock act) label artists Paul Horn, Steve Kindler and Joaquin Lievano are slated to perform. Gregory Dobrin When one hears Henry Johnson’s guitar playing, one hears a jazz style that’s washed in the blues. So it’s not surprising that Henry Johnson, whose debut album, “You’re The One,” was released late last year on Impulse!, grew up in two of the bluesiest cities on Earth: Chicago and Memphis. “I got the blues from Memphis, of course,” he says, “and when 1 came back to Chicago I worked on the South Side a lot. I always liked the blues, I always liked B.B. King and those guys. And, you know, being young in the ’60s, I’d end up listening to Isaac Hayes or Sly & the Family Stone. But every once in a while, you hear something that just turns your head around, and at that particular time I heard Wes Mont- gomery. This was right before he died, and it just freaked me totally out. So, after that, I just wanted to find out what this music was all about. I didn’t under- stand it, but the only thing I knew was there was just something about it that 1 just really liked. And the more I listened to it, the more I got addicted to it.” Henry’s addiction to Wes Montgom- ery is evident in his playing. He never did get to see the guitar great live, but he did get to work, at the age of 14, with an earlier influence: the aforemen- tioned Isaac Hayes. “That was my first professional gig, around the time of the ‘Hot Buttered Soul’ album. Before that I played churches, playing gospel stuff.” After resettling in Chicago, Henry Johnson began the various slate of ac- tivities: playing in top 40 bands, leading his own trio, working in society orchestras. “Then after that, about 1976, I went on the road with Jack McDuff for about a year, which really got the blues stuff happening. Then I stuck around Chica- go for about a year, before getting called by Donny Hathaway.” After Hathaway’s death, Henry be- gan working with Ramsey Lewis, the first of two stints in Lewis’ outfit, but his real formative years were from 1982- HENRY JOHNSON 85, when he worked around Chiq with hiw own quartet. By Brian Kassan LOS ANGELES -Love Tractor? Even the name of the band elicits chuck- les from the uninitiated, but those fans who are familiar with the positively bright, hap- py-go-lucky instrumental strains of this Georgian band probably chuckle frequently anyway. Love Tractor emerged out of Athens, Ga. in 1980, where a unique college party scene spawned from the lack of dance clubs in the area. The B-52’s, Pylon, R.E.M. and Love Tractor were among a handful of “dance” oriented bands who played at these “front- porch” parties, drawing a steady crowd of college students. “Athens had no clubs per se to really go to,” says Love Tractor guitarist Mark Cline in an interview with Cash Box, “and within the art school crowd there was a massive party scene. It was really a group of about 100 people in the core of it. When we start- ed, we were considered a dance band. You were a good band if people could dance to you. We were doing these bands for fun. No one was serious. ONJAZZ Terry Gibbs GIBBS—The best jazz big band album released in 1986 did not win a Grammy; in fact, it wasn’t even nominated for a Grammy. That may be because the best big band album released in 1986 — year in which the Grammy nominees in the category were the formidable bands of Lionel Hampton, Mel Lewis, Benny Goodman, Woody Herman, and Doc Severinsen — was recorded in March of 1959. “Terry Gibbs Dream Band” (Contemporary) is a smoking, wallop-packing album that features great charts (by Bill Holman, Bob Brookmeyer, Al Cohn, Marty Paich, and Manny Albam), great players (like Conte Candoli, Med Flory, Joe Maini, Mel Lewis), and great big band tunes (like “Don’t Be That Way,” “Cottontail,” “Jumpin’ at the Woodside”). “I’ll tell you the whole story,” says Terry Gibbs, in New York for a week- long engagement with Buddy De- Franco, his frequent partner. “When I moved to California, there were a few rehearsal bands — Bill Holman had one, Med Flory had one — and they were nice. 1 had a good contract with Mercu- ry where I could record what I wanted to record, so I decided 1 wanted to do a big band album. But I heard that this one guy got fined $1,000 by the union for rehearsing a band for an album. And I didn’t just want to record a band — because I did that in New York one time, just went in the studio and didn’t really know what the hell we were do- ing. I wanted a tight band. “At the same time, there was a club called the Seville, in Hollywood, that had some Latin music and they were bombing. So they called me up to come in with a quintet. I went in on a Tuesday night, and it went good. Then I heard that you could rehearse a big band for a nightclub engagement, which is ridicu- lous, but not for a record date. So I got an idea: why don’t 1 put a big band in ^ the club? That way I could rehearse my band. And they were paying me enough money — the scale was only $15 a night in those days — so I went to the club owner and said, ‘How would you like to have a 16-piece band for what you’re giving me for five?”’ So in came the Terry Gibbs Big Band, and, about five weeks later, in came Wally Heider to do some re- mote recording. And, voila, out came the best big band album of 1986. And, perhaps, the best big band album of 1987 — there is another live volume due from Contemporary in May. And — who knows? — maybe the best big band al- bums of 1988 and 1989. All told, Gibbs has been sitting on enough tapes for four albums. They didn’t come out when they were recorded, because the band recorded many of these same songs on their studio albums (Emarcy, out-of-print). They didn’t come out earli- er, because Gibbs says he didn’t want them on a fly-by-night label that would “have ripped it off and put it in their closet.” The reason the first album is so pow- erful — it explodes off the turntable — is that, according to Terry Gibbs, “for the first album, I took all my closing tunes and flagwavers, because 1 wanted to shock everybody. I knew how good the band was, but I wasn’t sure it would be accepted by anybody else.” It has been accepted. So accepted, in fact, that Gibbs — who has for years been concentrating on playing his vibes in small groups, these days with De- Franco at his side if it can be ar- ranged — has been fielding offers to reform the band, something he is reluc- tant to do “because it’s a headache.” Terry Gibbs has been playing the vibes professionally for some 50 years, ever since, as 12-year-old Julius Gu- benko — the son of “one of the biggest Jewish bandleaders” — he won a Ma- jor Bowes amateur contest in 1936. The next day, young Julius made his professional debut at the Stanley The- atre in Pittsburgh where. Variety re- ported, he “just about steals the show.” Somewhere along the line, Julius Gu- benko became Terry Gibbs, and the wunderkind of the bar mitzvah circuit became a fleet-handed bebop vibes man. He was a big attraction in the ’50s — his small band, with Terry Pol- lard on piano and, at times, second vibes — was a huge success. Perhaps Terry Gibbs’ name value, in the grand scheme of things, would be higher if he hadn’t moved to Southern California in the ’50s. But, then, the rootin’-tootin’ big band might have really been just a dream band. “The next album coming out, the tempos are more groove tempos, more toe-tapping tempos. Because the first album was like — how can I explain it? — it’s like watching Don Rickies: zing-bang-bang-zing. Could you imagine what it sounded like in person? You know what it was, it was a bunch of maniacs having fun.” It is possible, just possible, that if the next album receives a warm response, the Terry Gibbs Big Band — or some version of it — will be back in business. Under Terry Gibbs’ terms. “You can’t just have guys, they have to be of the calibre of Conte Candoli playing a solo. After hearing my library played that good, that’s how 1 want it played.” Lee Jeske '1‘ihBox March 21, 1987 15

ONJAZZ\ ORNETTE COLEMAN ORNETTE— After a couple of years of more-or-less public inactivity, Or- nette Coleman is currently on some kind of a roll. Most years don’t see a single Ornette Coleman album issued, last year saw two: “Song X’’ (Geffen), the brilliant collaboration with Pat Metheny, and “Opening the Caravan of Dreams” (Caravan of Dreams), with Ornette’s electric band, Prime Time. This year should also see the release of two Ornette Coleman albums on Cara- van of Dreams: the complete recording of his symphony “Skies of America,” performed by Prime Time with the Fort Worth Symphony, and an ex- traordinary-sounding project, currently in the mixing stage, which reteams Or- nette with the members of his original 1958 Quartet — Don Cherry, Charlie Haden and Ed Blackwell. The re- cord features the Quartet playing new Ornette Coleman music and Prime Time playing the same music. Called “Ornette,” it’s due in May or June., “1 did it because so many people think I’m playing different music with Prime Time,” says Ornette Coleman. The two bands are going to do a con- cert at New York’s Town Hall in June that promises to be one of the year’s most noteworthy jazz events. “1 haven’t played any of the old mu- sic with the Quartet,” says Ornette. “Don Cherry is always asking me, ‘Let’s play this, let’s play that,’ but I haven’t played any this year with them. I’m try- ing to get them to come up to ’87.” Although the album doesn’t have a full-scale harmolodic blow-out, with the two groups combined, it is a possibility for the concert. “That’s what we were thinking about doing in June. I had a piece that 1 was going to record with all of them, but the Quartet guys were in California when I had Prime Time here, so it didn’t work out. But we’re going to try something like that when we perform live.” Last weekend (March 14 & 15), Or- nette Coleman was present at Carnegie Recital Hall for a fascinating two-night retrospective of his chamber music (a taste of which can be heard on the re- cently-released Caravan of Dreams al- bum “Prime Design/Time Design”). This summer. Prime Time will tour Eu- rope, stopping in Verona for a full per- formance of “Skies of America.” Ornette credits a lot of his recent ac- tivity on the fact that he finally has a manager that he feels he can trust: his son. Prime Time drummer Denardo Coleman. “Since Denardo has been handling me — it seems that everyone likes him and he communicates to me very well — things are becoming more natu- ral. I’ve given up the idea that. ..the op- portunism of the day. In 1965, 1 played Berlin, at the Sports Plaza, with David Izenzon and Charles Moffett, and there were about 20,000 people there, it was sold out. And we were playing something — some song, 1 don’t know what — and right in the middle of it, while we were improvising, every per- son stood up at that very moment and started screaming and cheering because of how good it sounded to them. And, you know, when I got back to America, they said, ‘Well, you don’t have an audi- ence, nobody wants to hear you.’ So I say: well, I had my Madison Square Gar- den experience 20 years ago. What it made me realize about America was that the particular producers and en- trenpeneurs actually make whoever they want successful, because of the re- lationship they want to have with that person. And I just haven’t found that person who feels that way about sup- porting me. But at least the Caravan of Dreams has given me some light in the tunnel.” Indeed. The Fort Worth-based arts complex and, now, record label, is, it seems, dedicated to Ornette Coleman and his harmolodic progeny (Ronald Shannon Jackson, James Blood Ulmer). “In America, it’s true, you have to have someone to be able to relate to people that doesn’t necessarily want you to make them feel bad because they don’t know what you’re doing. Those are called managers and entre- peneurs, and lots of those people may not even be interested in what I’m do- ing. But now it’s gotten better.” Ornette talks of future projects with enthusiasm — his long-standing dream to have a harmolodic orchestra made up of some 140 musicians (two from each state and 40 from around the world). He’s been composing a piece, “The Old- est Language” for the orchestra, but he acknowledges it’s not likely to happen “unless money falls from the sky.” He also talks about writing a piece for his former uncle, 8Tyear-old trumpeter Doc Cheatham (who bought the teen- aged Ornette Coleman his first saxo- phone), to play with Prime Time. And what of last year’s acclaimed “Song X” album and tour. “I tell you, it was really good,” says Ornette Coleman. “I mean, I have the best admiration for Pat, he’s a really fine person. He really played beautiful- ly. From the experience we had togeth- er, from when he first started playing, it was like hearing a caterpillar turn into a butterfly.” Is the collaboration done? “I don’t know. We’ll probably play together again some time. There’s no reason to stop that right now for good.” Lee Jeske 8, 1981j Hash Box March 28, 1987 13

ON JAZZ PASSING ON— I’d like to note the recent deaths of two important figures in jazz: Eddie Durham, who died March 6 at the age of 80, and Allan Jaffe, who died March 9 at the age of 51. Durham, an original member of the Count Basie Orchestra, was a noted trombonist, a pioneer on the electric guitar, and a widely-respected compos- er and arranger. Jaffe was the founder of Preservation Hall and a guiding force in keeping the traditional jazz flame alive — by organizing, and touring as a tubaist with, the Preservation Hall Jazz Band. REISSUING ON— Hoo-hah, have the reissues been coming hot and heavy lately. For those who doubted the gen- uiness of RCA’s efforts in that depart- ment, the label has just issued a bundle of gems under the Bluebird banner. On double albums (single cassettes and, where available, CDs) are Dizzy Gil- lespie’s “Dizziest,” some of the bebop pioneer’s finest recordings, notably the essential late-’40s big band work; Louis Armstrong’s “Pops,” the greatest jazz musician of them all in some prime ma- teria! from ’4647; “The Complete Fats Waller Vol. IV,” continuing the long- delayed series of several years ago that intends to reissue all of that piano gi- ant’s massive RCA output; and “Short Stops,” the first in a proposed series that will issue all of the ’50s RCA work of “cool jazz” pioneer Shorty Rogers. On delectable single albums are won- derful works by two of the tastiest solo- ists in jazz history: Paul Desmond’s lovely “Late Lament,” ’61-62 sessions teaming the alto great with strings and Jim Hall’s guitar; and “Triple Play,” an album featuring three all-star 1967 sessions by alto colossus Johnny Hodges. From Blue Note comes three prime examples of the Blue Note sound from the ’60s: Academy Award nominee Dexter Gordon’s “Gettin’ Around,” McCoy Tyner’s “The Real McCoy,” and Lee Morgan’s “Search for the New Land.” From Delmark, which has been quiet in the jazz department of late, we get “The Albert Nicholas Quartet,” fea- turing the excellent traditional clarinet- ist in the company of Art Hodes, “All The Gin is Gone,” a properly low-down session led by tenor saxophonist Jim- my Forrest (and including, among oth- ers, Elvin Jones and Grant Green), and “Bouncing with Bud,” Bud Pow- ell in Copenhagen, vintage 1962. And from PolyGram’s Verve and MGM vaults comes CD versions (most with extra tracks) of Ella Fitzgerald’s “Ella at the Opera House,” “Stan Getz and J.J. Johnson at the Opera House” (73 minutes of music on that one), Charlie Parker/ Dizzy Gilles- pie’s “Bird and Diz,” Kenny Burrell’s “For Charlie & Benny,” Lee Konitz’s “Motion,” and three Clifford Brown albums: “Jams 2,” “Best Coast Jazz,” and “Clifford Brown All-Stars.” And, while we’re on the subject, Co- lumbia is beaming over its Jazz Master- pieces roll-out, claiming over a quarter- million units shipped on the first 12 releases, with another seven items due momentarily. SWING MOODS - NARAS/N. Y. recent- ly sponsored a seminar called “Big Bands Revisited" at N. Y.U. Here, remembering the good old days, are (I - r) trumpeter Roy El dridge, jazz historian George T. Simon, vo- calist Fran Warren, and arranger Sy Oliver. FESTIVITIES— It’s that time again, time to start thinking about jazz festi- vals. The first out of the box, the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival, is also the most fun, though it’s the one that has the least to do with jazz. Set for April 24-May 3, the music and food ex- travanganza — and I do mean extrava- ganza— will present thousands of musicians, among them Fats Domino, Branford Marsalis, the Neville Brothers, the Fabulous Thunder- birds, Robert Cray, Wynton Mar- salis, Carl Perkins, Leon Redbone, Rockin’ Sidney, Ellis Marsalis, the Timeless All-Stars, Toots & the Maytals, the Dixie Humming- birds, Delfeayo Marsalis, Clifton Chenier, Jose Feliciano, the Four Tops, Gatemouth Brown, the Timeless All-Stars, Johnny Riv- ers, Jr. Walker & The All-Stars, Jay McShann, Wilson Pickett, Rockin’ Dopsie and the Cajun Twisters, the Dirty Dozen Brass Band, King Sunny Ade, Allen Toussaint, Pete Seeger, and the Sa- maroo Jets. Did somebody say Jazz Festival? P.O. Box 2530, New Orleans 70176 is the place to write for the whole list. For those thinking summertime, the fantastic JVC Grande Parade du Jazz at Nice will run from July 9-19 on the French Riviera with, to name just a few, George Benson, Miles Davis, Chuck Berry, Dexter Gordon, Her- bie Hancock, the MJQ, Benny Car- ter, Stephane Grappelli, Wynton Marsalis, Stanley Jordan, and Stan Getz in tow. Write to 8ter, rue Traver- siere, 92100, Boulogne, France. And, around the same time (July 2- 18), the Swiss banks of Lake Geneva will resound to the sounds of the 21st Montreux Jazz Festival, featuring many of the same artists who will be at Nice, and many who won’t (like Brazil’s Joao Bosco, Nany Caymi, and Simone). Write to the CH-1820, Montreux, Switzerland. TAKE FIVE, NYET?—The Dave Brubeck Quartet is presently glas- nosting it through the Soviet Union. :agot Leaves Columbia, Joins Capitol; Benesch Named His Replacement 5 ANGELES — Long-time Columbia Re- is executive John Fagot is confirmed to saving his post as vice president of pro- ion to take a position as head of promo- for Capitol Records. He will leave umbia’s New York headquarters to join litol in Los Angeles. letails of his new position with Capitol e, as of last week, not finalized. He is ected to be named a vice president. At ;s time, Columbia Records would only firm that he was leaving; Capitol was not prepared to make an official confirma- tion of his appointment, though sources at the label confirmed the truth of his impend- ing move to the L. A. -based label. Bob Altshuler, vice president press & public affairs confirmed to Cash Box that Marc Benesch, a 10-year Columbia veteran, has been promoted to vice president nation- al promotion, replacing Fagot. Benesch will report to Bob Sherwood, senior vice presi- dent marketing. Benesch has been the local promotion man in several Columbia mar- kets, including Denver, Los Angeles, the Midwest and mid-central. Abrams SHINGTON — The American recording ustry opted for legislation that would re- e copy code scanners inhibiting home ying in recording machines over the im- ition of a royalty-producing fee in the s price of such devices. That position enunciated by Jason S. Berman, presi- t of the Recording Industry Association America (RIAA) on April 2, before a joint non of the Copyright Committees of n the Senate and House of Representa- s considering legislation relating to the ninent introduction of Digital Audio •e (DAT) machines. lerman’s choice was evoked by a ques- from Senator Dennis DeConcini (D AZ), irman of the Senate Copyright Commit- Representative Robert W. Kastenmeier A/I) is chairman of the House Copyright >-Committee. Siding with the RIAA president’s position b Ralph Oman, registrar of copyrights, 3 “reluctantly” endorsed the copy code finer device, although he noted his posi- i historically has been that the only equi- le solution in the royalty route. There e been moves in both audio and televi- i recording areas to require the imposi- i of an extra fee on the sales of recording :hines. These sums are to go into a pool >e distributed to copyright owners, ’ending legislation in both the Senate House would require all DAT machines nclude copy coding scanners to prevent ne taping. The bills (S-506 and HR-1384) pending committee consideration in h houses. Additionally, a House Com rce Committee trade legislation includes provision: that bill is awaiting clearance he House Rules Committee before it can taken up by the full House, lerman told the dozen legislators that r “poses the most significant technologi- threat to the American music industry r faces.” The reason, he said, is that DAT eliminates the distinction between originals and copies. With DAT he says, “every copy becomes a new original, the equivalent of a master recording ...” DAT he says, “is only a copying machine, serving no purpose other than home taping ...” Berman urged the enactment of the DAT legislation as a temporary measure until Congress can take up the basic issue: home taping. Charles D. Ferris, Washington attorney and spokesman for the Home Recording Rights Coalition (recording machine and tape manufacturers), argued that there is no justification for imposing a copy coding de- vice machines. DAT cannot allow perfect digital to digital recordings, based on an agreement among manufacturers, he noted. The fact the DAT machines can make ana- log copies is not germane, he contended, since home taping is not illegal if it is not for commercial gain. Ferris was backed by Leonard Feldman, owner of an electronics laboratory as well as a writer on audio technology. Feldman maintained that, “digital audio tape record ers . . . are a step forward in technology. The copy coding scanner is a step backward.” During a morning hearing, both sides demonstrated their respective systems with David W. Stebbings, CBS Technology Cen- ter, which developed the copy coding scan- ner system, rebutting Japanese demonstrations of the CBS device that os- tensibly degraded the music. Feldman also demonstrated the “flag” system used by the makers of DAT recorders that prevents digi- tal to digital copying. The source licensing bill, which would threaten the livelihood of songwriters and composers, has been re-introduced into the 100th Congress as H R 1195 in the house and S. 698 in the senate. Berman received a plaque from BMI, ASCAP, SESAC, The National Academy of Songwriters and the Songwriters Guild of America Los Angeles mayor Tom Bradley proclaimed March 27th as Howard Berman day. JVC Jazz Festival/New York Sets Ambitious Schedule By Lee Jeske NEW YORK -The JVC Jazz Festival/New York, which used to be the Kool Jazz Festi- val/New York, the Newport Jazz Festival/ New York, and, years and years ago, the Newport Jazz Festival, announced an ex- panded line-up of concerts for this year’s event, to be held June 19-28 in various ven- ues in and around the New York area. The expansion is seen as a deepening of JVC’s commitment to the Festival, which it took over at the eleventh-hour last year. Although the Festival is heavily-weighted towards traditional Festival favorites, there are several new twists. Perennial headliners Sarah Vaughan and Mel Torme will share concerts with recent Grammy winners Bob- by McFerrin and Diane Schuur, respective- ly. Dizzy Gillespie, who will be celebrating his 70th birthday later this year, will be at the helm of a stellar big band featuring Sam Rivers, Jon Faddis, Frank Wess, Steve Turre, James Williams and many others, in a concert that co-bills the bopmeister with Wynton Marsalis. The Modern Jazz Quartet will premiere a new work with the New York Chamber Symphony. Most of the concerts, as usual, will take place in Carnegie Hall and its Weill Recital Hall (unavailable to the Festival last year due to renovations), Avery Fisher Hall and Town Hall, with the Festival roaming as far afield as Waterloo Village, in Stanhope, New Jersey, and Stamford, Connecticut. The Festival is also affiliated with two other George Wein productions to be held concur- rently with the Festival’s final weekend: Newport Jazz at Saratoga, in Saratoga Springs, and Newport Jazz in Rochester, New York. Some of the other expected highlights of the Festival include a reunion of the original Ornette Coleman Quartet sharing a pro- gram with Coleman’s electric band, Prime Time; an evening with Ella Fitzgerald, who has spent a year inactive due to heart trou- bles; the Festival debut of Ruben Blades; and an all-star salute to Hank Jones. Returning are the series of one-hour pi- ano recitals at Weill Recital Hall, music cruises on the Hudson, the Waterloo tradi- tional jazz picnic, and an evening of David Chertok’s jazz films. As usual, several out- side producers will be used, including three record companies — CBS, Blue Note and Grama vision. ON JAZZ MORE MASTERPIECES—Colum bia Records has just released its second batch of “Jazz Masterpieces” — seven digitally remastered goodies from its large catalogue (these are not stricty re- issues since most of them have been in print continuously), each available in all three formats. They are the Dave Bru- beck Quartet’s “Gone With the Wind,” Miles Davis’ “’Round About Midnight” and “Porgy and Bess,” Duke Ellington’s “At Newport” (which features Paul Gonsalves’ gal- vanizing workout on “Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue”), Errol Garner’s “Concert by the Sea,” Charles Min- gus’s “Mingus Ah Urn,” and “The Quintessential Billie Holiday, Vol- ume I.” The Holiday is the only thing in here that is new — that is, that is new in this form. Over the years Columbia has issued Billie Holiday’s large output for the label in many different ways. What we have here, quite encouragingly, is simply the first 14 sides the great Lady Day made for Columbia, fully annotat- ed by the savvy Michael Brooks. If Columbia keeps this going apace, “The Quintessential Billie Holiday” will fill, perhaps, 14 albums, and that’s not in- cluding alternate takes and whatnot. It’s all worthy of rerelease. The Japanese, in fact, have reissued all of this al- ready— on an eight-disc CD set (with some 21 songs per disc) with somewhat questionable sound. I’d also like to men- tion something about the Mingus al- bum, which 1 think is one of Mingus’ true masterpieces. A few years ago, Co- lumbia put out a double-album, under its old Contemporary Masters Series, called “Nostalgia In Times Square,” containing restored versions of five of the nine songs on “Mingus Ah Um,” which apparently was subjected to seri- ous editing at the time of its release. The restored versions are now, sadly, out of print. It would have been nice if Columbia somehow included both ver- sions, a la the RCA Mingus reissue (“Ti- juana Moods”), either on a double album or on the single CD, but Colum- bia’s policy is strict on this — the LPs and the CDs will be identical. list. DISQUES CONTENT—DRG, which has been doing a fine service in issuing French sessions by American jazz greats that have never been available stateside, has just popped out four wor- thy new items (under their Disques Swing imprint). They are “Lionel Hampton in Paris,” a gently-swinging sextet date; “Benny Golson in Paris,” (actually mostly recorded in New York) featuring, among others, Lee Morgan, Bobby Timmons, and Philly Joe Jones; “Zoot Sims in Paris,” a bop- pish session with trumpeter Jon Eard- ley; and “The International Jazz Group Volume II,” an all-star set under French pianist Andre Persiany that includes Budd Johnson, Lawrence Brown, Eddie Barefield and Taft Jordan. Everything was recorded between ’56 and ’58 and everything sounds terrific. SCOTT’S DEAL — Saxophonist Tom Scott recently signed to GRP Records. Here, at the pacting pow wow, are (I - r) Larry Ro- sen, GRP co-president; Scott; and Scott's at- torneys Malcolm Wiseman and David Braun. I SEE A RHAPSODY—You say you want jazz films on videotape? Well, New York’s Rhapsody Films has quietly been releasing some fine jazz tapes over the last couple of years — there are now two dozen items in their catalogue — and, begorrah, they have just reduced their prices, to $29.95 for tapes under 30 minutes, $39.95 for the rest. Some of the better tapes available from Rhap- sody: The Last of the Blue Devils, Bruce Ricker’s Kansas City jazz epic; Talmage Farlow, Lorenzo De Ste- fano’s insightful portrait of the great guitarist; Sonny Rollins Live at Laren ; Jazz, a delightful session with Earl Hines and Coleman Hawkins; Different Drummer: Elvin Jones ; Jackie McLean on Mars; and Robert Mugge’s properly bizarre Sun Ra: A Joyful Noise. Harms Music Wins Copyright Infringement Suit Against Jem NEW YORK — The U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey has decided in favor of T.B. Harms Music Company in its copyright infringement action against Jem Records. Harms had sued Jem for infringing its copyright of “OR Man River” by import- ing records containing performances of the songs by Frank Sinatra without obtaining the consent or authority of Harms. Even though the records were lawfully made in New Zealand by WEA, and Jem had WEA’s permission to import them, the court held in ruling on Jem’s motion for summary judg- ment that such importation by Jem violated Section 602 of the U.S. Copyright Act and Jem is liable to Harms as an infringer. Judge John W. Bissel, in a 19-page opin- ion, determined that the copyright owner of a song has the exclusive right to authorize importation of recordings containing perfor- mances of the song. Beck, who comes out of the Austin jazz/blues scene, was responsible for bringing in Stevie Ray Vaughn, who plays guitar on the album’s first single, “First We Take Manhattan,” giving it a blues rock edge. Improving the aural quality of records was another ambition Sussman and Warnes shared from the outset, and many “tricks” were used to improve the album’s sound (most of which Warnes understandably pre- fers not to give away in print). The album was cut digitally at L A ’s Complex. “One of the unique things about this record is that it’s folk songs within a digital context,” she remarks. The album, which she says was much supported by the passion and enthusiasm of all the musicians and technicians who worked on it, gave her that long awaited chance to blossom, a thing too often ham- pered by corporate over-involvement. “Art- ists who are living experimental lives - like Leonard Cohen - have social information that’s very useful for the people who want to buy the records,” she says, “and if the corporation puts five a&r people between that process, it dilutes the information, and the telegram gets garbled. “What I’m in this for is the exchange of new information. It’s a communications thing, that’s what we’re all doing. I would (now) plead and beg with the corporations, that when an artist is ready - and maybe 1 wasn’t ready until now - to stay out the way. Stay out of the way and just let it go! Let it roll . . . Some artists you need to just leave alone.” A video to “First We l ake Manhattan” is in the works, and a tour i; .heduled for this summer. Warnes also plans to complete an album of her own songs, which she was in the midst of when she jumped at the chance to record the Cohen material. Cohen, Warnes maintains, has been strangely battered by critics in this country, and indeed, comparisons between his deliv- ery and wet cement have not been uncom- mon. Certainly, our national obsession for surfaces has much to do with such artist- bashing (Cohen may have been relegated to cult status here, but he’s widely acclaimed in Europe, as well as his native Canada, where his writings are even taught in schools). If there is a last laugh to be had in this story, it’s Warnes’ and Cohen’s, but bit- terness plays no part here. Human ness does, and music. Warnes, armed with the songs of one of the world’s great songwrit- ers, has set about restoring a sense of inti- macy that’s been sorely missed. IN CASHBOX* April 13, 1957—JOHANNESBURG, SOUTH AFRICA — For the first time, the music of the modern urban African has been introduced to the public on high-fidelity long-playing records with the release of Trutone Africa Limited’s “Music was Born in Africa.” This re- cord was conceived as an ideal souvenir for tourists visiting the Union who want- ed to take away some memento of their stay. The music of the urban African is a blend of ancient tribal chants and modern jazz idioms that results in a dif- ferent type of listening. “Music was Born in Africa” was compiled from re- cordings made in all the major centres of South Africa during 1956... Buddy Rich’s Drums Stilled By Gregory Dobrin S NGELES — Battle lines were drawn ; lain between rock music and those I pose its content during a panel on C ifluence on society at the recent Mu- ) ness Symposium at the Ambassador a two-hour plus debate over the per- 3 avils of rock lyrics and the rights of n ns, top professionals of the music il 5, including Geffen Records presi- J Rosenblatt, Spin publisher Bob jie Jr., BAM publisher Dennis Ero- e RIAA’s Trish Heimers, publicist \ 1 Bloom, Goshen Indiana’s Rock Rag is >r Marianne Hatfield and recording t Yank Zappa and Jello Biafra, vol- i I le issue with representatives of the r tering side, which included PMRC il /e director Jennifer Norwood, PTA I nn Kahn, Back in Control director ; >denhamer, minister A1 Menconi and jbeords’ David and Melissa Beaudoin. » Friday afternoon panel delt with 11 1 f the same issues that have been an t concern since the PMRC waged its igton-based attack on rock lyrics » wo years ago, such as the stickering fns deemed harmful to youngsters. < ile the issue remains a potent topic on both sides, the panel featured few impas- sioned outbursts. The newest information revealed during the debate was two of the sources of the PMRC’s funding - Merrill Lynch and Occi- dental Corporation - named by the PMRC’s Norwood when cornered as to the mystery surrounding her organization’s financial backing. Norwood also provided the afternoon’s most enduring plea, asking that lyrics be printed where parents can see them, giving them a chance to judge records at the point of purchase (an argument which lasted through much of the discussion until the RIAA’s Heimers finally shot it down with the reality that record companies don’t al- ways own the lyrics the PMRC would have them display). Norwood’s request, echoed by several panelists on her side, called for “tools” with which parents might familiarize themselves with what their children are listening to. Cit- ing the bushels of reading material available (such as rock publications) Heimers re- sponded, “You’ve asked for tools - you’ve got tools.’ Melissa Beaudoin of D&L Records of- (continued on page 25) By Lee Jeske NEW YORK — Buddy Rich, one of the most technically adroit drummers in the history of jazz, died April 2nd in California at the age of 69. Rich, who had a history of heart trouble, was found to have a brain tumor earlier this year, after he suffered a mild case of paralysis while performing. The tu- mor was removed in an operation March 16 at the UCLA Medical Center where Rich underwent subsequent chemotherapy ses- sions. His wife, Marie, and daughter, Kathy, were with him when he died. Born Bernard Rich in Brooklyn in 1917, Buddy Rich was in show business at the age of 18 months — as part of Wilson & Rich, his parents’ vaudeville act. Just a few years lat- er he was touring Australia as “Traps, the Boy Wonder.” The June 12, 1925 edition of the Mel- bourne Sun-News Pictorial carried a picture of young Rich over the caption, “Traps, the six-year-old jazz musician at the Tivoli The- atre, is beating his way into the hearts of patrons. Next to Jackie Coogan, he is, it is stated, the highest paid juvenile in the world.” The adult Rich began gigging in New York in 1938, and, in quick succession, played with bands led by Joe Marsala, Bun- ny Berigan, and Artie Shaw, before joining the Tommy Dorsey Orchestra in 1939. In his first three years with Dorsey — before he left for the first time in 1942 (shortly before become a Marine) — Rich received great praise for his overwhelming technique. “He propels a tremendous, natural beat under the impetus of one of the most mag- nificent drum techniques dancebandom has ever known,” wrote George T. Simon in a 1942 Metronome Magazine review of the Dorsey band. Rich’s roommate in the Dorsey Orches- tra was the band’s male singer, Frank Sina- tra, with whom the hot-headed Rich often did battle (Sinatra liked his drumming softer than Rich cared to play). After two post-War years with Dorsey, Rich formed his first big band, in 1946, with financial assistance from the same Frank Sinatra. But the Big Band Era was kaput, so Rich worked as a star journeyman — touring with Jazz at the Philharmonic and recording with the likes of Art Tatum, Charlie Parker and Lester Young. During the ’50s, Rich was in and out of the Harry James Orches- tra, periodically leading his own big bands or small ensembles (and recording celebrat- ed drum battles with Gene Krupa and Max Roach). In 1966, after several more years with Harry James, Buddy Rich formed the big band that would ensure his stardom. The Buddy Rich Band was, not surprisingly, a hard-driving, drum-driven ban*! that re- mained true to its jazz big band format while contemporizing with electric guitars, basses, and keyboards and by playing ar- rangements of popular rock tunes (their ver- sion of “Norwegian Wood” became one of the band’s most requested numbers). The Rich Band rarely had any star solo- ists except for the leader (though two saxo- phonists — Pat La Barbara in the early-’70s and Steven Marcus off-and-on until Rich’s death — were featured prominently). Mostly made up up fresh-faced, recent college mu- sic school graduates, the Rich Band played with a fiery swagger. The highlight of every set, however, was The Drum Solo. Usually contained in an extended composition (of- ten “The Channel One Suite” or a “West Side Story Medley”), Rich’s solo forays were breathtaking masterpieces of percus- sion technique — lightning-fast, firecracker- crisp and fiercely rhythmic. The Band was under strict instructions to not look bored here — they were all under orders to fix their gazes on their spotlighted leader — but that wasn’t necessary: the Rich solos, which al- most always drew standing ovations, were marvels. Buddy Rich became best known, per- haps, thanks to his frequent appearances on The Tonight Show, where his acerbic ban- ter with host Johnny Carson established him as a wit and raconteur. Never humble, Rich wouldn’t blink when he was referred to, as he often was, as “the world’s greatest drummer.” In fact, as his Tonight Show ap- pearances made clear, it was an appellation that he didn’t have any qualms with whatso- ever. In terms of pure technical ability, it probably was true. Lang THE ROXY, L.A. — The kid’s got talent. Does she ever! Sire’s K.D. Lang has a voice that can prod cattle to polka or make other- wise composed folk get all dreamy-eyed. Is she country, is she pop ... is she kidding? These and other questions permeated the pre-show buzz here recently. The answer, delivered with raucous energy by Lang and her frolicking band The Reclines, was all-of- the-above and none-of-the-above: Yes, the sound is country, but not purely; and yes the sound has a rock/pop edge, but not much; and yes, Lang does have fun with the corni- er aspects of country, but her heart seems to be in the right place while she’s doing so. What Lang and her band proved here was that there is indeed an intersection where Patsy Cline’s country blues, Frank Yankovic’s polka, Rose Maddox’ western swing and Gene Vincent’s rockabilly can meet and intertwine in a barn-shaking square dance of styles. COLLINS & “BRUNO " ROCK OUT—A! bert Collins, recent Grammy winner for his Alli- gator LP, ‘‘Showdown!" (also featuring Robert Cray and Johnny Copeland), performed his hot ‘‘cool’’ sound of blues before two sold-out crowds at Los Angeles’ Music Machine. Join- ing Albert on stage for a few numbers was TV's “Moonlighting ” co-star Bruce ‘‘Bruno’’ Willis. Pictured (l-r) are: Collins, Willis, (c) and saxman Sam Franklin. Lang’s rich, voluminous voice is a plea- sure. With apparent ease and considerable stage poise, the former performance artist from the Canadian sticks nearly blew this venerable Sunset Strip venue off the boule- vard with her deliciously resonant pipes. It’s true, Lang does sound a bit like coun- try legend Patsy Cline (to whom she’s been continually compared by the press), espe- cially when covering the late singer’s materi- al. Lang opened the show with her own bluesy, downtempo rendition of Cline’s torchy, barroom-busting “Don’t Ever Leave Me Again,” which she milked for every note while casually leaning on the keyboard stand singing to keyboardist Michael Creeber. Much of the humor in her act - criticized for its apparent irreverence toward country music - was so subtle that it took sharp ears to catch it, while some was so broad that it was impossible to miss (such as the three cigarettes Lang manipulated while singing Cline’s “Three Cigarettes In An Ashtray” - a romantic ballad whose ashtray imagery is so bizarre that it’s funny). The evening’s line-up of tunes included the Joanie Sommers ‘60’s pop hit “Johnny Get Angry,” which was given particularly campy treatment. Working the tune into a violent climax (in which an imaginary “Johnny” finally hauls off and whallops her), Lang lay prone in silence for a good two minutes, only to bounce back and finish the song. Lang and The Recline’s country single, a EMIA. rockabilly cover of Joe South’s “Rose Gar- den” was delivered with infectious impact, featuring guitarist Gordie Mathews’ strong instrumental lead. “To dance is human,” the singer ex- claimed before charging into one of several polka numbers, “but to polka is devine!” And indeed, Lang and The Reclines, aided by Ben Mink’s fiddle, brought enough vitali- ty to this rather quaint (albeit rip-roaring) country dance tradition as to make it seem new. Lang and her band’s L.A. debut was re- freshingly original. Much more than the mere novelty act much of this material might well have constituted in the hands of a less talented, endearingly witty singer and less superbly proficient musicians, this show had that ineffable magical edge that spells quality and longevity. Gregory Dobrin on Pullen THE PUBLIC THEATRE, N.Y.C.-Don Pullen, the volcanic modern jazz pianist and co-leader, with George Adams, of one of the finest bands in jazz, turned to his roots last Monday night for a terrifically entertaining evening at the Public Theatre. Nancy Weiss Hanrahan, who initiated a series of New Jazz at the Public Theatre commissions last year, had the ingenius idea of having Pullen organize a band around his organ playing — an instrument he used quite a bit in the or- gan-heavy ’60s but had ignored in recent years. From the first notes of the first tune, “Zet,” Pullen made it clear where he was coming from — he was coming from the jukeboxes of the 1960s. For the most part, Pullen and his bandmates could have been recording for the Blue Note of 20 years ago. It was a refreshing, exceptionally enjoyable night of music. Opening with a septet — drummer Bobby Battle, guitarist Melvin Sparks, trumpeter Joe Gardner, pianist Jeremy Bacon, alto saxophonist Charles Williams, and trom- bonist Frank Lacy — that was vintage Blue Note, Pullen churned out swirling, thick or- gan chords, stomped-off fine sturdy organ bass, and generally unleashed the down-ho- meist organ sound this side of Brother Jack McDuff. Right in there with him were Sparks, who cooked like crazy on “Blues at Hanna’s House;” Williams, who cooked like crazy on a deep-fried “Send Me Someone To Love;” and Battle, who cooked like crazy every second of the way. FURTHER FESTIVITIES— Well, as was detailed in the news pages last week, the upcoming JVC/New York Jazz Festival looks like a good one. The programming is relatively imaginative, and I’m already looking forward to such treats as the reunion of the original Or- nette Coleman Quartet, the debut of the star-filled (Sam Rivers, James Williams, Daniel Ponce, Frank Wess, Jon Faddis, Britt Wood- man, etc.) Dizzy Gillespie Big Band (Ornette and Dizzy are on the same night, at the same time — can you be- lieve that? — but, hopefully, a late show will be added to one of them), the team- ing of Sarah Vaughan and Bobby McFerrin (if they don’t do a number together, I’ll cry), Sun Ra’s solo piano concert, and the evening in tribute to Hank Jones. Last year, JVC didn’t commit to the New York affair until rather late, but this year their commit- ment seems strong and, according to Festival producer George Wein, they’re is committed to at least a couple of years in New York. Bravo! JVC, which also sponsors several of Wein’s other festivals around the world, is stepping up that department as well. Three cities have been added to the U.S. JVC Jazz Festival Tour: Minneapo- lis, Madison, Wisconsin, and Houston. They will be joining Chicago, Atlanta, Newport, Concord, California, and Los Angeles. And JVC will do another PBS special from the Newport Festival. JVC also sponsors major jazz festivals in The Hague, Holland, Nice, and London. A very impressive commitment to jazz that may not last forever — what does? — but it’s good to have it as long as it’s here. Other festivals on the slate are the Jazz on the Lake Festival, set for June 27 in Garberville, California and head- lining Pete Escovedo; and Gresham, Oregon’s Mt. Hood Festival of Jazz, set for Aug. 1 & 2 and featuring Doc Se- verinsen and the Tonight Show Orchestra, Mel Torme, George Shearing and Wynton Marsalis. BOPPING AROUND— Hey, good for Herbie Hancock. Not only did he win an Oscar for Round Midnight, but he made a damned fine acceptance speech. It’s not everyday that Charlie Parker, Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, Lester Young and, for that matter, Dexter Gordon get touted in front of a billion people. ..Outer space, get ready. New York’s WKCR-FM (89.9), coming off impressive mara- thons of the blues and the music of Bil- lie Holiday, is about to unloose 116 hours — that’s 116 hours non-stop— of the music of Sun Ra and his various Arkestras. It all begins on April 16 at noon and continues through April 21 at 1 a.m. A cosmic time is guaranteed for all. ..And speaking of the former Her- man Blount, the Brooklyn Academy of Music will host Sun Ra with a 100- plus piece Arkestra, playing the music of Basie, Henderson, Ellington, and Ra, some time this falL.WBGO- FM, the other jazz voice in town, has been holding Friday night jazz concerts at Newark’s Symphony Hall, sponsored by Gilbey’s Gin. Coming up are Arthur Prysock (4/23), the Art Farmer/ Benny Golson Jazztet (5/8), Tito Puente (5/22), and Abbey Lincoln (5/29). I guess I’ve heard of stranger ideas, but New York’s Blue Note — the jazz club that thinks of itself as some sort of jazz kingdom — has inaugurated a series of star tables. That’s right, you are very likely to be sitting at a table imbedded with the name of a Blue Note headliner — sort of like Graumann’s Chi- nese Theatre on four legs — and, if you turn out opening night, you can witness the elaborate presentation-of-the-table ceremony . The Illinois Jacquet Big Band, a rough-and-tumble jazz ensem- ble if there ever was one, is about to head off for a European tour: they open in Lyon on May 4th... Books, books, books. I will be going on at length about these in a couple of weeks, but, in the meantime, I’d like to point out that the following jazz books have recently been issued: Jazz: Myth and Religion by Neil Leonard ($16.95, Oxford University Press), Buck Clayton ’s Jazz World by Buck Clayton ($19.95, Oxford Universi- ty Press), Queen of the Blues: A Biogra- phy of Dinah Washington by James Haskins ($16.95, William Morrow), Alberta Hunter: A Celebration in Blues by Frank C. Taylor ($17.95, McGraw-Hill), and / Remember Jazz: Six Decades Among the Great Jazzmen by A1 Rose ($24.95, Louisiana State University Press). MEWS Beatles Lose Six Of Nine Actions In Capitol/EMI Suit ANGELES — New York Supreme l Justice Michael J. Dontzin ruled last to dismiss six of nine charges brought st Capitol Records and EMI Records by Beatles label Apple Records and iffs George Harrison, Ringo Starr and Ono, John Lennon’s widow. (Paul : irtney is not a plaintiff in the suit), long the actions dismissed in the April sion were charges of fraud and conver- which sought $50 million in punitive ges. Though Capitol and EMI sought ssal of seven causes of action, one of a claim for breach of fiduciary duty, in chose not to dismiss. The Capitol/ notion didn’t address two remaining s for alleged breach of contract. The suit is a longstanding one, filed in 1979, and charges the record companies with defrauding The Beatles by not paying them royalties on sales of various record- ings made over the last 18 years. Fundamentally, last week’s ruling re- duces the case to allegations of breach of contract, which could be pursued by the plaintiffs. Said Capitol and EMI Music Worldwide chairman and chief executive Bhaskar Menon, “Plaintiffs are now left with claims for additional royalties under a 1969 record- ing agreement with Capitol. It is Capitol’s firm position that the royalty claims lack merit and we will continue to vigorously de- fend that position in court.” DEBATERS—Bob Guccione, Jr., publisher ofSpin Magazine, recording artist Frank Zappa, and former Dead Kennedy Jello Biafra took part in the rock censorship panel at Music Business Symposium 3, held recently at the Ambassador ffotel in L.A . Blue Note Rolls Out The Compact Discs By Lee Jeske YORK — A couple of years ago, vin- 31ue Note albums were so hard to by that jazz fans eagerly snapped up ese and French imports for up to 20 an LP. Amnesty Int’l & Tower Records Join Forces LOS ANGELES — Amnesty International, the Nobel Prize-winning human rights orga- nization that works for the release of prison- ers of conscience, fair trials for political prisoners and an end to torture and execu- tions, has kicked off a major campaign in a unique collaboration with 75 Tower Record & Video retail outlets across the country. During the campaign, each Tower Re- cord or Video store will adopt a prisoner of conscience and work to free that individual. A number of recording artists have also con- tributed their talents for the video compo- nent of the campaign. “It is an honor for Tower Records & vid- eo to be involved with an international pro- ject of this magnitude. Our involvement in this project stems from a feeling that every- one should be free and uncensored,” says Tower president, Russ Solomon. “The mu- sic industry is involved with many urgent and important causes and each time I be- come aware of the level of our involvement, from the recording artists to the top level executives, I feel that much prouder of our industry’s commitment to helping the imme- diate, critical issues and problems of our times.” The goal of the campaign is to generate as many letters as possible to facilitate the release of the adopted prisoners, men and women imprisoned in countries all over the world, solely for their race, religion or politi- cal beliefs. While in Tower stores, custom- ers will be asked to sign a prepared letter on the prisoners’ behalf. “This remarkable expression of support for Amnesty International’s work is an un- precedented opportunity for hundreds of thousands of record buyers to help free pris- oners of conscience with just a moment of their time and a stroke of their pen,” says John G. Healey, executive director of Am- nesty International, USA. Coordination of the Tower outlets is be- ing handled by the Music Stock Market. “We’re proud to be a catalyst for this cam- paign materializing for the retail communi- ty. The people working within retail in the music industry have always shared an enor- mous sensitivity for human rights. This cam- paign will be the first of its kind to demonstrate the magnitude retail can have on social issues when they are allowed to be directly involved,” says Babs Stock, of the Music Stock Market. Steve Pollutro of Tower’s Art Depart- ment has designed an in-store Amnesty In- ternational display which features a photo of that store’s adopted prisoner, informa- tion about the case, and a brochure on the work of Amnesty. The color poster used in the display was created by artist Jean-Fran- cois Podevin. To accompany the display, Amnesty has developed a video reel that will play in most outlets. Created by Johnson/Klein Produc- tions, the reel features Jackson Browne, Whoopi Goldberg, Daryl Hannah, Colin James Hay, Hiroshima, Little Steven, Maria McKee of Lone Justice and Run-D.M.C. “One of the issues that Larry Johnson and I feel strongly about is prisoners of con- science. These video spots became a tangi- ble way to use our skills and resources to express our emotions,” says Bobby Klein of Johnson/Klein Productions. On this special video, the artists talk about the effectiveness of Amnesty’s work (continued on page 31) CBS Sees Profit; Booming Record Sales Cited LOS ANGELES — Healthy record sales and declining interest expenses gave CBS high- er profits for the first quarter of 1987 even though its television network has ran at a loss for the second straight quarter. Earnings rose 200 percent to $48.7 bil- lion, up from a profit of $16.3 million on revenue of $1.17 billion for the first quarter of last year. CBS has recently cut its payroll in the past year by approximetely 2,000 to 20,000. The cutbacks, they say, were the only way to offset the network’s losses. An- other reason for the gains was the ad reve- nue from the network’s broadcast of the National Football League’s Super Bowl XXI. The CBS Broadcast Group’s revenue increased only 4 percent. CBS Records posted a 16 percent year to year increase largely due to the blockbuster foreign and domestic sales of the Bruce Springsteen live package which increased revenue to $413 million with a 30 percent profit increase to $68 million, an all-time high for the Records Group. While CBS has not specified how much the network stood to lose this year, chief executive Laurence Tisch estimated last year that it could lose as much as $20 mil- lion dollars this year. The Beastie Boys Set To Get Stoopid On Film By Paul Iorio NEW YORK — The Beastie Boys — cellu- loid heroes? Celluloid anti-heroes may be more like it once they unveil their first film, The Beastie Boys Scared Stupid, later this year. It’s the second production by Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin’s new company, Def Films, and it promises to be the cinemat- ic equivalent of “Licensed To 111” (Def Jam). The first film from Def, Run-D.M.C.’s Tougher Than Leather, slated for August release, also features the Beasties, in a com- ic cameo. Scared Stupid not only stars the Boys but is also being scripted by them along the lines of a Three Stooges C-movie. Auteur Michael Diamond (aka, Mike D, the guy with the VW medallion) explains: “It’s sort of a horror comedy type of thing star- ring us. I inherit a haunted mansion from my great uncle and (in order) to claim my for- tune we have to stay in it overnight. We basically play ourselves. Take it from there.” The Beasties next album will be the soundtrack to Scared Stupid. “The next al- bum is gonna be the soundtrack to the mov- ie,” says Diamond. “We were thinking of sort of a beatnik and disco revival type al- bum. And we’re gonna do one song record- ed live on Macdougal Street (in Manhattan). Just a lot of disco dancing. The main thing we’re gonna do is make what we want and not really listen to anybody,” he says laughing. Apparently, Adam Horovitz (King Ad- Rock) will add the beatnik-folkie flavor, while Adam Yauch (MCA) rekindles the flame of Studio 54. “Ad-Rock is really the most promising illiterate of our generation,” says Diamond. “He’s the beatnik poet of the band. The inspiration is just choked into his mind since he’s the surreal beatnik poet of the group. Yauch’s the madman of the group. He also does disco dancing the best and wears the most polyester. When it comes to the Latin hustle, he’s the best.” Diamond is fully aware of the fact that the Beasties can now get away with just about anything they want musically. Their mega-platinum “Licensed To 111” is the fast- est-selling debut album in the history of Co- lumbia Records and recently spent more than a month in the number one spot. He is also fully aware that an album as undiluted as “Licensed To III” isn’t theoretcially sup- posed to have such mass appeal. “I think this is truly the great rock ‘n’ roll swindle,” he says. “It’s cool thinking that we’re the only punk group to ever have gone number one in America.” Their absorption into the mainstream, culminating with an appearance at the Grammys, has been unusually swift. Dia- mond says that the downside of this accep- tance is that people now ask them to be outrageous on command. “People expect it of us now,” he says. “It’s almost weird because they want you to be the Beastie Boys and act outrageous so they definitely get the mileage out of it- Six months ago we would have been thrown out of the Grammys.” Indeed, there was a time when their com- ic-book delinquency was not so welcome. As the opening act for Madonna in 1985, the Beasties were booed and jeered. “A lot of people say we were booed offstage. I’d like to say that we were onstage for the booing at all times. Not once did we ever pussy under and leave the stage,” says Dia- mond. Today, they play sell-out shows national- ly and have had the honor of being banned forever from Holiday Inns. Underway is a co-headlining tour with Run-D.M.C that starts in Europe and opens in the U S. June 12 in Honolulu, Hawaii. Meanwhile, The Beastie Boys Scared Stupid tentatively be- gins shooting in July, with a release date set for around Christmas. TICKERTAPE I NEW YORK — BMI and the NYU. ONJAZZ \ MAXINE AND CO. - The late Maxine Sullivan was joined during a gig at the Holly- wood Roosevelt's Cinegrill earlier this year by fellow vocalists Diane Schuur (I) and Nellie Lutcher (r). PASSING ON— Maxine Sullivan, the ever-swinging, ever-delightful vocal- ist who came to fame chirping “Loch Lomond” some 50 years ago, died April 7 of heart failure. Maxine Sullivan was a small woman with a small voice. Her singing style was so easy, so effort- less, that it almost seemed as if she was casually conversing on her stoop. She didn't scat, didn’t swoop across oc- taves, and didn’t cause jaws to drop with her vocal prowess. But, boy, could she swing! She gained her fame in the late ’30s as a star of 52nd St. and starred with Louis Armstrong in the final Cotton Club Revue, in 1939. Re- cently, Maxine Sullivan had been espe- cially active — she recorded numerous albums, several of which were nominat- ed for Grammy Awards; sung in jazz clubs and at jazz festivals throughout the world; and, generally, brought the same cheerful elegance to songs as she had been doing for 50 years. Maxine Sullivan died in the Bronx, not far from The House That Jazz Built, a communi- ty center that she founded and was ever-so proud of. She was 75. CLASSIC—The Smithsonian Institu- tion, that repository of old airplanes and flags, is also a repository of old mu- sic. In fact, the six-LP “Smithsonian Col- lection of Classic Jazz” has, since its release in 1973, stood as the definitive set of its kind. The Smithsonian, thanks to its unique status, was able to acquire recordings from numerous rival labels, and Martin Williams, thanks to his unique stature as one of jazz’s finest critics and historians, was able to as- semble those recordings into a sensible anthology that, without too much chest- beating, walked the listener — Williams’ informative annotations in hand — through the history of jazz; “classic jazz,” in this case, referring to classic recordings from the entire spectrum of jazz history. Now the Smithsonian and Williams have updated and expanded their work. “The Revised Smithsonian Collection of Classic Jazz” is now avail- able on seven-LPs or five cassettes (what, Smithsonian, no CDs?), all pack- aged with a 120-page booklet (a book, really) containing notes on the music by Williams and thumbnail biographies by Ira Gitler, for $49.96 plus $3.49 post- age— a bargain. This set — which be- gins with Scott Joplin and ends with The World Saxophone Quartet (the only representatives of the last 25 years in jazz, by the way) — is the place to go for anybody who wants to learn about jazz, to hear how Louis Armstrong relates to Charlie Parker, how Char- lie Parker relates to Ornette Cole- man, etc. It is an indispensable collection and it is available from Smith- sonian Collection of Recordings, P.O. Box 23345, Washington, D.C. 20026. SPARE CHANGE— I wrote a couple of weeks ago in this space about the new RCA Bluebird and Novus reissues ai d issues, but I’d like to add a couple of things. First of all, I’d like to point out that trie CD of each of the superb new releases on Novus — the Henry Threadgill Sextet’s “You Know the Number” and Hiton Ruiz’s “Some- thing Grand” — has an extra track. The Threadgill has a nice four-minute piece called “Paille Street,” but the Ruiz has a marvelous extended composition called “Infinity,” over 17 minutes of modal grit where that wonderful horn section (Sam Rivers, Steve Turre, Lew So- loff) gets to stretch out. A bonus, for sure. As for the Bluebirds, the Fats Waller, Dizzy Gillespie, and Louis Armstrong sets are not available on CD — they are from the acoustic era, and, apparently, the masters were not good enough to transfer to digital. How- ever, the Paul Desmond, Johnny Hodges, and Shorty Rogers albums are available on CDs and here’s the deal: the sound is great on all of them, and the Desmond has two extra tracks on the CD, but the Shorty Rogers is the screwiest reissue I’ve ever seen in that the double-LP has 32 tracks, the single- cassette has 28 tracks, and the single CD has-20 tracks. Say what? The next volley from Bluebird, due in June, will be 16 CD-only reissues. Closed Monday ENC1NO 17410 Ventura Blvd. Encino, CA 818-783-CRAB SANTA MONICA 25th & Pico Blvd. Santa Monica, CA 213-450-5555 Suzanne Vega (continued from page 10) lead guitar work is tasty and to the point. Hester and Seymour provide a solid rhythm section especially on the more propulsive numbers. The name, Crowded House, came about after they relocated to Hollywood, rehears- ing and searching for a deal in the world’s tackiest and most famous suburb. The band had taken residence in a house, run by a nervous landlady, keen to sell, who let a “parade of bizarre and strange” would-be buyers in at all hours of the day. “I’d come home and find people sliding down the stairs on trays — stair surfing!” said Finn. “So it just evolved. I really like that sort of domestic imagery, where the most peculiar things happen in seemingly normal surroundings.” The group is currently touring as a four- piece with Split Enz Keyboardist Eddie Rayner. They have performed Split Enz songs as well as almost anything requested as an encore. They plan to record their sec- ond album some time this summer after the tour. “We want to start it as soon as possible,” said Finn, “but it really depends on what happens with this one and the rest of the tour. We’ve got a lot of new material togeth- er. Meanwhile, we want as many people as possible to hear the first one.” April (‘86) in relatively small theatres and suddenly be playing the Royal Albert Hall for two nights in the fall was sort of shock- ing. I don’t know if I was quite prepared for that. But the funny thing is that it happened with ‘Marlene On The Wall’ and not ‘Left Of Center,’ which was definitely more pop.” Vega first gained note in the early eight- ies through performances in Manhattan folk clubs. For many, she came to represent the new wave in folk music, even though her influences come from an earlier era. “I lis- tened more to Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie and Cisco Houston,” she says. “I wasn’t really into Dylan or Joni Mitchell. I don’t think I really got into Joni Mitchell until I was twenty. So many people com- pared me to her that I started to think, well maybe I should listen to her once or twice to see what everybody’s talking about.” “I don’t try to write a lot of love songs because I feel like most people have written them much better than I could do. So I try to find the odd angle to write from, like ‘Small Japan (continued from page 12) ty system. Of course, this system would col- lect royalties from hardware (audio and video tape recorders and blank tape). On the contrary, the representatives from hard- wares including E1AJ (Electrical Industries Association of Japan) are opposed to the royalty system, arguing that this system Blue Thing,’ and deal with feelings like fear and pain but also tenderness and compas- sion. And try to mix all those feelings together.” “Solitude Standing’”s mixture of moods and feelings is unified by “Tom’s Diner,” a song which brackets the album. The diner serves as a setting, a sort of shadow-world in which such enigmatic characters as “Luka,” “Calypso,” and the personification of “Solitude” tell their stories. If all of this sounds somewhat filmic, that’s because it is. “1 had wanted ‘Tom’s Diner’ itself to have the feel of one of those French movies from the 1960’s where the music is kind of sad and kind of happy at the same time and a little funny,” she says. “And definitely when we had the reprise at the end it was as though you can imagine the credits coming up.” Vega is currently on a seven month inter- national tour in support of the album, and will play two shows at the Shubert Theatre in Manhattan May 3d. would be against the interests of users. Now as the label approaches its second anniver- sary, the same Turtles are just coming off another monster disk, their million- selling, ex-chart-topping “Happy To- gether” . . . Epic Records has signed the popular British group, the Hollies, to an exclusive recording contract . . . The veteran songwriting team of Mike Stoller and Jerry Leiber has provid- ed the music for the upcoming ABC-TV special, Twiggy In New York, sked‘ed for network broadcast on April 27 . . . The second annual KHJ-Hollywood ra- dio appreciation concert at the Holly- wood Bowl on April 29 will feature the Supremes and the Buffalo Spring- field . . . Steve Winwood, lead singer of the Spencer Davis Group, left the group on April 2. Winwood has been the nucleus of the group since its forma- tion three-and-a-half years ago, playing lead guitar, piano, organ and singing. His departure can only be regarded as a serious blow to the Spencer Davis Group, who are also losing his brother, Muff, who played bass. Winwood is now going into virtual retirement for six months with the members of his new group, Traffic, who are David Ma- son, lead guitar and percussion, James Capaldi, drums and percus- sion, and Christopher Wood, tenor, flute and percussion. Although still only 18 years old, Winwood is widely regard- ed as one of the most gifted and cre- ative artists to emerge on the British music scene in the past two years. Al- though his departure may well signal the end of the Spencer Davis Group, who will find him impossible to replace, it seems certain that the career of Steve Winwood is only just beginning . . .
