ONJAZZ\ CLASSIC, PART TWO—Last week 1 discussed, and recommended, “The Revised Smithsonian Collection of Clas- sic Jazz.” This week I’ve got something to add about the set. Martin Williams, who organized and annotated the seven-LP set, has, as 1 said, provided as good a thumbnail guide through recorded jazz history as is available anywhere under one roof. However, in listening to the set and reading Williams’ excellent commen- tary, something troubled me. That is, though the course through the first 40 years of recorded jazz is succinctly de- tailed. Williams has absolutely gone to sleep on us after 1966, with the excep- tion of a single 1981 track from the World Saxophone Quartet. Now 1 don’t want to get into the old argument of whether or not there has been a ma- jor single innovator in jazz since the death of John Coltrane. but I’ll happi- ly tussle with anyone who insists that there hasn’t been a single innovation in jazz since the death of John Coltrane. According to Williams, there has been at least one notable advance in jazz in the past 20 years: The World Sax Quar- tet’s abandonment of the jazz rhythm section. But, according to the implica- tions of this set, that’s it. Aside from the WSQ (and 1 don’t think “Steppin”’ is nearly the best pos- sible example of what the WSQ is all about), Williams gives up the ghost af- ter the innovations of free jazz. The final six cuts on the set are by, in order, the Cecil Taylor Unit (from ’66). the John Coltrane Quartet (’63), the Or- nette Coleman Quartet (’59), the Or- nette Coleman Quartet (’59), the Ornette Coleman Double Quartet (’60), and the World Saxophone Quartet (’81). Beginning with Miles Davis’s mode-stretching Quintet of the ’60s (Herbie Hancock, Wayne Shorter, Ron Carter, Tony Williams). Wil- liams ignores the entire AACM, the Art Ensemble of Chicago, solo perfor- mances (Steve Lacy and Anthony Braxton eliminated a lot more than the rhythm section), the coming to terms of jazz with rhythm & blues and rock & roll (the WSQ is a good example of that), jazz fusion (The Mahavishnu Orchestra’s “Inner Mounting Flame,” Return to Forever’s “Light as a Feather,” several Miles Davis albums, and numerous other examples of classic jazz fusion), the blending of jazz and classical music in the works of, among others, James Newton and Anthony Davis, the innovations of such young players as Stanley Jordan and Bob- by McFerrin, each of whom has found a new way of expressing himself on an old instrument; harmolodics, Qrnette Coleman’s extension of his earlier inno- vations; ensembles dedicated to jazz repertory, and, yes, the neo-classicism of the likes of Wynton Marsalis, Scott Hamilton and so many others. For example. Qkay, 1 would be the first to admit that not all of the above belongs in a definitive set of “classic jazz;” in fact, maybe none of it does. The point is, if Williams had ended this set on the Or- nette Coleman Double Quartet the set’s intentions would have been clear: the history of “classic jazz” from ragtime to free jazz. Period. But, by including a sin- gle example of the World Saxophone Quartet (who took a further stride to- wards respectability with a lengthy piece by Rick Woodward in the New York Times Sunday Magazine a couple of weeks ago), Williams has attempted to be complete, to be up-to-date and inclusive. He fails. What’s needed here is a follow-up: “The Smithsonian His- tory of Classic Jazz, 1965-1987” or, a much better title, “The Smithsonian Survey of Contemporary Jazz, 1965- 1987.” However, like 1 stated last week, for a set surveying the backbone of “classic jazz,” this is the cat’s meow. It is not by any means the whole story. WHAT A PERE - Ellis Marsalis (1) and Branford Marsalis recently joined for- ces for a cross-generational jam session at the Studio Museum of Harlem. FESTIVALITIES— Here’s a couple more for those of you who are keeping a running tally on the upcoming jazz festivals: The Queen Mary Jazz Festival, held in Long Beach, CA at the foot of the boat of the same name, is set for the weekend of May 15-17. Qn the slate are the Duke Ellington Orchestra, Diane Schuur, the Rippingtons, Leslie Drayton & Fun, Lee Riten- our, George Howard, Poncho San- chez, Rare Silk, Charlie Byrd/ Herb Ellis/Barney Kessel, the Louie Bellson Big Band, Wishful Thinking, Spyro Gyra, the Yellow- jackets, Alphonse Mouzon and Larry Carlton. Sounds like there’ll be a whole lot of fusion going on. Call them at (213) 435-3511 if there’s anything else you’d like to know. In the same general vicinity (Califor- nia), but further on down the line (Au- gust 22 & 23) is the Concord Jazz Festival, which will field Chick Corea, the Crusaders, Michael Brecker, the Timeless All-Stars, Herbie Hancock, Kenny G, Joe Williams, Flora Purim & Airto, Jessica Wil- liams, and others. Their number is (415) 762-2277. And Oregon’s Mt. Hood Festival, which was discussed here a couple of weeks back, has added Herbie Mann, Monty Alexander, Phil Woods, Hi- roshima, George Howard and Tom Grant to its line-up. BLACKCONTEMPORARY THAT GIRL-Bobby Brown (1), whose current LP “King Of Stage’’ has sold in excess of a half million copies proves he is not afraid to strut an in- spired funk during the shooting of his video Girl Next Door. The song, his second single from the album, was produced by Larry Blackmon (r) of Cameo, who also directed the clip. ABBOTT GOES PLATINUM - Columbia Records recently honored Gregory Abbott with a party to celebrate the world-wide platinum success of his “Shake You Down’ LP and single. Pictured (I - r): Jane Berk, assoc dir prod mkt’g, Columbia; Danny Yarbrough, vp sales, Columbia; Mickey Eichner, sr vp A&R, Columbia; Abbott; Al Teller, pres CBS Records div; Ruben Rodriguez, vp black music andjazz promo, Columbia; and Bob Sherwood, sr vp mkt’g, Columbia. GOOD CAUSES-Recording star Jean Cam received a bouquet of roses from Boris Oglesby, Miller coordinator for young adult marketing, at a Miller Genuine Draft reception for Cam and Anita Baker at Valley Forge Music Fair. Baker followed three sold-out performances at Valley Forge with an encore show that generated more than $20,000 in charitable contributions for the United Negro College Fund and the Philadelphia Tribune charities. ALRIGHT, OKAY, HE SIGNS - Joe Williams (c) recently signed an ex- clusive contract with the newly reactivated Verve label; he’ll record his first album at LA’s Vine Street Bar & Grill later this month. Here with Williams at the signing are (I - r) Donald Elfman, PolyGram Jazz promotion manager; session producers Miriam Cutler and David Kreisberg ofHemisphere Produc- tions; and Ron Berinstein, owner ofVine Street. CTI-The race to pour jazz CDs into the market continues apace, with CBS As- sociated Records recent release of 14 titles from the CTI catalogue, Creed Taylor’s pioneering fusion label of the ’70s. CTI Records had classy packaging and crisp sound, and, though the albums weren’t to everybody’s taste, CTI seems a perfect candidate for the CD push. Out now are George Benson’s “White Rabbit,” Fred- die Hubbard’s “First Light,” Ron Carter’s “Blues Farm,” Deodato’s “Prelude,” Esther Phillips’ “What a Dif- ference a Day Makes,” “Freddie Hub- bard and Stanley Turrentine In Con- cert,” Chet Baker/Gerry Mulligan’s “Carnegie Hall Concert,” the CTI All- Stars “California Concert,” Johnny Hammond’s “Higher Ground,” Hubert Laws’ “The Rite of Spring,” “The Joe Farrell Quartet,” Don Sebesky’s “Giant Box,” Hank Crawford’s “Wildflowers,” and “Fire Into Music,” a sampler. On deck are Hubbard’s “Red Clay,” Jim Hall’s “Concierto,” Paul Desmond’s “Pure Desmond,” and Kenny Burrell’s “God Bless the Child.” NAJ-The Los Angeles-based National Academy of Jazz, which is “dedicated to the advancement and artistry of jazz and to establishing chapters throughout the country so that we can become a major force in helping make more Americans aware of the complete spectrum of the music we call jazz,” has expanded its board. Currently serving are Ray Avery, Frank Capp, Allyn Ferguson, Bob Florence, Terry Gibbs, Red Holloway, Phil Hulsey, Ralph Jungheim, Sandra Kimberling, Mauri Lathower, Luis Conti, Bernie Lewak, Mundell Lowe, Marty Morgan, Chuck Niles, Kirk Pasich, Dave Pell, Sue Raney, George Rappaport, Pancho Sanchez, Jim Shatz, Terri Hilton, Jim Washburn, LaRue Brown Watson, and Jack Wheaton. STRUTTIN’ WITH SOME BLINI- The other side of the Soviet jazz coin is coming stateside this spring. Last year we had the Ganelin Trio, the avant-gardist of the avant garde. This year it’s, believe it or not, the eight-member Leningrad Dixieland Jazz Band, led by one Oleg Grigoriyevich Kuvaitsev on alto sax (not your typical dixieland instrument that). The tour will begin where it should-at the Sacramento Dixieland Jubilee (5/22-25)- and will continue in San Francisco (5/27), Los Angeles (5/28 & 29), Central City, CO (5/30 & 31), La Crosse, WI (6/3), Mil- waukee (6/4), St. Louis (6/6), Rockford, IL (6/7), Rochester, NY (6/13), and Washington, D.C. (the Smithsonian, 6/14). BOPPING AROUND-Dr. Charles Kelman, a noted cataract surgeon and a once-in-awhile vocalist, has recorded an album with one of his patients, Lionel Hampton, in tribute to Benny Good- man. ..Leonard Feather has begun host- ing a one-hour Sunday program on L.A.’s KKGO; he can be found there from 8-9 p.m....Michel Petrucciani Live at the Vil- lage Vanguard is being released on video this month by Pioneer Artists. ..Five col- lege jazz groups, wiimers of a national competition sponsored by Walt Disney World and the National Association of Jazz Educators, will hold forth at Epcot Center, May 22-24; the North Texas State 2:00 Lab Band, the Fullerton (CA) Col- lege Vocal Jazz Ensemble, the Central State (OK) University Jazz Ensemble, the University of Kansas Vocal Ensemble, and the Eastman School of Music’s (NY) Saxology...The Newporter Resort and KLON Radio will present their annual All- American Jazz Festival at-where else?- Newport Beach, CA. On the slate are Pancho Sanchez, Don Menza, Matt Catingub, Melba Joyce, Ann Young, Judy Lori, Dan Jacobs, Alan Rowe and the Orange Coast College Big Bands...New York City’s Universal Jazz Coalition will present a “Tribute to Maxi- ne Sullivan,” May 9, hosted by Abbey Lincoln, and, the following weekend, the popular (in Sweden) Swedish fusion group Mwendo Dawa, May 15 & 16. ..The “Festival De Jazz Uno” is about to bring Billy Taylor, the Modern Jazz Quartet, Betty Carter, Jimmy Heath, and Jimmy Owens to South America for a five-day tour.. .The Second Annual Great Woods Jazz & Blues Festival is set for that lovely Mansfield, MA venue, June 20 & 21. Max Roach, Chuck Green, the MJQ, Carmen McRae, and the Count Basie Band will headline the first day, with a blues extravaganza-John Lee Hooker, Koko Taylor, Roomful of Blues, the Neville Brothers, Albert Col- lins, the Nighthawks, Johnny Winter, and Luther “Guitar” Johnson-on tap for Sunday. il ONJAZZ^^m NOTES ON TOMES-A ton of jazz books have come thudding onto my desk in recent weeks and I’ll try to report on them aU as I read them. Here are some thoughts on a few of them: Jazz: Myth And Religion by Neil Leonard ($16.95, Oxford University Press) is one of the dopiest jazz books I’ve ever read. Basically, it attempts to equate jazz with religion. Here’s an example: “Jazz sects start out in the cultic ferment of prophetic figures, like Bix Beiderbecke, Charlie Parker, and Ornette Coleman, men with mes- sages and auras powerful enough to break through accepted customs and beliefs. Such charismatics change not only musical tastes but the out- looks and life-styles of listeners who fall under their spell. Before long the prophet acquires a small, elite follow- ing, mostly musicians, but gradually, as his message spreads in personal ap- perances by word of mouth, and through recordings, he attracts a high- ly personalized and unstructured fol- lowing composed of aesthetically ad- venturous individuals whose taste is volatile but who remain zealous while in the fold. Cultists demand stylistic purity of their idols and shun listeners who accept tainted music or musicians. For the most part, however, they readily tolerate other beliefs-including those of other art forms (including modem classical music) or religions (Christianity, Judaism, Islam, as well as more ex- otic faiths)-so long as they do not threathen the jazz hfe. ’ ’ Read enough? This goes on for a couple of hundred pages-detaihng the cults, coming up with numerous examples of musicians and listeners who experienced near religious fer- vor while playing or listening, describing how the critics are like priests, etc., etc. What strikes me is how easily all of this can be applied to any art form. Just substitute the three names above with, say, Paul Gaughin, Pablo Picasso, and Jasper Johns, for example, or Elvis Presley, Mick Jagger, and Michael Jackson. It works. In fact, almost anything works-any thing with followers and leaders, anything where aesthetic judgements need to be made. This could have been Acting: Myth And Religion or Poetry: Myth And Religion and, who knows, maybe it will be. I Remember Jazz: Six Decades Among The Great Jazzmen by A1 Rose ($24.95, Louisiana State University Press) is a gentle, pleasant set of anecdotes from a steadfast chronicler of traditional jazz. Rose, who lives in New Orleans, has been around a long time and this is a breezy, enjoyable set of written snap- shots of the likes of Jelly Roll Mor- ton, Sidney Bechet, Jack Teagar- den, and W.C. Handy. At times Rose becomes ridiculous, beginning I j Cash Box May 1 6, 1 987 a profile of Dizzy Gillespie with the line “In a book about real jazz you wouldn’t reasonably expect to find anything about Dizzy Gillespie, but I’ve included him to make a point.’’ The point, as Rose brings out a few paragraphs later, is that “I was right about be-bop. It was a musical deadend. I hoped when it was over that some of the excellent musicians it produced would turn their atten- tions to genuine jazz, but that never happened.’’ He gives moldy figs a bad name. Da Capo Press, which lives, it seems, to revivify dead or dying jazz books of note has just brought out paperback reissues of a few items, in- cluding Benny: King of Swing, which is more or less like looking through Benny Goodman’s photo album, something only the most devoted Goodmanphile will want to do; and The Enyclopedia of Jazz in the '70s by Leonard Feather and Ira Gitler, a book that I’ve praised here before-it’s the third (and, so far, the last) in Feather’s remarkable series of jazz encylopedias and, like the first two (also in paperback from Da Capo), it’s flawed but absolutely in- dispensable. A TABLE NAMED MARIA - Tania Maria glows over her recently-in- stalled “star table,’’ the Blue Notes answer to footprints in cemertt. Sal Maries, manager of the N.Y. club, beams at the star and her table. MELLON HEADS-Philadelphians who journey to New York for the JVC Festival are hereby instructed to stay put. During the same 10 days (June 19-28), the same producer (George Wein), will bring many of the same artists (Sarah Vaughan, Wynton Marsalis, Stan Getz, Bran- ford Marsalis, Herbie Hancock, etc.) to the City of Brotherly Love for the second annual Mellon Jazz Fes- tival (that’s a bank, folks). The Fes- tival is dedicated to the Heath Brothers (Jimmy, Percy, and “Tootie”), one of the city’s preeminent musical families. Tlie full schedule-and it’s a big one-can be had by calling (215) 751-9883. The thing will kick off this week, however, when Wynton Marsalis, Jimmy and “Tootie’’ Heath, Paquito D’Rivera, David Amram, John Blake, Ron Carter, Pieces of a Dream and others participate in some master classes, symposiums, and free public performances at Philadelphia Colleges of the Performing Arts and Penn’s Landing, May 15 & 16. TWO JOE HENTERSON (Blue Note BT 85126) 38 YOU KNOW THE NUMBER 35 7 HEN"RY THREADGILL SEXTETT (Novus/RCA 3013-1-N9) 39 TONIGHT SHOW BAND 36 6 VOL II (Amherst 521 01 40 WHIZ KIDS 37 9 GARY BURTON (ECM 831 110) JAZZFEATURE PICKS LESS THAN DIVINE^PolyGram Jazz has completed its massive program reissuing everything that the great Sarah Vaughan waxed for the Mercury label. Last year, you’ll recall, PolyGram gave us three boxed sets covering the sessions from the ’50s. Now, on two boxed sets of LPs or a single boxed set of CDs, comes “The Complete Sarah Vaughan on Mecury Vol. 4, 1963-1967.’’ Like the first three sets, this material is spotty. Unlike the first three sets, this material is mostly spotty. One thing is certain-Sarah Vaughan’s singing is magnificent eveiy inch of the way. But in the ’60s Mercury attempted to cast her as more of a pop singer, and this set is stuffed with schmaltz and com- Sarah singing covers of the hits of the day (“What the World Needs Now Is Love,” “A Lover’s Concer- to,” etc.), Sarah singing with the soupy Sevend Saaby Choir, Sarah singing something called “Domini- que’s Discotheque.” Great singing, awful material, mostly awful arrange- ments. There is some fine Sarah here however, some of the finest avail- able. “Sassy Swings the Tivoli” was a delightful live LP, recorded in Copenhagan, produced by Quincy Jones, and featuring only la Vaughan and her trio. In ‘ ‘Volume 4,” we not only get the original ten songs from the LP, but an additional 22 numbers never before available in the States (some of it has been out in Japan). That, and a nice pair of dates original- ly released as “It’s a Man’s World” and “Sassy Swings Again,” are ex- ceptionally worthwhile. The rest of it has its moments, but only Sarah Vaughan completists are really going to fmd very much other divine material in here. StiU, completeness is the key and, for that, PolyGram Jazz and Kiyoshi Koyama, who put aU of the sets together, deserve another deep bow. PERUGIA-The good folks from Italy’s Umbria Jazz Festival, which takes place in the lovely town of Perugia, recently threw a fancy-schmancy party at the Whitney Museum here in New York to unveil the line-up for this year’s festival. At the July 10-19 festival will be, among others, Wynton Mar- salis, Pat Metheny, Ahmad Jamal, Gil Evans, Cab Calloway, Miles Davis, Branford Marsalis, the Man- hattan Transfer, George Benson, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Stan Getz, Michael Brecker, Gary Burton, Tito Puente, Celia Cruz, Stanley Jordan and Dexter Gordon. At the party were, among others. Sting, Roy Haynes and Hilton Ruiz (who performed). UNDER THE SKY-The good folks from Japan’s “Select Live Under The Sky Festival” recently threw their own fancy-schmancy party in town, at the Parker-Meridien, to an- nounce their line-up for this summer. This festival will tour-hitting six cities (five in Japan and Hong Kong) for nine performances between July 25 and August 8. On tap for the tour are groups led by Miles Davis, Wayne Shorter, Jack Dejohnette and Steve Gadd (aU on hand for the party), the World Saxophone Quar- tet (a third of whom were on hand for the party), and something called SXL, led by Bill Laswell (who skipped the party). Also schmoozing by the Parker-Meridien pool were Sonny Rollins, Herbie Hancock, Tony Williams, Roberta Flack, and other movers and shakers. YOCK IT - Herbie Hancock and CBS Records Group president Wal- ter Yetnikoff laugh it up at a recent CBS gala. DEXTERITY-Dexter Gordon, who hasn’t performed in public in years, will not only be touring Europe this summer, but will be ap- pearing with the New York Philhar- monic at Avery Fisher Hall, June 4- 6, in an evening called “Gershwin & Ellington: American Masters.” Dexter will be playing David Baker’s “EUingtones: A Fantasy for Saxophone and Orchestra.” And speal^g of the Academy Award nominee for Best Actor, Dexter copped the Italian equivalent of the Oscar recently for his performance in RoundMidnight. BOPPING AROUND-Bobby McFerrin will be hosting VH-l’s New Visions on May 24. ..Hank Crawford and Jimmy McGriff will set sail on the DeWitt Clinton, May 31, the first in a series of jazz boat rides out of N.Y.’s South Street Seaport benefitting WBGO- FM...JazzVideo International has just released a VHS master class with bebop pianist Walter Bishop, Jr., who discusses and demonstrates fourths, jazz comping, chord voic- ing s, etc., and even recites a little poetry. Tapes are available for S34.95 by writing to Suite 33-Q, 400 W. 43rd St., New York, NY 10036...ECM has just issused a CD compilation, “ECM Spectrum Vol. I,” a sampler containing 68 minutes of various ECM stuff...Tickets are now on sale for the JVC Jazz Fes- tival/New York at the various box of- fices around town or by calling Tick- etron...Two more new jazz books are available (I’ll get to them at length in a couple of weeks): a paperback reprint of The Jazz Word by Dom Cerulli, Burt Korall and Mort Nasatir (S9.95, Da Capo) and The Music: Reflections On Jazz and Blues by Amiri and Amina Baraka (S22.95 , William Morrow). Lee Jeske FOR OLIM-Cecil Taylor-Soul Note SN 1150-Producer: Giovanni Bonandrini Taylor in absolute peak solo piano form: brilliant, inventive, explosive, virtuosic and surprisingly subtle and spatial. Sublime! BRIGHT MOMENTS-Max Roach Double Quartet-Soul Note SN 1159-Producer: Max Roach The drum great’s Double Quartet is his post-bop jazz quartet combined with a jazz-sawy string quartet. This is no cut-and-paste job: the quar- tets are well-integrated and the whole sound is fresh and invigorating. REFLECTIONS IN BLUE-Sun Ra Arkestra-Black Saint BSR 0101-Producer: Giovanni Bo- nandrini The wild, wooly, always unique, usually swinging Arkestra in a wild, wooly, unique and swinging album of pithy originals and prismatic ver- sions of standards. Simultaneously down to earth and out in the cosmos. NEW LIFE-David Murray Octet- Black Saint BSR 0100-Producer: David Murray The prolific tenor saxophonist returns to his best format: the Octet. Like the three previous Octet dates, this is a stomping session with a foot in the past, a foot in the future, and its body firmly in the present. ROLES-Joe Sample-MCA 597^- Producers: Joe Sample, Wilton Felder Contemporary soul jazz, with Sample playing mostly acoustic piano in a toe-tapping light funk set- ting. Bobby Hutcherson guests. FOUR CORNERS-Yellowjackets- MCA 5994-Producers: Yellowjack- ets, David Hentschel Four-on-the-floor jazz fusion from the popular quartet and a num- | ber of guests. Slick, latinified and bubbly. ALBUM RELEASES OUT OF THEBOX HEART-Bad Animals-Capitol PJ- 12546-Producer: Ron Nevison-List: 8.98-Bar Coded The Wilson sisters return with another slickly produced collection of gutsy rockers and soul-searing ballads. The lead single, “Alone,” is already burning up AOR, A/C, and Top 40 radio nationwide, and looks to be a major hit. Songwriting contributors in- clude Diane Warren and Stein- berg/Kelly, who have written enough hits between them to get Heart off on the right foot here. OUT OF THE BOX\ 4 BY FOUR-4 By Four-Cap- itol/EMI ST- 12560-Producers: Various-List: 8.98-Bar Coded An appealing air of innocence per- vades this record; from the clean cut yomig musicians to the sugar sweet pop harmonies they produce, this quin- tet resembles nothing less than an 80’s Jackson Five. Their smokin’ dance grooves (“You Changed”) and silky- smooth ballads (“Come Over,” “This Time I Know It’s For Real”) are tailor- made for mass appeal radio airplay, and the teen-age market should jump on this all summer long. OUT OF THEBOX LITTLE STEVEN-Freedom No Compromise-Manhattan ST-53048- Producer: Little Steven-List: 8.98- Bar Coded One of the most committed and pas- sionate artists of our time returns with his third full-length album. Conceptual in nature, the themes focus on three inter-related problem areas - South Africa, Latin America, and Native Americans. Written, arranged, and produced by Little Steven, this is a wondrous example of the power of rock music to awaken and inspire. NEWAND DEVELOPING FIRE TOWN-In The Heart Of The I i Heart Country-Atlantic 81754-1- I Producer: Fire Town-List: 8.98-Bar i I Coded Strong debut effort from this Mid- ^ western quartet. Their music blends | sublime 60 ’s harmonies with homespun 80’s pop sensibilities, and j the result is destined for major Alterna- tive radio acceptance. The heartfelt strumming shimmers under the plain- tive vocal harmonies on such cuts as j “Carry The Torch” and “Rain on i You.” MTV exposure is helping, too. FEATURE PICKS MASON RUFFNER-Gypsy Blood-CBS Associated BFZ 40601-Producer: Dave Edmunds-List: 8.98-Bar Coded Hot blooded guitar workout from New Orleans club legend. Dylanish vocals add depth to these explosive rave-ups, and his stinging fills echo the legacy of Hendrix, Clapton, and Keith Richard. Adds a new chapter to the book of original Southern blues/boogie guitarists. JILL JONES-Jill Jones-Paisley Park/WB 25575-1-Producers: David Z.-Jill Jones-Prince-List: 8.98-Bar Coded The latest Prince protege checks in with this wonderful collection of dance grooves. As per usual Paisley Park, the material is highly carnal, but with enough humor to smooth over the rough edges. Jones’ voice is cloud-light, but deeply ex- pressive and sensuous. THE COLOURFIELD-Deception-Chrysalis BFV 41546-Producer: Richard Gottehrer-List: 8.98-Bar Coded Sprightly, synth-oriented pop with a distinctively British sense of style. The lavish, lush texture combines with the dark lyrical outlook to produce a shimmer- ing and accessible set of tunes. DIVINE WEEKS-Through And Through-Down There/Restless 72206-1- Producer: Vitus Matare-List: 8.98-Bar Coded Urgent guitar rock with a message. This debut LP features a sense of lyrical in- sight far beyond this band’s tender years, and their music combines the vocal in- stincts of the 60’s with a slight twist of hardcore thrash, just for fun. The overall treatment is rough, but their promise shines through brightly. MOTLEY CRUE-Girls, Girls, Girls-Elektra 60725-1-Producer: Tom Wer- j I man-List: 8.98-Bar Coded ] Plenty of head-banging metal here to please the Criie’s legions of teenage fans. Nikki Sixx’s lyrics of backseat sex, underage sex, and striptease sex should cut straight to the heart of young America. TSOL-Hit And Run-Enigma ST-73263-Producer: Howard Benson-List: 8.98-Bar Coded Relentlessly hard-driving rock-and-roll from L.A. underground favorites. i Recalls the knife-edged desperation of early AC/DC, with more fulfilled produc- i tion than TSOL’s earlier efforts. The payoff is the mix of lyrical introspection with ; anthemic choruses. GLENN MEDEIROS-GIenn Medeiros-Amherst AMH 3313-Producer: Jay Stone-List: 8.98-Bar Coded The debut album from a 16 year-old Hawaiian prodigy, discovered in a high- | school talent contest. His winning single, “Nothing’s Gonna Change My Love For ! You,” has been all over radio for months now, and the LP reflects similar seam- less style. STAN CAMPBELL-Stan Campbell-Elektra 60734-1-Producer: Stan ; Campbell-List: 8.98-Bar Coded Stylish and jazzy pop from guitarist Campbell. ON JAZZ PASSING ON-Bassist Wilbur Lit- tle and pianist Victor Feldman both succumbed to heart attacks in the past couple of weeks. Little was a big-toned, flexible bassist who was widely admired; he worked with Kenny Dorham, Elvin Jones, J.J. Johnson and many others before moving to Europe, where he became one of the most in-demand bassists on the continent-backing visiting Americans and enlivening local groups with his sohd work. He was 59. Feldman was a British-bom pianist and vibes-player who lived and worked in California. He was a popular studio musician, a pioneer in the fusing of jazz and classical music, and a sideman who worked with Miles Davis, amongst many others. He was 53. A memorial service was held last week at New York’s St. Peter’s Lutheran Church for Buddy Rich, who died last month. Except for an outrageously vulgar and incoherent outburst from Steve Gadd, the two- and-a-half-hour afternoon was filled with gentle reminiscences and swing- ing music. Max Roach, Roy Eldridge, Sonny Igoe, Burt Korall, and Chico Hamilton were among the speakers; Stan Getz, Ruby Braff, Joe Bushkin, Jane Harvey, and a Rich alumni band under the baton of Rich stalwart Steve Marcus were among the performers; and David Chertok supphed appropriate film chps. COMPACTION-EolyGram Jazz has unveiled its fust midline CD release. Called, naturalmente. Com- pact Jazz, the series is to feature best- of compilations from PolyGram’s vast jazz holdings (you know. Verve, Mercury, MPS, etc.)-a CD version of the new Walkman Jazz series. Each CD will hold nearly an hour’s worth of music, and the first mid- liners on the block are Ella Eitzgerald, Count Basie, Chuck Mangione, Dinah Washington, Wes Montgomery, Gerry Mul- ligan, Jimmy Smith, the Singers Unlimited, and a pair of anthologies- a general sampler and a disc called “The Best of Dixieland.” The SlO CD barrier continues to crumble. IMPROVISATIONS !-That’s the name of a worthwhile June festival of “contemporary' American music” being launched in Manhattan by the World Music Institute, a worthwhile orgartization. The festival features some of the leading lights in contem- porary jazz and, wisely, George We in has seen fit to include the dates that coincide with his JVC Fes- tival (June 19-27) into the JVC wing- ding. Scheduled are the Billy Bang Quintet/Henry Threadgill’s Windstring Ensemble (June 6, Merkin Concert Hall), The Black Swan Quartet/Muhal Richard Abrams’ Quartet (13, MCH), New Winds/T)ewey Redman’s Quartet (19, Greenwich House), Anthony Davis’ Episteme/John Carter’s Octet (24, MCH), Leroy Jenkins’ Stingi/Gerry Hemingway Trio (26, GH), and the Amina Claudine Myers Quintet/Craig Harris & Tailgater’s Tales (27, MCH). ALBAM~IANS -BMFs Stan Catron (1) and Burt Korall (r) congratulate composer-arranger Manny Albam, following a recent tribute to Albam at the Peekskill (NY) Center For The Arts. LJUB FOR SALE-Look, I know its a schlep, but the Ljubljana Jazz Fes- tival, held-where else?-in Ljubljana, Yugoslavia, wanted me to pass along the information that the festival is being held June 15-20 and will in- clude, along with a number of European groups, Paul Bley, Cecil Taylor, Billy Bang, the Art En- semble of Chicago, Abbey Lincoln, Billy Harper, and a Duke Ellington “Sacred Concert” conducted by Mercer Ellington. Now you know. SAIL FOR SALE-For those New York-based seafarers who can’t af- ford those expensive one-week jazz cruises on the S.S. Norway, there are a couple of summer alternatives. Musiccruise ’87 features a Hudson River Dayliner steaming around Manhattan with a musical notable firmly ensconced on board. The cruises, which leave from Pier 81 (41st Street and the Hudson), wiU headline Stanley Turrentine/Fred- die Hubbard (6/5), Albert Col- lins/David “Fathead” Newman (6/19), Tania Maria (6/26), Pieces of a Dream (7/4), Ben E. ONJAZZ FANTASY-IZES^G4f Fantasy Re- cords is still issuing OJCs then vinyl can’t really be dead, can it? The latest batch of the midlme goodies have just arrived and, in a pair of new twists, the albums are all culled from the same label-Fantasy-and the first 2,000 copies of each are pressed on red vinyl. Fantasy, founded by Max and Sol Weiss, was the label of San Francisco jazz and, in the mid-’50s, was quite an influential operation, thanks in great part to Dave Brubeck, their biggest-selling artist. But Fan- tasy had a number of other influential performers on their roster-including Lenny Bruce-and they recorded some of the then-popular fusions of jazz and latin music spearheaded by the likes of Cal Tjader and Mongo Santamaria They also had the inter- esting habit of issuing their albums on colored vinyl, years before this be- came an au courant practice in the rock game (among my souvenirs are several red vinyl Lenny Bruce LPs). Well, these 20 new OJCs include no Brubeck or Bruce, but they are rich in a sweet, innocent, percolating sound- a soimd that very much reflects the ’50s and early-’60s, but a sound that holds up very nicely today. So, forget the compact discs for now. It’s time to head for the turntable, with, per- haps, a Kerouac novel by your side, a jug of cheap Italian wine, and the sounds (and red vinyl sight) of Cal Tjader’s “Mambo with Tjader,” “Tjader Plays Mambo” (snappy tit- les, those), “San Francisco Moods,” “A Night at the Blackhawk,” “Con- cert on the Campus,” “Cal Tjader Plays, Mary Stallings Sings,” and “Plays Harold Arlen,” Bola Sete’s (he was the early bossa nova guitarist who died this year) “Bossa Nova,” “The Incomparable,” “Autentico!,” and “Vince Guaraldi & Bola Sete Live at El Matador,” Guaraldi’s “Jazz Impressions,” “The Mont- gomery Brothers In Canada,” “A Date with the Mastersounds” (Buddy and Monk Montgomery minus brother Wes), “Swinging with the Mastersounds,” Mongo San- tamaria’s “Sabroso,” and “Yambu,” “Stan Getz” (featuring, who else?. Cal Tjader), “Gerry Mul- ligan/Paul Desmond, and “Modem Music From San Francisco,” a com- pilation featuring Guaraldi, the Ron Crotty Trio, and the Jerry Dodgion Quartet. During this 50th anniver- sary of the Golden Gate Bridge, it’s nice to remember that San Francisco was a hot-bed of musical activity long before the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane and Huey Lewis & The News. S’COOL DAYS-Look, forget the Hamptons and Fire Island. Manhat- tan is the place to be this summer-the jazz clubs are aU cool and open, the jazz concerts on boats and in parks will start coming hot and heavy, and, at NYU, you can even get smart while thinking jazz thoughts. Arnold Jay Smith, the one-time jazz critic and this-time jazz publicist, is going to the head of the class for the fifth year of his “Jazz Greats/Great Jazz.” Join- ing Smith, with cases full of an- cedotes and, perhaps, an instrument or two, will be Paquito D ’Rivera (6/10), Max Roach (6/17), Phil Woods (6/24), Hank Jones (7/8), Jay Leonhart (7/15), Amy Duncan (7y^2), and “surprises” (7/29), plus registrants will be taken to a pair of JVC Jazz Festival concerts. It’s $180 for aU of this (hey, this is college) and one can call (212) 598-3091 or 998- 7 130 for info. INTIMA-CY — Trumpeter!band- leader Maynard Ferguson (1) has signed with Intima Records. Here he pens his contract in the company of Enigma founder Jim Martone (c) and Enigma Records CEO William Hein. IN THE PARK-One of those free concert series in the parks will be SummerStage, running throughout the summer at the Central Park BandsheU. Lots of great per- formers’ll be aroimd for this chock- fuU extravanganza (including Ladys- mith Black Mambazo, a must-see). Jazzwise, one can look forward to Sun Ra (6/20), the Microscopic Sex- tet/Wilberforce (6/27), Olu Dara & The Okra Orchestra (7/4), the Henry Threadgill Sextet (7A1), and Leroy Jenkins’ Sting! (7/18). SEPTEMBER SONGS-I know it’s a httle early, but some of us do our planning in advance. The Delaware Water Gap (Pennsylvania) Celebra- tion of the Arts will hold its 10th an- niversary Celebration, September 11- 13. It will feature, among others, Manny Albam, Phil Woods, Bob Dorough, A1 Cohn, and Urbie Green. The Sedona, Arizona Jazz on the Rocks Festival will take place on September 26 and on the rocks will be Nancy Wilson, Terry Gibbs and the Capp-Pierce Juggernaut, Derek Smith, Milt Hinton, Jon Faddis and others. BOPPING AROUND-Byron Stri- pling (boy, is there a guy with a bad name—he’s enormous), a trumpeter with the Count Basie Orchestra, has been chosen to play Louis Armstrong in Satchmo, a musical about the greatest jazzman of them all that opens in New Orleans July 14 before hitting the road en route to a five-week run at Washington, D.C.’s Kennedy Center...New on the jazz bookshelves (and adding to the large list of books I want to review here) are Nights In Birdland: Jazz Photographs 1954-60, photos by Carol ReifT ($10.95, Fireside Books), The Giants of Jazz by Dave Geliy, with drawings by David Smith ($19.95, cloth; $9.95, paper, Schirmer Books) and It Ain’t Neces- sarily So, the autobiography of Larry Adler ($17.95, Grove Press). Australian Robert Parker started fid- dling around with acoustic-era jazz a number of years ago and now, final- ly, the fruits of his incredible labor are getting stateside distribution. These three CDs feature the hkes of Louis Armstrong, Earl Hines, JeUy Roll Morton, King Oliver, and the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, all recorded in the early days of record- ing (the ODJB track is from 1918) and all gloriously clear and rich. Parker calls his “digital stereo” “a subjective balancing act for the trans- fer engineer, juggling opposing fac- tors such as high-frequency response and surface noise on one hand, and deep bass response and rumbles on the other.” No matter, you’ve got to hear it to believe it. SEXTET-Carla Bley-Watt/ECM 831 697-Producers: Carla Bley, Steve Swallow Carla Bley continues her explora- tion of latin-tinged, guitar (Hiram Bullock) and electric bass (Steve Swallow) based mood music, and while it’s good of that type, it ain’t up to the rollicking, unique and great- ly missed Carla Bley big band. MEANS OF IDENTTFICATION- Valery Ponomarev-Reservoir RSR 101-Producer: MarkFeldman New label debuts with ex-Jazz Messenger and, not surprisingly, it’s a hard-bop date, with the trumpeter helming a tough-as-nails quintet in- cluding tenor saxophonist Ralph Moore and drummer Kenny Wash- ington. ONJAZZ^^m SOVIET GARAGE?-Pat Meth- eny’s latest tour will be opening tonight at the Jubilee Hall in Leningrad. Leningrad? Yep, Meth-, eny and his band left last week for an unusual tour of the Soviet Union. Un- usual in that this is working hke a real tour-the Metheny Group is play- ing 13 concerts in three cities, each in a 7,000 seat haU; is bringing their own sound and lighting; and is actual- ly getting paid by the Soviets (that’s Goskontsert, the official goverment concert agency). For those who want to know such things, the tour is at Jubilee Hall, June 8-11; Moscow’s Dynamo HaU, June 13-17; and Kiev’s Sports Concert Hall, June 20- 23. The concerts, Metheny proudly notes, were sold out in no time-and to regular paying customers at that. After the Soviet Union, the Metheny Group (Lyle Mays, Steve Rodby, Paul Wertico, David Blamires, Mark Ledford, Armando Marcal) plays Europe before beginning a U.S. tour (including Radio City) in August. This wiU all coincide with the release of “Still Life (Talking),’’ the first Geffen album by the Metheny Group. Metheny, you’U recall, began his Geffen deal last year with the fantastic “Song X,’’ the col- laboration with Ornette Coleman. The plan was for this album to be a collaboration with Milton Nascimen- to, but, says Pat, that has been put off for the next album (he and Geffen figured it’d be better to slip a group album out in-between). Metheny, by the way, says he will not be flying into Moscow in a Cessna. MANSFIELDALITIES-Look, if you don’t want to cross an ocean, and you don’t want to come to New York for the JVC Festival, fret not, there’s yet another jazz festival worth men- tioning. The Great Woods Center for the Performing Arts, a nice new cen- ter in Mansfield, Massachusetts, is holding their own jazz and blues fes- tival, June 20 & 21 (I went last year- it was real nice), and I can mention aU the participants. The jazz day, June 20, wiU feature Max Roach, Barry Harris, the MJQ, Carmen McRae, the Count Basie Or- chestra, and a host of tap dancers. The blues day, however, sounds like the thing to go for: John Lee Hooker, the Nighthawks, Luther “Guitar Junior” Johnson, Room- ful of Blues, Albert Collins, the Neville Brothers and Johnny Winter will get things hopping. A call to Ticketmaster 1-800-682-8080 gets the poop. PASSING ON-Turk Murphy, one of the most steadfast keepers of the traditional jazz flame, died May 30 of cancer in San Francisco. Murphy came to prominence in 1940, during the heart of the traditional jazz revival, playing trombone in Lu Wat- ters’ Yerba Buena Jazz Band. Mur- phy formed his own band in the ’40s and has performed constantly since then, sticking to his traditional jazz guns. He never left San Francisco- playing long engagements in residence at various San Francisco boites and hotels. Last year, the Mur- phy band participated in a sold-out Carnegie Hall concert in tribute to the trombonist. His burly, tailgating sound was spry and uplifting, and the music was pure and lovely. Turk Murphy was 71. JAZZ TIMES-The Jazz Times Con- vention is scheduled for October 14- 17 at New York’s Roosevelt Hotel and I’ll be going into more detail about it later on. However, if you’d like to save a couple of dollars, a 10% discount on registrations is available to those who sign up before July 8. Write to Jazz Times, 8055 13th St., Silver Spring, MD 20910 for all the details. A NIGHT AT SAM'S - Shannon (c), whose debut album is due later this year from Soul Note, recently warbled at N.Y.’s Mr. Sam's, where PolyGram Special Imports’ Paul Del Campo (1), and Gilbert Hetherwick, PolyGram Regional Classics manager, came out to greet her. MONTREALITIES-Say you’ve read enough about jazz festivals? Well, here’s a bit about two others. The Montreal International Jazz Fes- tival has quietly turned itself into one of the major events on the jazz fes- tival calendar. There’Ll be some 10 concerts a night for ten nights, not to mention films, plays, aU sorts of things. Now, I can’t possibly men- tion everybody who’s booked on it here, suffice it to say that everybody is booked on it (the schedule booklet is 56 pages long). The thing takes place June 26-July 5 and if you want to go to an international jazz festival this summer, but you don’t want to cross an ocean, hey, this is the way to go. Call (514) 871-1881 for the low- down. BOPPING AROUND-Billy Tay- lor, the most ubiquitous jazzman around, adds another job to his resume. He has been named the Tampa Bay Performing Arts Center Music Director for Jazz Programs. “The position of jazz in American culture and musical history is sig- nificant,” said the always eloquent Taylor. “Activities which present the best of jazz, national and interna- tional, will become part of our plan- ning. Jazz education workshops and awareness opportunities will also be- come a priority. ’’...Herbie Hancock will be making a rare club ap- pearance when he puts in five nights, June 17-21, at Fort Worth’s worthy Caravan of Dreams, with A1 Foster and Buster Williams. ..Add one more book to the pile: the long-awaited Stormy Monday: The T-Bone Walker Story by Helen Oakley Dance ($24.95, Louisiana State University Press). PROFILES KLSX - “Classic Rock” Here To Stay On September 27, 1986, Los Angeles radio listeners were in- troduced to an inventive, new radio concept, "Classic Rock.” The inception of KLSX 97.1 FM in the L.A. marketplace quickly proved successful, and soon many stations across the country followed suit. The demise of one-time L.A. market kingpin KMET only aided the cause - freeing up many of that stations popular on-air talent to fill positions at the infant KLSX. "I think what we have done with KLSX is we’ve been able to fill a void that existed in this marketplace,” stated the sta- tion’s General Manager Bob Moore during a recent interview with Cash Box. He continued, “ ... a void that we talked about for two and a half years and didn’t know what it was, fortunately the audience has labeled it 'classic rock.’ ” A programmer’s definition of classic rock, according to Moore, " ... is music that has outlasted a fad or a popularity of a particular time.” Yet he credits one of the stations listeners with the ideal analogy, "He told me, ‘An oldie is ‘Sugar Sugar,’ a clas- sic is ‘Layla.’ ” I think that is the perfect definition of a classic.” He emphasized, "We are expos- ing product to people that they haven’t been able to hear in years.” One myth Moore would like to shatter is that of the narrow reach of the classic format. “Too many people try to categorize classic rock as a handful of ar- tists, it isn’t a handful of artists - it’s over 35,000 songs, that’s our library.” He continued, “What we have done is solidified that once and for all to the world that there is a format called classic rock, and it is a real format. It isn’t 25 records, it isn’t a morning show, it’s a very, very intricate, com- plex format that reaches a mass of people - and if you do it cor- rectly it is something that can continue to grow and continue to expand. Our goal is to have over a million listeners, have them all happy and interactive with the radio station. And I think that that’s a very realistic goal for us to achieve. The bottom line is that the audience feels very favorable to what we’re doing and showing tremendous sup- port of the station. The station is being programmed on a daily basis utilizing our audience and their reaction to everything, and that’s the single most important thing. Radio is a part of the entertainment industry, but it’s really a part of the communica- tion industry. We encourage not only praise, but criticism.” “ an oldie is ‘Sugar Sugar, ’ a classic is ‘Layla’ . ” Although on the air only a few short months, KLSX has refused to remain dormant and familiar. One major shift has been that of programming a heal- thy dose of current rock within the playlist. "We play a lot of currents, I personally think that there are a lot of classic acts today that make classic rock - the Talking Heads is one of them, U2 is on the border of that right now. The Police are definitely classic artists ... At this time we are playing five cur- rents an hour out of fifteen records an hour. We play Paul Simon, we play a lot of Eddie Money, we’re playing a lot of the new Greg Allman. The currents have to be by an established art- ist or an artist that has outlasted a fad. We have tried to carve out the music that has lasted throughout whatever that initial fad was.” He assured, “We are constantly testing the water, what we will do is see what lasts KLSX prides itself on its “no repeat days,” never playing the same song in one 24 hour period. Moore recalls “ ... when we started in the market, one of our friendly competitors had a no repeat Thursday. I was talk- ing to their General Manager and he was telling me how dif- ficult it was to have a "no repeat day” - because you have to be really careful, you can burn out your library real quickly. I kind of snickered in the back of my mind and thought, ‘our approach is going to be no repeat weeks!” On the subject of KMET (now KTWV - new age format, no disc jockeys), Moore ex- plained that “The greatest benefit we received from KMET’s demise, was the freeing up of some incredible talent: Jim Ladd, David Perry, Jack Snyder, Paraquat Kelly, Cynthia Fox, etc.” He continued, "KMET, un- fortunately, died a long time ago, they just buried the body recent- ly. It did have another effect, be- cause it gave us the opportunity to reach another level of people that I think had hung on to KMET much longer than the norm. KMET, I think, was one of those caring, concerned, in- volved radio stations - and when they went away, there was a part of certain people’s hearts that went with it. ” KLSX has made a point of devoting itself to community ser- vice and public awareness. The station has been active in aid for Vietnam veterans, L.A.’s home- less, and many other aspects of involvement. KLSX recently sponsored The Doobie Brothers reunion concert benefiting the Vietnam vets, and donated much on air time devoted to the cause via auctions and public service announcements. Moore commented, "We’re not taking out our costs. We don’t have ad- ministrative costs or overhead, we’re happy to turn over the proceeds because it’s a cause we believe in very much. We are very, very involved with the L.A. homeless, it has become a major problem. We are what 1960’s FM radio was all about - being concerned, getting in- volved. We are not a music machine. The worst thing that could happen to us is a billboard saying ‘New format, no disc jock- eys’ - that is not us. The enter- tainers that we have on the air are definitely aware of what’s going on in the world and they definitely speak their piece about it.” Moore insists “My radio sta- tion is not ‘60 minutes,’ it’s not in- vestigative reporting, it’s not changing the face of America. But I think it’s making people aware that besides this music there were some very powerful statements made with this music, and still being made with this music.” He concluded, “and not only is it an entertainment medium, but it’s also an informa- tion medium, and that’s what radio is supposed to be.” Tom De Savia KLSX 97.1 FM 7^/4 " S •40^ IllOam

40REUNITED 36 10 ELVIN JONES McCOY TYNER QUINTET (Blackhawk 52101) JAZZFEATURE PICKS DEXTER GORDON T ONG TALL REDUX-Dexter -^^Gordon is back. Again. After a four year lay-off due to ill health (“My health was very rundown after all these years of my life,” says Dex- ter), Dexter Gordon, saxophone in hand, faced a hve audience the week before last, as a guest soloist with, of all things, the N.Y. Philharmonic. He played on a new David Baker piece called “Ellingtones,” and, after a second or two, it was clear that Dexter Gordon’s sound was still in- tact. The real sharp chops, perhaps, will follow; the chops at Avery Fisher Hall were, in fact, not bad at all. Dexter, of course, comes and goes. In 1960 he came back, after years of obscurity and a prison term. In 1976 he came back, after 14 years of living and working in Europe. Last year, of course, he came back on film, cop- ping a Best Actor nomination for his troubles. This year, the six-foot-five- inch bebop giant is back in the flesh. The weekend before the Philhar- monic gig, Dexter guested on the up- coming Tony Bennett album. At the end of the month, he embarks on a tour of Europe with Bobby Hutcher- son, Cedar Walton, Billy Higgins and Pierre Michelot, four players who participated in Round Midnight. At the end of the tour, the band wiU wax a live album for Blue Note (the first Dexter Gordon album, not count- ing the two Round Midnight soundtracks, in five years). And after that? “I haven’t really thought too much about that,” says Dexter slowly, very slowly. “I’ve been thinking about getting myself back together, which I seem to have done. I’m in better shape than I was in four years ago. “I’m not really planning on getting back on the circuit and playing aU the joints. Mostly I’ll do concerts. But, you know, we just talked to Max Gordon [the owner of the Village Vanguard, where Dexter made his much-acclaimed 1976 “Homecom- ing”] and he wants us to come into the club. Basically, there will be very few clubs that we’ll be doing. But maybe we can do a special weekend later in the year at the Vanguard just to pay our respects. Because he did a lot for me, you know. When I came back from Europe in ’76, not too many people remembered me, and he gave me a shot. And it turned out fan- tastic.” And what about taking another ac- ting assignment? Certainly, the Academy Award nomination must have caused a couple of scripts to waft Dexter’s way. “Oh yes, no hesitation, as long as it’s in my bailiwick. It wouldn’t have to necessarily be a jazz musician. I don’t want to be typecast all my life. ’ ’ '^UBE-BOP-The amount of jazz ^ on TV is a joke, right? Right. This is a shame, right? Right. Slow- ly, however, some action is being taken, right? Right. Finally, Public Television (you taow, the guys who bring us tons of baUets and operas) is waking up to the much-abused, much- neglected art form called jazz. At least it’s happening here in New York. Last year, WNYC (Channel 31) gave us a Jazz Hot Summer, and they’re doing it again on Monday nights this summer. Now, the Big Daddy, WNET (Channel 13) has come around. Beginning July 2, Jazz Tonight will unspool every Thursday night for 18 weeks. Now the 11:00 p.m. airing time isn’t exactly prime time, but it does give you a chance to catch a set at a jazz club (or a Mets game) and be installed in your recliner just in time. T/\LENT T he Kinks/Joan Jett THE GREEK THEATRE, L.A.- Joan Jett’s appearance here sharing the bill with legendary British rockers the Kinks was like drinking a Coke before tasting an excellent champagne: Both are enjoyable in their own way, but you wish you’d tasted them on separate occasions. As with Coke and that other fizzy beverage, Jett’s style, with its heavy metal chum, is geared toward a younger, seemingly adolescent crowd, while the Kinks, a thinking man’s rock band whose songs are often laced with social and political statements, are a baby boomer’s band with age-defying appeal. The trouble at this Friday evening show was that Jett’s audience seemed far out numbered by older, yuppie- looking Kinks fans, who appeared to be about as excited about shouting “Yeah, Oh Yeah’’ at Joan’s bidding during “Do You Want to Touch” as cats are about swimming. Jett’s rabble- rousing efforts didn’t have the affect they could have - or should have. Musically, Epic’s Jett and her band flew in tight formation. Ricky Bird’s lead guitar churned with heavy metal intensity, as did Jett’s. Paul Harkins’ drums and Bret Cartwright’s bass were also in fine form. StUl, there was a cer- tain energy missing from the set, due partly to the band’s droning, electric guitar sound, and partly to Jett’s lack- luster performance style, which was mirth-free even during such uptempo, energetic shakers as the Stone’s “Star Star.” Tommy James and the Shondel- les’ “Crimson and Clover” was the Jett set’s high point, delivered with haunting poise. The evening took a sharp turn when MCA’s Kinks took over. Frontman Ray Davies proved himself a seasoned pro from the outset, when he, brother Dave Davies on lead guitar, Ian Gib- bons on keyboards, Jim Rodford on bass and Bob Henrit on drums, kicked into a highly-charged set that drew from material both ancient (1964’s “You Really Got Me”) and recent (tunes from their latest album, “Think Visual”), but never seemed to ride on laurels from the distant past. In fact, the refreshing thing about watching these British invasion originals per- form is that while one is conscious of their ’60’s Golden Oldies aspect, one never doubts for an instant that the creative energy that set them in motion more than 20 years ago has never ceased to fuel them. As lead singer and focal point for the band, Davies is a captivating, world-class rocker. His sly, gender- bending sexuality, a device used by many an English popster, seemed fresh. And the band’s rebellious. East End sensibility was as alive and genuine as could be, especially on this night, which happened to be the eve of Britain’s national election (which Davies admitted the band takes very seriously). Dave Davies’ guitar provided rol- licking, electrifying interludes to the entire show. Both Davies have con- siderable stage presence, and both brothers sing, but Dave’s primary con- tribution is that he, and a handful of other brash Englishman, play as if they invented the art of scintillating guitar riffs. They certainly redefined them, and Dave Davies played like an original during Friday’s show here. Traditional Kinks themes of pover- ty and national decay, of loneliness and political deceit - conveyed with equal parts ethos pathos - plus pensive, romantic ballads (such as the mes- merizing “Lost and Found”) aU mingled to form that rarity of rarities: a thoroughly captivating, thought provoking and high energized show. Gregory Dobrin GREAT DIRTY PLATINUM - CBS Records Canada band Gowan was visited after a recent Toronto show by CBS execs, who presented him with a gold album for Gowan’s “Great Dirty World” album. Pictured (i - r): Ray Daniels, Gowan’s mgr.; Bunny Freidus, sr vp, creative ops, CBS Int’l; and Gowan. W olf Trap Celebrates Dizzy Gil- lespie WOLF TRAP, VA-It was the headiest, most dazzling tribute to a single living jazz musician one could imagine. Dizzy Gillespie, who will turn 70 years old in October, was the centerpiece of a star-studded, jam-pack- ed Wolf Trap program that, despite its five-hour length, only scratched the sur- face of his incredible jazz career. PBS’ Great Performances, to its credit, was on hand to record the whole event-the concert, the rehearsals, the special American Zephyr train carrying Dizzy and company from New York to Washington, the works-but, no doubt, the program, which will air in the fall, won’t scratch the surface of the weekend. This review won’t scratch the surface of the concert. Chronologically, this is what hap- pened: Lalo Schifrin led a sensational big band (we’re talking sensational-the trumpet section was Wynton Marsalis, Freddie Hubbard, Jon Faddis, Jimmy Owens and Vaughn Nark!) in the “Fan- fare” and “Toccata” from his “GU- lespiana Suite.” Wynton, Benny Carter, J.J. Johnson, Hank Jones, Rufus Reid and Mickey Roker (with Dizzy on the sidelines) es- sayed “Groovin’ High” and “Birks Works.” Dizzy and Sonny Rollins (I!!!!!!), with the same rhythm section, un- corked smoking versions of “Wheat- leigh Hall” and “Stella By Starlight.” Dizzy and Sonny Rollins! Imagine! Dizzy and Carmen McRae teamed up for lovely and delicate versions of “Round Midnight” and, with Carmen at the piano, “A Beautiful Friendship.” Dizzy, James Moody, Jimmy Owens, Slide Hampton, Mike Longo, Chris White, and Charli Persip played “Con Alma” con alma. Mongo San- tamaria was added for a lush “Kush,” and Jon Hendricks joined Dizzy and Moody for a madcap scat “Oop-Pop-A- Da.” And then Marsalis, Hubbard, Faddis, Owens, Nark and Gillespie strutted their high-flyingest stuff for “Tour de Force.” Faddis, with a heavy dose of Louis Armstrong, took the honors. And that was the first half. The first half! And even the intermission had music-films of Dizzy and his ’40s big band, Di 2:zy and Charlie Parker, Dizzy and Louis Armstrong, and just plain Dizzy. The second half began with the Blues Alley Youth Orchestra, con- ducted by the honoree, scraping through ‘ ‘A Night in Tunisia. ’ ’ Dizzy and Oscar Peterson then in- spired each other to rare heights on a couple of duets: “All the Things You Are” and “Autumn Leaves.” Dizzy, Ignacio Berroa, Candido, Mongo, Nicky Marrerro, John Lee, Ed Cherry, Dave Valentin, Sam Rivers, Amie Lawrence, Jimmy Owens, and David Amram then bubbled-we’re talk- ing percolated-through a Cu-bop drenched “Tin Tin Deo. ’ ’ Then a funny thing happened: Flora Purim and Airto Moreira led a three- song set of their own. Dizzy didn’t par- ticipate, and his connection to it was, at best, a little hazy. And, to close, that beautiful big band, with all those percussionists, played “Things to Come,” “A Night in Tunisia,” “Olinga,” and, of course, ‘ ‘H appy B irthday . ’ ’ In case you’re wondering. Dizzy Gil- lespie, at the age of 69, played superbly throughout. The long concert, moreover, firmly established the wide- range of his talents and the long shadow of his influence-he is so much more, so very much more, than Charlie Parker’s straight man in the creation of bebop. Dizzy Gillespie is one of the dozen most important jazz musicians of all time. It was one hell of a night. Lee Jeske V ernon Reid’s Living Color CBGB, NY - Vernon Reid’s Living Color goes for a Zeppelinish brand of imperial bombast, the kind that works best when it’s bouncing off stadium walls. Though they mix it up with reg- gae, calypso, and funk, they still sound like an updated version of a kickin’ early- ‘70 ’s hard rock band. In concert (June 2d), they overpowered this small club, sounding not loud but big, far too big to remain unsigned for long. The clincher was “Desperate People,” which foreplayed like a Jour- ney song, got into some AC/DC chord- ing and Ozzy “Wicked World” Os- bourne vocals, and climaxed with Reid’s baroque guitar wizardry. For a generation informed by punk but raised on Zep, this was Johnny Lydon making peace with Jimmy Page at the wedding of Prince and Journey. The marriage works because Reid hears the link between generations; his guitar work is pure Hendrix without being retro, if one accepts the fact that Hendrix pretty much created metal and its latter-day mutations. After all, it’s not a long jump from “Purple Haze” to the guitar solo in “Beat It” or from “Crosstown Traffic” to Prince’s “Lady Cab Driver” and even AC/DC’s “You Shook Me All Night Long.” For a generation informed by punk but raised on Zep, this show was John Lydon making peace with Jimmy Page at the wedding ofPrince and Journey, Indeed, Living Color’s “Glamour Boys” may start off sounding like a great lost track from “1999,” but it’s powered by a progression straight from Clapton’s “After Midnight.” Though Reid uses reggae to get the song’s funk across, it rocks along basically genre- less, with loyalty only to the groove. The groove often became unstop- pable as when drummer Will Calhoun soloed with staggered rhythms and Muzz Skillings plucked along on bass. Vocalist Corey Glover meanwhile pounded the stage, jumped into the audience, screamed, and crooned for aU he was worth, proving himself a bet- ter showman than musician, with an onstage razzle dazzle that recalled both James Brown and Mick Jagger. Living Color’s got the chops and moves for a bigger stage, and in fact it might be more appropriate if the band’s next showcase were at Giants Stadium. Paul lorio Cash Box June 20, 1987 15

Capitol and Cinema Launch New Venture Paullorio Mazza Out, Licata In EMI America and Manhattan Merge By Stephen Padgett LOS ANGELES-The long-rumored dissolution of EMI America finally took place last week. Joe Smith, vice chairman of Capitol Industries-EMI, Inc., announced on Thursday (June 18), that EMI America Records would merge with Manhattan Records. The new label, now called EMI America/Manhattan Records, will be based in New York. Sal Licata, current- ly president of RCA-Ac&M-Arista Dis- tribution, has been named chief execu- tive officer and will report directly to Joe Smith. Bruce Lundvall, who headed Manhattan, will now become president of the new label, reporting to Licata. Licata told Cash Box that he expects to begin his new position sometime toward the middle of July. Jim Mazza, formerly president of EMI America, resigned his post and does not figure in the realignment. He is said to be pursuing “other interests’’ Plan Begins In ‘88 according to a statement. Lundvall was out of the office and could not be contacted. According to a company statement, his duties will be supervising the A&R and creative aspects of the new merged label, in- cluding the Blue Note jazz division. Sue Satriano, director, public rela- tions/communications for EMI Music, North America & Japan, told Cash Box that the futures of other EMI America executives and employees was still un- determined. “What has happened is that some people are being asked to move to New York,’’ she said, “some people will be needed here in L.A. in the newly combined label. And some will, hopefully, be assimilated into Capitol.’’ The fate of EMI America’s Sunset Blvd. headquarters is also not known. Abrams WASHINGTON - A system for peg- ging mechanical royalty fees for the next decade to the Consumer Price Index becomes official July 15th and will apply to records made on or around January 1, 1988. The system, accepted by The Copyright Royalty Tribunal and published in the June 15th Federal Register, is a result of negotiations that began more than six months ago among the Recording Industry Associa- tion of America, TJie National Music Publishers Association, and The Songwriters Guild of America. The plan gained the support of SESAC and Music Royalties, Inc. In essence, the measure calls on the C.R.T. to figure the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index every two years and to adjust the mechanical royalty rate accordingly. It also specifies that the adjusted rate shall be no greater than 25 per cent of the then- current fee, and no lower than the exist- ing fee. It also calls for the adjusted rate to be rounded to the nearest l/20th of a cent. The first change is to be based on the percentage difference between the Con- sumer Price Index published for December, 1985, and that published for September, 1987. Thereafter, the C.R.T. is required to use the Index published for September, 1987, and bi-annually to 1995 to deter- mine the percentage change, and to an- (continued on page 18) Atlantic To Begin Issuing Classic Jazz CDs NEW YORK-This week, Atlantic Records wiU release the first titles in an extensive reissue program of compact discs culled from its enormous and in- fluential jazz catalogue. 23 titles are due in June and July, with a projected 100 titles due by year’s end. Nesuhi Er- tegun, who produced many of the original sessions, is supervising the transfer to digital, with Ilhan Mimaroglu and Bob Porter active in the program. “We’re ver>' excited at the prospect of having these great recordings now available in the brilliant sound quality offered by the compact disc,’’ said Dave Glew, Atlantic’s executive vice president/general manager. The discs will include the original artwork and liner notes and, where possible, addi- tional tracks. CASH BOX JAZZ ALBUMS B opping AROUNi>=odds and ends, flotsam and jet- sam, kibbles and bits. ..Since we are right now smack dab in the middle of the WC/New York Jazz Festival (first reports due next week), it seems a good idea to mention that tickets are now on sale for the Newport Jazz Fes- tival. Now you need a genealogist to figure all of this out, of course, since the Newport Jazz Festival moved to New York in 1972 and has been there ever since: called, in order, the New- port Jazz Festival/New York, the Kool-Newport Jazz Festival/New York, the Kool Jazz Festival/New York and, as of last year, the JVC Jazz Festival/New York. (Why nobody ever thought to just call this the New York Jazz Festival I’ll never understand.) In any case, JVC, a few years back, began sponsoring jazz festivals, including one in, of course, Newport, Rhode Island. That, of course, is called the JVC Jazz Fes- tival-Newport though, as all jazz buffs know, the Newport Jazz Fes- tival is the JVC Jazz Festival/New York. Got it? Forget it. In any case, the weekend event in Newport is set for August 15 and 16 this year and will feature Nancy Wilson, Stanley Jordan, Kenny G, the Crusaders and Wynton Marsalis on day one, and George Benson, Branford Mar- I salis, Dianne Reeves, Michael Brecker and the Dizzy Gillespie Big Band on day two. ONJAZZ^^m The JVC/New York Jazz Festival Day-by-Day, Part One: F riday-The JVC/New York Jazz Festival started off this year like it starts off every year-with hot dogs at Gracie Mansion (that’s the official home of our scandal-ridden mayor). Nathan’s did not supply the wieners this year, a big mistake. Officially, things got under way (as they always do) with the first of the one-hour piano recitals at Weill (formerly Carnegie) Recital Hall. Marian McPartland had the lead- off spot and she played a pretty, florid hour that mixed a couple of rhythmic swingers into the balladic brew. Carnegie Hall, two hours later, was the site for some vocal muscle-flex- ing from Sarah Vaughan and Bobby McFerrin (separately, of course). La Vaughan sang a no-nonsense set of ballads-the voice magnifique, naturalmente, the phrasing perfec- tion. McFerrin did his delightful solo thing—a couple of haunting jazz stand- ards, a couple of wordless improvised explorations, and such items as “The Beverly Hillbillies Theme’’ and his capsulized version of The Wizard of Oz. The audience, mostly Vaughan’s crowd, was on its feet screaming. Next year, they’ll buy tickets to see McFerrin alone (which, in jazz terms, is known as building an audience). Then Miles Davis, the grand old man of fusion, shared an Avery Fisher Hall bill with Kenny G, the new superstar of fusion, and there were some surprises. First of all, Miles’ band was surprisingly tight and funky-saxophonist Kenny Gar- rett, guitarist Joe McCreary, and drummer Ricky Weldman are wel- come new members, and the band was more cohesive than any Davis unit since his comeback. However, old Miles hardly played at all, and when he did it was the tired “Human Nature’’ and “Time After Time” (after time, after time, after time...). The other surprise was Kenny G, who’s got some serious soprano sax chops, though his music ain’t meaty enough (maybe he should have played with Miles’s band). Saturday-Town Hall hosted a double bill of the World Saxophone Quartet, which played, without ques- tion, the best set I’ve ever heard them play (and that’s saying a lot); and Branford Marsalis, who, with a quartet including ex-Wyntonians Kenny Kirkland and Jeff Watts, played watered-down John Coitraneisms that were boring at best. Sunday-A Carnegie Hall evening with the Modern Jazz Quartet is al- ways an enticement, and, during the second half of the show, it was clear why: the MJQ is still one of the most musical small bands in jazz, and they played a model set of blues and stand- ards and John Lewis tunes. During the first half of the show, the MJQ was joined by the New York Cham- ber Symphony for the Lewis pieces that sound so good on “Three Win- dows” (Atlantic), but sounded so dull -I in the flesh. 2 Monday-A solo piano concert, at the Recital Hall, with old Sun Ra, who dug into his roots for some mossy blues, heady stride piano, fril- ly romanticism, thunderous avant crashes and all sorts of other things. It was an expansive, let’s say Arkestral, performance. George Shearing then presided over a Town Hall concert called “Musical ‘Amusements’ of Chef George,” that was broken into three sets: dixieland, piano duo and bebop. The dixieland set was spirited and in- fectious, thanks to the fine players on hand (Kenny Davern, Warren Vache, George Masso, Slam Stewart and Oliver Jackson) and the leader’s cheerful good humor. The set of piano duets with Hank Jones was musical, but not that successful (their styles didn’t really come together). The bebop set-with Dizzy Gillespie, Jimmy Heath, Eddie Gomez and Jimmy Cobb-was some- thing of a mess. GOlespie’s chops were off, and Shearing ain’t a bebop pianist. Heath, Gomez and Cobb, however, got some good hcks in. Tuesday-Dick Hyman-that walk- ing repository of jazz piano styles- played an inspired hour of Irving Berlin tunes (inspired, somewhat, by the death the previous day of Fred Astaire). The tunes were mostly from the ’10s, ’20s and ’30s-eras that are right in Hyman’s rag- time/stride/swing wheelhouse, and the hour purred. And then the eagerly-awaited “Or- nette In All Languages” program at Town Hall that was, almost, worth the wait. The problem was that the concert was too short. The set with the “original Quartet” (which saw Ed Blackwell, the real original drum- mer, replacing Billy Higgins, who replaced Blackwell shortly before the band came to New York in ’59) was only 45 minutes long. It was brilliant and, surprise of surprises, they not only played Ornette’s lovely new music, but they whipped “Lonely ’Woman” and “The Sphinx” out of their memory banks. Ornette has moved on to other things, of course, but his collaboration with Don Cher- ry, Charlie Haden and either Hig- gins or Blackwell is too good not to continue, even sporadically. Prime Time, the other things, played the first set of the concert and Ornette seems to be coohng them down-the set was filled with high- flying funk rhythms and zipping electric basses and guitars, but the music was subtler, less frenetic than in recent years. Again, the set was too short-there’s nothing like listen- ing to Prime Time smacking you in the ears for a couple of hours. The closer was a combined Prime Time/Quartet blow-out on “Theme From a Symphony” that was just as you’d imagine it-spewing rhythms like some kind of harmolodic vol- cano. Afterwards, at a post-concert party, I complimented Ornette on the con- cert and new album. ‘ ‘It was a good idea, wasn’t it?” he asked. CB—When had you finalized your decision to to ahead with the merger? Smith-It had been discussed over a period of time, I guess over a period of two years they had been thinking of doing something like that. When we got here in February we let everything remain in place but it soon became clear, to me anyhow, and anybody in management, that it didn’t work well. We had this promotion force out there, both pop and black music, being directed from two sides. The priorities got mixed up. We ran into some tremendous collisions where David Bowie vis a vis Robbie Nevil, Richard Marx and John Waite, things that were happening out there and we had no con- trol. The geography didn’t work well. Here we had enough artists, a really solid artist roster to make one great company, and here was Manhattan who was doing very well breaking new acts—Richard Marx, Nevil, Glass Tiger, a few others-but a long haul to really get in there with no catalog to back them up. When we merge them we have the enormous United Artists agreement with EMI America. The deal includes such artists as George Thorogood and the Destroyers (three times gold for EMI America), the Neville Brothers ( whose recently released LP is in a critical stage of its promotion according to Rounder) and the True Believers (whose record is ready to be released pending comple- tion of artwork, a problem exacerbated by the dissolution of the west coast of- fice). “Bruce Lundvall called this morn- ing,’’ said Marian Leighton, president and co-owner/founder of Rounder, last Wednesday (June 24). “Everyone has been very cordial, very supportive, wanting to get things moving along. But right now, it’s so transitional, I don’t think anybody on either end has any answers to just exactly how it is going to function day to day,’’ she added. According to Leighton, Rounder ex- pects to continue its relationship with the new company. “We like the brief contact we’ve had with the new people at the company,’’ she said, and is glad that the overall bureaucracy of the new label is basically small, similar to EMI America. catalog, the Liberty, the Imperial catalogs, and along with that you add the Blue Note, and now you’ve got a catalog company. Plus, you’re adding George Thorogood and Pet Shop Boys, and David Bowie and a whole bunch of other artists to the mix. Now you’ve got a real up and going record com- pany that can afford the services that each one of them alone could not af- ford. Now you can really give yourself some meat, where each company split. It’s just a business judgment that it doesn’t work well with two. When Warners put together Warner, Elektra and Atlantic, they bought three com- panies. They had bought Warner Bros., it was already running. They bought At- lantic which was already miming. And then they bought Elektra which was al- ready miming. Here, we started two of these labels from nothing. EMI America and Manhattan. And so they have never really matured as yet into two full blown labels. And the wait was going to be a long one. And so this just made sense, it’s not hurting anybody. All of the artists have the same promotional representation out there that they always did. It’s not a case of us throwing all this product out. They were working on all these artists anyhow. CS-When you made Thursday’s an- nouncement, how soon before that had you decided to do the merger? Smith-We had finally closed the situa- tion with Sal Licata just a couple of days before that and were not able to announce it, for RCA’s own reasons, they asked us not to announce it, imtil that Thursday. The speculation was on. Anytime you start the planning of something like this, a lot of people know about it, and then all the rumors started for six or seven weeks. But, there was no way for us to shortcut that process. We had identified the man we wanted, Licata, and we had to now wait until he could get clear. Cfi-Was there any pressure on you to hurry up your decision as a result of the rumors that had escalated in the last few weeks? Smith-I would have loved to have done this the moment the first rumor hit. It was impossible to do, so we had to live with it. The pressure, of course. It was self-imposed pressure. You can’t let people hang like that. It was affecting everything. Artists were call- ing, and nervous about whether their records were going to come out. To everybody’s credit, they kept it going. The John Waite and Nona Hendryx records look terrific. Bowie had a hit single all during this period and another big AOR record. Everybody hung in there. And they’re still hanging in there, only Jack Sattcr has moved into national promotion, Gerry Griffith has moved into A&R, and Sari Becker has taken over press, and all these department heads, they’re all out here this week, meeting everybody and look- ing into these projects and reviewing what we’ve got on the boards here. C/J-Another rumor that we’ve been hearing is that president of Capitol Don Zimmerman’s job might be in jeopar- dy. Any truth? Smith-No, no. No- CB-Aie, there any oi in the works? Smith-It’s possible (lauglu,). can talk about now. I’ll .va rumors to start. CJ5-Whcn you came to Car’’* January, it was one of your expressed purposes to improve Capitol’s north American market share. Are you meet- ing your objectives? Smiths think so. We’ve had a rcmtrk- able jump. But I’m not kidding myself Some of that’s attributable to the Beatles. But everybody takes credit for whatever they sell, so I shouldn’t be ashamed of it. Whatever you sell, you seU. But, no, we’ve had a remarkable jump. You can’t do that quickly. What you can do is make a better record company. And the rest fol- lows. I think anybody whose been ob- serving this business feels that Capitol is a much stronger label than it was four months ago. It’s a player out there now. In the talent market it’s very ag- gressive in promotion and marketing. And that’s with the infusion of a few new people. And there’s a great new feeling about Capitol Records. I think the same feeling is starting to hit Man- hattan and EMI, certainly—I’ve been working out of EMI for the last couple of days—those pieople are really pumped about the new feeling. We’ve now removed the clouds, and here’s a very positive motivating guy, Licata, coming in. And Lundvall remains and he’s a beloved and a very effective talent guy. I think its a terrific team and I hope it works out well. And then the talent flows and then the records go. But the first thing is to build a structure. CB—Was former EMI America presi- dent Jim Mazza ever given anything like an ultimatum to perform? Smith-No, no. I had a meeting with EMI people, not with Mazza there, but with everybody there, and explained to them that the clock was ticking here, and that there had been a sentiment to move ahead with this and it had been going on for some time. But I would have preferred not to do it if things went well and it looked like it could work. It just became clear to me after that that it was never going work really well. And we just had to bite the bullet and do this. Cfi-Would a better performance out of Bowie, Wolf and Hendyrx have cauterized the hemorrhage and saved EMI America? Smith-Nah, I don’t think so. You’re still talking about a structure that is not efficient and doesn’t work well. And that would be with Bowie and Hendryx and anybody else selling twice as many records. CB-Wc had heard that Bowie needed to do a minimum five million? Smith-No, not at all. I think I passed that in a remark, you know, ‘Gecz, if Bowie had sold five million albums, maybe we’d have been ok.’ But that’s a lot of pressure to put on David Bowie, or anylxxiy.
