iPROFiLES ROCKLINE: Six Years And Still Gain’ Strong In the world of syndicated rock adio, one show has continued to ;et the precedent for all that have ollowed, Global Satellite Network’s lockline. The show, presented by ^BC Radio Networks, recently celebrated its sixth successful year )n the air. Rockline has certainly carved the mold for similar-styled chone in radio shows, and has ijarnered a reputation for consistent- ly booking the top acts in rock and oil today. Recently, Cash Box spoke to Bob Soburn, the show’s host, and Cindy Tollin, producer of Rockline and Operations Manager of the Global |5atellite Networks. The two dis- icussed the program’s past, present und future; the responsibility of put- ling out a a live, weekly, syndicated ;how; and what has made Rockline successfully survive in a sea of syn- ficated radio. Global Satellite Net- vork has evolved itself as quite a lorce in the radio industry, currently hey deliver three high quality week- y satellite delivered programs in ad- iition to Rockline, "Power Cuts,’’ Reelin’ In The Years,” and ‘‘Let "he Good Times Roll.” When Rockline first hit the air- vaves, air personality B. Mitchell ^eed served as host, but was orced to resign due to failing lealth. Shortly thereafter, Reed Dassed away. Coburn remembers ind acknowledged his predecessor ... he always served as a mentor 0 me. He was somebody that I lighly respected - he really taught ne a lot about how to handle nyself on the air. I’ve tried to carry )n in his steps ... ” Coburn em- chasized his love for his job, "It’s he most fun thing that 1 do, I really injoy doing the program. It’s terrific 0 meet the artists who make the nusic, and let’s face it, it’s a thrill to ce on over 160 radio stations at )nce. There’s nothing like it ...” Tol- n couldn’t be happier working with ;)oburn on the show, she ex- cressed, ‘‘ ... he, himself has be- come a star. People look at him as he ‘Rockathorian,’ they ask him all hese questions about all the dif- erent bands. He generates tons of an mail ... ” She continued, explain- ng the show’s continued appeal. Rockline has built a very, very oyal listening audience of people vho, we believe, tune in every Mon- iay night whether they know who’s in or not because they like the .how, they like Bob Coburn and hey way he does interviews - as do ill the artists which is why we con- sider him our greatest asset.” The audience are not the only ines loyal to the show, Tollin ex- ilained, "We pride ourselves on the fact that every artist that has ap- peared on Rockline has always come back or has always said they will come back, which means ob- viously, that everyone’s really pleased.” Why is such a feat so im- portant to the most successful phone-in program on the air? " ... if we didn’t have repeat business we would be out of business - because there are not 52 new superstars every year. It has become almost automatic, from the point of the management company and the record label, that when an artist puts out a new album they’ll do Rockline it’s just a matter of which Monday night are they going to do it.” Global has maintained success- ful business relationships and they owe a great debt to that gift. Said Tollin, "We have the reputation with management and labels so they all know we’re- out to make everybody look good - so everybody wins. The artist wins because they have a really fun time doing something that the record company and the management company love ... it’s tough to get some artists to do any type of interviews.” Cindy Tollin & Bob Coburn Although geared towards the AOR listener. Rockline offers a wide appeal to nearly all demo- graphics, each show is presented in a slick, well produced, entertaining package - accessible to nearly every listener, "We are the only program that goes out live all over to the United States and Canada. So we literally cover all of North America.” Tollin continued, "We primarily hit the major market AOR radio stations but we also have in smaller markets a lot of what we call contemporary stations, theoreti- cally they are the only CHR in the market so they can rock out as much as they want to. We are heard on everi^hing from hip A/C to CHR to AOR to Classic Rock sta- tions. We program many shows featuring ‘crossover* artists, i.e. Huey Lewis, Genesis, Bryan Adams, etc. Our program is definite- ly rock radio - no question about it.” "To me it’s easy to believe it’s been six years (on the air) because Rockline has become such an in- stitution that it’s hard to believe that we haven’t been on the air for sixty years!” She continued, "On the other hand, sometimes I think to myself ‘52 Monday nights a year for six years’ - it’s a personal statement for me and what I’ve been doing with my life! It has become such a mainstay that it’s hard to remember a time when Rocklined\6n'\ exist.” “We were first, we had a head start. But I don’t think that would have helped us if we weren’t really good at what we were doing. ’’ Rockline has continually re- mained successful due to a team ef- fort according to both Tollin and Coburn. She emphasized the team- work at Global as she stated, "I think it’s everybody involved in put- ting together Rockline. Bob Coburn is the best at what he does, and I think that the artists absolutely adore him. We are a full service net- work, we don’t just produce shows, we personally deal with every one of our affiliates for every one of our programs ... We have a winning show, radio stations have a winning show, listeners have something they look forward to and love to lis- ten to, the artists have fun which makes the labels and management happy and they promote the heck out of the record. We were first, we had a head start. But I don’t think that would have helped us if we weren’t really good at what we were doing. onjAzzmmm The JVC/New York Jazz Festival Day-by-Day, Part Two: EDNESDAY-Kenny Barron had the solo slot at Weill Recital Hall, va- cated at the last minute by an ailing Dave McKenna. Barron played rollicking versions of standards, everything un- derpinned by a nicely percussive left hand and a scintillatingly effective right Good stuff. Ella Fitzgerald, who hadn’t per- formed in a year (she’s had heart trouble), had the main slot at Avery Fisher Hall and she turned up in good voice and, obviously, quite strong. She did two sets and they were swing- ing, no two ways about it. Ella’s voice isn’t what it once was—she’s 69, folks-but she is in tune and, when she scats the bejeezers out of “Flying Home,” there’s no question that the woman belongs on a concert stage. After several erratic performances a few years ago, Ella turned in her third fine JVC/New York performance in a row. THURSDAY-Cedar Walton had the Weill slot and he played a pretty hour, but it was too pretty. Even a medley of Monk tunes was too pret- ty, too impressionistic. I waited for Cedar to bop out, but he never did. Joe Williams, Nancy Wilson and the Count Basie Orchestra were the headliners at Carnegie later that night, but, oy, where there problems. First of all, the amplified sound at Carnegie Hall, which stunk all week, was at its stinkiest-at times it was al- most like a mime show. That aside, I thought Nancy Wilson was going to avow herself of the opportunity to sing some jazz with the Basie Band. She didn’t-she avowed herself of the opportunity to sing some pop schmaltz with her own band (and string section) and then to bring out Carl Anderson for some pop schmaltz duets. Then, with time a-wasting, Frank Foster led the Basie Band through a full six numbers, including two by the band’s vocalist, Carmen Brad- ford. Were there not enough vocalists on this bill? By the time Joe Williams hit the stage, there was about a half-hour of concert left. What he sang sounded okay (what you could hear of it)-he and that band are still a supreme combination- but it was over too fast. He didn’t do “Every Day” and he didn’t do “Cherry Red,” which he had even promised some loudmouth in the audience. I then slid over to Avery Fisher for Ray Charles. Ray turned in a good set-Ray usually (but certainly not al- ways) turns in a good set. How he can still sing “I Can’t Stop Loving You” and “Georgia On My Mind” with such feeling, such, well, soul, I’ll never understand. But who wants to unders tand—owwwwww! FRIDAY-Mel Torme is always on the New York Jazz Festival. Always. Usually he’s paired with some com- bination of George Shearing and/or Gerry Mulligan. On this night, at Carnegie and called “A Grand Night for Singing,” he was joined by Diane Schuur, Lonette McKee, the Mel Lewis Orchestra and Stan Getz. It was a jam-packed, but quite good, concert. Mel was in good voice. Diane was not only in good voice, but she seems to be shaving some of her tendency to oversing from her perfor- mances (and, backed by the Lewis Band and Getz, she had some first- class accompaniment). McKee was in good voice, but she’s a Broadway belter, not a jazz singer. (She was good as Lena Horne in “The Cotton Club” because, as a singer, she resembles Home.) The Lewis Or- chestra, by itself and behind all of the singers, was in good instrument. A good concert. SATURDAY-Roger Kellaway made like Keith Jarrett and played a numbingly boring, pretentious hour of neo-classical noodling at the Reci- tal Hall. Yawn. Ruben Blades turned in a solid two-plus-hour concert at Carnegie that featured excellent singing, excel- lent streamlined salsa playing from Seis del Solar (actually Siete del Solar), and genuine emotion, anger and concern. Not only did Blades sing about injustice, racism and the serious problems of Latin America, but he made sure everybody had English translations so that us gringos in the crowd would not just sit there and groove to the music—and it was music to groove to-but would under- stand as well. I hope Ruben doesn’t decide to become president of Panama, he’s too good a musician. And good musicians always make more of a mark on the world than leaders of countries. I closed the night at Merkin Con- cert Hall, where an ambitious series called “Improvisations” (co-spon- sored by the World Music Institute) was coming to a close. Craig Harris and Tailgater’s Tales was who I heard, and I liked what I heard quite a bit. Harris is a splendid trombone player with a burly sound (he plays the trombone like it’s a trombone, not as obvious an observation as you’d think) and this updated dixieland in- strumentation (Don Byron on clarinet, E.J. Allen on trumpet, An- thony Cox on bass and Pheeroan Ak Laff on drums) is an excellent vehicle for his wide-ranging writing, which, like most good jazz writing, looks forwards and backwards at once. SUNDAY-Hank Jones was the sub- ject of a Town Hall concert called “The World of Hank Jones” and it’s about time. Ask any jazz fan for a short list of favorite pianists and Hank Jones’s name is on it nine times out of ten. Yet Hank has spent his career quite quietly-he’s never really made a name for himself as a leader, but his playing is always superb and always improves any band he’s in. Here he was featured in numerous set- tings: from solo (fantastic) to duo (with George Mraz and Kenny Bar- ron) to trio (with Eddie Gomez and Keith Copeland) to quartet (the trio plus Frank Wess) to various sextets, septets and octets (with a revolving cast of hom players-Al Cohn, Urbie Green, Joe Wilder and Wess-and Marvin “Smitty” Smith, Ray Drummond and Rodney Jones), to backing two singers, Jackie Paris and Bob Stewart. It was a low- keyed, elegant and exceptionally musical concert. NEWS UNIVERSALELTON-MCA recording artist Elton John celebrated his return to the label and new release, ‘ ‘Elton John Live In Australia with the Melbourne Sym- phony Orchestra ” by holding a press conference on the Universal Studios lot recently. Shown afterwards (l-r): James Newton Howard (arranger and conductor for Australian concerts), Bemie Taupin (songwriting partner), John Reid (John s manager), Elton John, MCA' s Irving Azoff (president, MCA Music Entertainment Group), Richard Palmese (executive vice president, marketing and promotion), Jheryl Busby (executive vice president artist acquisition and development), and Larry Solters (senior vice president, artist development). Former Elektra Mrktng & Promo Head Bone To Replace Craigo As Chrysalis President NEW YORK - Mike Bone has been named president of Chrysalis Records, replacing Jack Craigo, it was learned this week. Bone most recently served Elektra Records as senior vice presi- dent of marketing and promotion. It is not known whether Craigo left volun- tarily or was relieved of his duties. Reasons for the change were unan- nounced, and representatives at Chrysalis had no comment at press time. R.I.A.A. Backs DAT Scanner LOS ANGELES-The Recording In- dustry Association of America (R.I.A.A.) announced plans to better ac- quaint recording industry executives with the copy-code scanner technol- ogy. Scanner requirements in Digital Audio Tape (DAT) machines are part of proposed in legislation now in com- mittee on Capitol hill. Demonstrations of the copy-code system developed by CBS Records Technology Labs will take place for in- dustry executives in Nashville on July 21, in Los Angeles on July 23 and in New York on July 28. The system is scheduled for an im- partial testing by the National Bureau of Standards. Members of Congress have asked that equipment manufac- turers refrain from importing DAT machines and that recording companies refrain from encoding product until a legislative decision has been reached. Marantz, a maker of DAT machines, has already pledged to begin introduc- ing DAT into the U.S. in October. Critics have said there is audible sound degradation in the copy-code scanner system. The demonstrations in the R.I.A.A. offices are meant, in part, to show this criticism to be groundless. BMI SALUTES HANCOCK — Herbie Hancock, the award-winning composer/in- strumentalist, was recently saluted by the international music press at a party hosted by BMI. Pictured here with BMI pres and CEO Frances Preston and Han- cock are (l - r): Branford Marsalis; Tony Reedus; Darius Brubeck, (obscured), James Williams, Dave Brubeck, Bob Cranshaw, George Coleman, Jimmy Owens, George Shearing, Herbie Hancock, Frances W. Preston, Harold Mabern, Lionel Hampton, Donald Byrd, Buster Williams, Bob Brookmeyer, and Tony Williams. Seeks Injunction, $50 Million Songwriter Sues Lionel Richie LOS ANGELES-Michael Frenchik, a Los Angeles-based songwriter, has filed a $50 million lawsuit against Lionel Richie claiming that Richie’s song “Dancing On The Ceiling’’ was an infringement of his copyright. According to Frenchik, Carlos Rios, an employee of Richie and the law firm of Manatt, Phelps, Rothenberg, Tunney & Phillips, also named in the suit, un- duly influenced him to relinquish authorship rights in his original musi- cal work to Richie for inadequate com- pensation. The law firm, according to Frenchik, represented both himself and Rios, knowing their interests were ad- verse to each other. Frenchik claims that a demo tape of his song was given to Rios in Decem- ber, 1984 and that Rios “appropriated said musical composition without Plaintiff’s lawful authority, right, title or license and converted” his song over to Rios, Richie and Richie’s publishing company, Brockman Music. Richie released “Dancing On The Ceiling” in July 1986, and, according to the suit, did not credit Frenchik for writing the song. Frenchik seeks an injunction enjoin- ing the defendants from further dis- tribution of “Dancing On The Ceil- ing,” $50 million for copyright infr- ingement, unfair competition and con- version and a full accounting of all defendants’ profits. Named as co-defendants in the law- suit are Richie, Brockman Music, Motown Records (Richie’s label), Rios, Jody E. Graham (an attorney with Manatt, et al) and Manatt, Phelps, Rothenberg, Tunney & Phillips. A Guide To The New Music Seminar Shows By PauIIorio NEW YORK - When Mark Joseph- son called this year’s New Music Semi- nar “a music festival,” he wasn’t kid- ding. Josephson, an NMS director, helped shape this year’s Seminar around performances by over 250 acts. In many ways, these shows mean more than the panel discussions taking place this week at the Marriott Marquis Hotel (13 - 15). A wide variety of music is scheduled, and nearly every genre is represented, from rap and ska to country and rock. As might be ex- pected with an event of this size, there are a few glaring omissions. For ex- ample, Tim Beme, wrongly excluded from Columbia’s recent JVC show- case, should have been given a hearing at NMS. And bands such as Sonic Youth, The Young Fresh Fellows, The Feelies, and others should also have been featured. But, overall, the choice of bands is superb and the amount of talent is stag- gering; you won’t be able to attend a single show without missing another one that’s just as good. This guide is a semi-hopeless attempt at simplifying matters. MONDAY, JULY 13. TOP SHOWS: Two shows stand out: Homestead’s showcase at CBGBs and Relativity’s at Nirvana. The former includes performances by Phan- tom Tollbooth, Live Skull, Salem 66, Big Dipper, and others. Live Skull, a particularly hot live act, and the other I bands can be sampled on a new Homes- tead compilation called “The Wailing Ultimate.” Relativity’s show features Scruffy The Cat, Thelonious Monster, Bleached Black, and The Brandos. Best bet is Scruffy, whose second album, “Tiny Days,” translates well on stage. Vernon Reid’s Living Color, the pride of the Black Rock Coalition, per- forms at 1018 with hardcore bands the (continued on page 11) POST-CONCERTCELEBRATION-As part of an extensive 35th Anniversary in- ternational tour, Atlantic recording group The Modern Jazz Quartet recently gave a concert at New York’s Carnegie Hall. The concert coincided with the release oj The MJQ’s latest album, “Three Windows,” which marks the group’ s return to the Atlantic label after a 13-year hiatus. Following the show, Atlantic Records and WEA International hosted a celebration in honor of the MJQ at the Russian Tea Room. Shown toasting the legendary quartet' s 35th anniversary and continued suc- cess are (l-r): Atlantic vice president of creative marketing services Mark Schul- man, The MJQ’s manager Monte Kay, and The MJQ’s Percy Heath, Connie Kay, Milt Jackson, and John Lewis. 6 Cash Box July 18, 198 --

Nippon Columbia Co. ( Ltd., Tokyo, Japar rh ANNIVERSARY PETER ERSKINE COMBINES ELECTRONICAND ACOUSTIC SOUNDS ON HIS NEWDENON CD. He's a veteran of Weather Report, Weather Update, and Steps Ahead. He's played extensively with the likes of Maynard Ferguson and Stan Kenton. He's drummer/composer Peter Erskine and his latest CD, "Transition" is his first on the Denon label. Erskine told us that "Transition" is a live direct-to-2-track digital recording. "The advantage of going direct is a subtle one. There's an element of excitement and risk. You capture much more of the live perfor- mance quality' When we commented that Denon has been recording digitally longer than any other label, Peter nodded. "The first digital recording I ever bought was a Denon classical sampler. I think it was in 197^ on my second trip to Japan." We asked Erskine about the players on "Transition." "It's a marvelous band— John Abercrombie and Marc Johnson, Joe Lovano, Bob Mintzer" he enthused. "We have Don Grolnickand Kenny Werner on keyboards, and Peter Gordon sitting in on french horn. I can't say enough good things about the musicians and Vince Mendoza, who did some of the arranging." "I think we represent the jazz tradition quite well. But to me, the music sounds like something new. The album sounds like itself." Peter reflected for a moment. "The most important thing for a musician is to play the music that he hears inside of himself" he said. "And Denon encourages that 100%." In jazz and classical, the important new music is on Denon. As it should be. DENON The first name in digital recording. DENON SUPRAPHON Interface. ON JAZZ VC REFLECTTONS-I would say that, on the whole, the 1987 JVC/New York Jazz Festival was a success. I know it was a commercial success, but, on le whole, I believe it was an artistic uccess as well. The “on the whole” usiness refers to two things: the atro- ious amplified sound in Carnegie lall, and the problems for a jazz fes- val that insists on using such halls in le first place. That aside, the rogramming was somewhat more im- ginative than in years past (yes larah Vaughan and Mel Torme osted Carnegie Hall shows again, but ith Bobby McFerrin and Diane Ichuur on their respective bills; thus iuilding an audience for the younger ingers from the audience for the ilder singers). The idea of musical etrospectives (Ornette Coleman euniting his original Quartet, Dizzy jSillespie heading up a big band, George Shearing and Hank Jones Presiding over musical auto- biographies) worked well-audiences :ame and the concerts were well- lone. And the use of the World vJusic Institute’s “Improvisations” series to bring some more adven- uresome jazz to the Festival was :ound (as was the sound, and the am- bience, in Merkin Concert Hall, vhere the “Improvisations” series ook place and where more JVC con- certs should be planned in the future). Hiat’s all. Not a perfect jazz festival- md still not a “festival” in the festive ways of such festivals as those held tnnually in New Orleans, Nice, and nany other locales- but a solid one lonetheless. PARTY ALL THE TIME-One hing that did return at this year’s Fes- ival was the party-record companies, rnd others, throwing little celebra- ions for their artists. Most elaborate was BMI’s Tavern on the Green unch for Herbie Hancock, which 'eatured-along with the food, drink rnd speeches-some jamming from he likes of Hancock, Lionel Hampton, Donald Byrd and Jimmy Owens. Second most elaborate was Atlantic’s Russian Tea Room bash complete with blini table) for the Modern Jazz Quartet-a classy party (or a classy ensemble. Least ela- borate was Caravan of Dreams’ Cen- :ury Cafe party for Ornette Coleman-sort of a harmolodic party. And I can’t speak for the Columbia party at the NYU club, having not been there (scheduling conflicts, you know), but I’m sure it was a killer. Welcome back to jazz, largesse. OJCDs-Lots of jazz reissue com- pact discs coming out-lots and lots- and I’m trying to keep up with them all (but I’m not complaining). MCA pushed up their CD-only-twofers June release to August, and RCA pushed up its CD-only Bluebird release to the same month, but Atlan- tic’s finally come around on the CD stick, and Columbia has just rolled out some more Jazz Masterpieces. But let us not forget the indies, espe- cially the biggest, baddest jazz indie of them all-Fantasy. They’re becom- ing increasingly more bullish on CD; case in point-Original Jazz Classics CDs. Now these are like the Original Jazz Classic LPs, in that they list for a couple of bucks less than the regular Fantasy CDs and they are drawn from the vaults of Prestige, Riverside, Milestone, Contemporary and Fan- tasy and feature original artwork, liner notes, etc. (unlike the LPs, though, they do include an extra track here and there). Hot off the presses (do CDs come hot off the presses?) are “Milt Jackson Quartet,” Miles Davis’s “Dig” and “Collector’s Items,” “Clifford Brown Me- morial,” Eric Dolphy’s “Outward Bound,” “Thelonious Monk Plays Duke Ellington,” “Thelonious Monk & Sonny Rollins,” Rollins’s “Moving Out” and “The Sound of Sonny,” Bill Evans’s “New Jazz Conceptions,” Coleman Hawkins’s “The Hawk Flies High,” Art Blakey’s “Caravan,” Dave Bru- beck’s “Jazz at Oberlin” and “Jazz at the College of the Pacific,” Tadd Dameron’s “Fontainebleau,” Abbey Lincoln’s “Abbey is Blue,” “Red Garland’s Piano,” John Coltrane’s “Settin’ the Pace” and “Traneing In,” Wes Montgomery’s “Wes Montgomery Trio” and “So Much Guitar!,” “King Pleasure Sings/Annie Ross Sings,” Paul Gon- salves’s “Genin’ Together,” Lucky Thompson’s “Lucky Strikes,” Gene Ammons’s “Blue Gene,” Benny Carter’s “Jazz Giant,” “Vince Guaraldi Trio,” “The Cannonball Adderley Sextet In New York,” Chet Baker’s “Chet” and “Barney Kessel Plays Standards.” Great sound on them all, too. In other Fan- tasy news, Richie Cole has just signed with Milestone, Barney Kessel has resigned with Contemporary, Frank Morgan is in the midst of his first European tour and Sonny Rollins is, finally, set to release a new album: “G-Man,” due later this summer. r Tl—1 wm n MEDITATION - Antonio Carlos Jobim (seated , l) was recently at NY's Record Plant mixing his forthcoming Verve album, “Passarim,” in the company of (l - r) Richard Seidel, vp, PolyGram jazz; Jacques Morelen- baum, co-producer ; and studio owner Roy Cicala. LIKE A VIRGIN-Yep, another jazz festival to report on. The Virgin Islands Jazz Festival will swing the Is- lands of St. Thomas, St. Croix and St. John, August 10-16. Dizzy Gillespie, Freddie Hubbard, Gary Bartz, Richie Cole, Bobby Hutcherson and Paul Horn will be on hand and a note to P.O. Box 6201, St. Thomas, V. I. 00801 (or a call to [809] 776- 2874) will bring details. ON JAZZ VSOParty - Herbie Hancock was the guest of honor at a recent BMI party at New York's Tavern-On-The-Green. Here, hanging out on the patio with BMI pres and ceo Frances Preston, are some of the musicians who turned out: (I - r) Branford Marsalis, Tony Reedus, James Williams, Dave Brubeck, Bob Cran- shaw, George Coleman, Jimmy Owens, George Shearing, Hancock, Preston, Harold Mabern, Lionel Hampton, Donald Byrd, Buster Williams, Bob Brook- meyer, and Tony Williams. C lassic, live - “Classi- cal Jazz” is the name of Lin- coln Center’s first concert series devoted exclusively to jazz and, needless to say, it’s high time. August 3-5 are the dates and Wynton Marsalis is the artistic adviser. The breakdown is like this: “Ladies First-A Tribute to the Great Ladies of Jazz,” with Betty Carter, Janis Siegel, Sasha Daltonn, Carrie Smith and Marian McPartland and others (8/3); “A Tribute to The- lonious Monk,” with Carmen McRae, Barry Harris, Walter Davis, Sphere and others (8/4); and“Bird Night-A Tribute to Char- lie Parker,” with Tommy Flan- agan, Jay McShann, Hank Jones, Charles McPherson, Frank Mor- gan, Vi Redd, Percy Heath, Red Rodney, Billy Higgins and Roy Haynes (8/5). The series is presented in association with WBGO-FM and (212) 362-1911 is the number of call for the lowdown. Speaking of ’BGO, they have a new general manager: AnnaKosof. CLASSIC, ON DISC - “Colum- bia Jazz Masterpieces” continues apace with 12 interesting new items— some reissued, one previously-unis- sued, others reissued in new con- figurations. In the latter category comes “The Essential Count Basie Volume 1” (’36-39 performances, but by no means complete—they don’t even include the complete Jones- Smith, Inc. session, one of the great recording sessions in jazz history); Benny Goodman, “Roll ’Em Volume 1” (airchecks, mainly); “The Quintessential Billlie Holiday Volume 2” (complete so far); and four compilations-“The 1930s-The Big Bands,” “The 1940s-The Singers,” “The 1950s-The Singers” and a sampler. In the first category comes Thelonious Monk’s “Monk’s Mood” and “Underground,” Duke Ellington’s “Jazz Party,” and Miles Davis’ “Miles Ahead.” In the first category comes “Live Miles” (see review this page). EMARCY REDUX - PolyGram Jazz, which reactivated the Verve label not long ago, is about to start up another jazz label from the past, Emarcy Records (which was a division of MerCurF). Up first on the new Emarcy are “Ray Bryant Plays Basie and Ellington” and “Billy Ecstine Sings with Benny Carter,” both due next month. Coming soon from Verve, by the way, are new al- bums by Antonio Carlos Jobim, Shirley Horn, Joe Williams and Paco de Lucia. BOPPING AROUND - Kid Thomas Valentine, one of the last New Orleans trumpeters from the ear- liest days of jazz, died June 16 in New Orleans at the age of 91...By the way, in all the tributes to Fred As- taire’s dancing, not enough people paid tribute to Fred Astaire’s singing. He was a swinging, elegant singer- one of my favorites.. .Felix Grant, the veteran Washington, D.C. jazz disc jockey, will have a new home come August 1. He’s moving from WRC, which is going to all talk, to WDCO..Bting has not turned tail on jazz. In fact, he’s been collaborating with the great arranger, Gil Evans, on some Jimi Hendrix tunes, which are due on Sting’s next album and should get a live airing this month at Italy’s Umbria Jazz Festival...New Blue Note signings: Charnett Mof- fett (whose name combines the first names of his father, Charles Moffett, and his father’s mentor, Ornette Coleman), Jack Walrath and Dianne Reeves.. .Westport, Connec- ticut’s Levitt Pavillion will host the annual Don Elliot Memorial Concert, July 19, with Mike Abene, Jay Leon- hart, Phil Bodner, Teddy Charles and many, many others taking part. ONJAZZ\ P ASSING ON-Trumpeter Howard McGhee died July 17 in New York after a long illness. McGhee was a fiery first generation bebopper whose vigorous, keening attack graced hundreds of bandstands and record sessions. Although McGhee was inactive for a number of years, I remember attending a record session in the late- ’70s in which he and Benny Bailey snarled through some fiery two-trumpet pieces. Howard McGhee, “Maggie” as he was fre- quently known, was 69. Photographer Bob Parent died in New York June 5. Parent photographed the jazz scene from the 1940s until shortly before his death, amassing over 100,000 photos, some of them the most famous images ever taken of jazz musicians. Bob Parent was 63. CALLING COLLECTORS-The International Association of Jazz Record Collectors will hold its 23rd convention August 12-15 at the Atlas Pacifica Hotel and Convention Center in Culver City, California. There will be concerts, speeches, films, records and books for sale, and a whole lot of talk about 78s, 10-inch LPs, maybe even CDs. For informa- tion about the event, contact the lAJRC at (213) 660-9061 or by mail to Box 1571, Glendale, CA 91209. DOCTOR BUHAINA - Art Blakey (1) and Phil Ramone congratulate each other after copping honorary doctorates at this year’s Berklee School OfMusic commencement. KEY NOTES-What could be bet- ter than the 21 -record boxed set, “The Complete Keynote Collec- tion,” that PolyGram put out last year? That’s right, “The Complete Keynote Collection” on CD, and now, not surprisingly, PolyGram has begun releasing a good hunk of that collection on compact disc under the banner of “The Essential Keynote Collection.” The first five sets have just been issued, with five more due in August. They are ‘ ‘The Complete Lester Young On Keynote” (which immediately takes its place as one of the most essential jazz CDs yet released), “The Complete Lennie Tristano On Keynote,” “Early Be- bop” (Red Rodney, Dave Lambert etc.), “Roy Eldridge and the Swing Trumpets” (dates by Roy, Charlie Shavers, Jonah Jones, Buck Clayton, Joe Thomas and Emmett Berry, and the only double-CD of the first issue) and “The Fabulous El- lingtonians” (dates by Johnny Hodges, Rex Stewart and other El- lington alumni). Much of this music, as I explained here last year in a review of the boxed set, is brilliant. filled with a majesty and grace that is often breathtaking. The transfers (al- though, as always, when they crackled on record, hoo-boy, do they crackle on CD) are quite excellent. Other recent jazz CD reissues in- clude “For You For Me For Ever- more,” tracks by the Artie Shaw Or- chestra with strings and a 21 -year- old Mel Torme (Musicraft), and a pair of two-CD compilations from DRG’s Disques Swing line: “Ridin’ in Rhythm,” featuring some excep- tional early Coleman Hawkins and Benny Carter, and “Jazz in the Thir- ties,” featuring, among others, Joe Venuti, Benny Goodman and Gene Krupa NAJ NOTES-The Los Angeles- based National Academy of Jazz, which is “dedicated to the advance- ment and artistry of jazz and to estab- lishing chapters throughout the country so diat we can become a major force in helping make more Americans aware of the complete spectrum of music we call jazz,” has upped its two-year-old Board of Directors from 15 to 25 members. The NAJ brain trust now consists of Ray Avery, Frank Capp, Allyn Fer- guson, Bob Florence, Terry Gibbs, Red Holloway, Phil Hulsey, Ralph Jungheim, Sandra Kimberling, Mauri Lathower, Luis Conte, Ber- nie Lewak, Mundell Lowe, Marty Morgan, Chuck Niles, Kirk Pasich, Dave Pell, Sue Raney, George Rap- paport, Pancho Sanchez, Jim Shatz, Terri Tilton, Jim Washburn, LaRue Brown Watson and Jack Wheaton. The NAJ’s next member- ship meeting will take place on July 30 at the Hollywood Musician’s Union, 817 N. Vine St., and Bill Henderson, Jimmy Witherspoon and the Britt & Brown Sextet will perform. ROUND MIDI-In one of the great ironies of the day, Dexter Gordon, in Europe on his first jazz tour in four years, was prevented from entering Paris earlier this month when the computers at immigration control turned up a 20-year-old drug rap. Ironic because not only has Dexter Gordon been in France numerous times since then but that, of course, is where he filmed “Round Midnight” and, to boot, where he was last year made a chevalier in France’s Ordre des Arts et des Lettres, a highly- prized honor. In any case, after five hours of moping in the airport. Long Tall Dexter was loosed upon France. Dexter told the International Herald Tribune’s Mike Zwerin that next time he comes to France, he’s going to be wearing his chavliermeda.1. BOPPING AROUND-In the hip- pest major label signing of the year, RCA Novus was pacted a deal with soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy, one of the towering giants of modem jazz...Bandleader Bob Florence was presented with the Los Angeles City College’s “Outstanding Alumnus Award” at that school’s recent graduation ceremonies. died July 24 of heart failure in Palo Alto, California, where he had gone to play at a jazz party. Wellstood was one of a group of traditionalists who came up during the bebop era and, since then, his Fats Waller-influenced piano styl- ings have been a constant joy— whether heard solo in New York’s piano bars, or as part of such tradi- tional groups as the Classic Jazz Quartet. IT’S THAT TIMES AGAIN- “Jazz and the Media: Past, Present and Future” is the working title for this year’s JazzTimes Convention, set for October 14-17 at New York’s Roosevelt Hotel. Joe Williams will be this year’s Guest of Honor and Billy Taylor will deliver the Keynote Address, but that ain’t the half of it. For those who’d like a sampler, here are some of the things (and several of the people) in-store. October 14: Registration, general opening session, “I Paid My Dues” (Ira Gitler, Chubby Jackson), Blue Note party (Jack Walrath). October 15: Keynote, “Promoting Your Jazz Station: A Reality” (Rick Petrone), “Television: Past, Present & Future” (Leonard Feather, Steve Allen), “Jazz Radio Today: Syndi- cated Shows & Networks (Ben Sidran, Andy Denemark), David Chertok’s jazz films, CBS Records (Terence Blanchard & Donald Har- rison). October 16: “Increasing Media Coverage for Jazz with a Series” (Frank Malfitano, Brad Simon), “Jazz in Print Today” (Gary Gid- dins), “Ad Agencies Look at Jazz” (Hal Davis, Elliot Lawrence), “Joe Williams on Jazz,’ ’ RCA party. October 17: Record Fair, “The For- ces Behind the Continued Growth of Jazz” (George Wein, John Con- yers), “New Age and Fusion in the Media” (Roger Lifeset, Lee Abrams), “New Technologies” (Ken Furst, Larry Rosen), “Media Conclusion Session,’ ’ PolyGram party (Joe Williams). For information about all of this, get in touch with JazzTimes at 8055- 13th St., Silver Spring, MD 20910 or at (301) 588-4114. FESTIVALIA NEAR-The Green- wich Village Jazz Festival is set for August 28-September 7, the only jazz festival in the world that takes place where jazz is bom and bred: the jazz clubs of New York City. See, the Vil- lage Festival is, for the most part, real- ly not a jazz festival, since the clubs of Greenwich Village are a per- manent jazz festival. What the Fes- tival allows is the ability to save a bunch of money on club-hopping. A $15 Festival Pass (on sale now at the Village Gate) gets the bearer a 50% discount on the first and second sets at the participating clubs and free ad- mission to the third sets. All mini- mums, however, apply. Check the local listings, as they say, for exactly who is playing at the clubs in ques- tion (Arthur’s Tavern, the Blue Note, Bradley’s, Carlos 1, Fat Tuesday’s, Sweet Basil, the Village Comer, the Village Gate, the Village Vanguard, Visiones and the 55 Bar). Other ac- tivities involving the Festival are a free kick-off concert with Sun Ra and Jack Walrath at the Gate, a jazz film series at the Bleecker Street Cinema, Sweet Basil’s “Music is an Open Sky” series and a number of other free performances. FESTIVALIA LESS NEAR-The 10th Chicago Jazz Festival, which has earned the right to call itself the largest free jazz festival in the world, will fill Grant Park’s Petrillo Bandshell for five nights beginning September 2 with, among many others, Stephane Grappelli, Wynton Marsalis, Woody Herman, a tribute to Art Blakey, Dave Brubeck, and a tribute to JATP. Won’t cost you a far- thing. FESTIVALIA FAR-It will cost you a farthing to attend the McEwan’s Edinburgh International Jazz Festival, which will swing out in the beautiful Scottish city, August 15- 22. On tap (so to speak-the festival is sponsored by a brewery) are Jay McShann, Bob Wilber, Buddy Tate, Acker Bilk, Ken Colyer, “Sweets” Edison, Humphrey Lyt- telton and many others with a tradi- tional bent. LAND OF THE FAT-Fat City Productions has been formed to provide a weekly syndicated radio series recorded live at New York’s Fat Tuesday’s jazz club. “Fat City Jazz” is the name of the show, and it’s intended as a 52-week series, with the initial program airing the first week of October. Charles Brandt president of Fat City, says, “‘Fat City Jazz’ is not a disk jockey spinning records. Our program cap- tures the top artists in the field per- forming at a hot New York jazz club, so our audience can sense the adrenalin and experience the true es- sence of the artists’ work.” Fat City Productions is at 150 E. 74th St., New York, NY 10021 (212-517- 1640). T he Grateful Dead/Bob Dylan GIANTS STADIUM, N.J. - The Grateful Dead/Bob Dylan show here (7/12) broke all previous attendance records at Giants Stadium, attracting 71,598 fans, most of them teenagers in tie-dyed t-shirts. Sure, there were a few fortyish granola types, but for the most part it looked just like the Haight in ‘68, back when going to a Dead show was an act of rebellion. Today, however, going to a Deadfest is an act of conservatism by a new generation that listens to its parents’ music and wears its parents’ clothes. In fact, one can imagine fans rushing home after the concert to trade notes with mom and dad, and to hear them reminisce about Watkins Glen and Woodstock. Apparently, teenagers don’t have heroes particular to their own genera- tion anymore (even the Beastie Boys are modeled on the rebel stance of a previous era), and they seem content with hand-me-down icons. Still, the pairing of Bob Dylan with the Grateful Dead promised to be the big American folk music event of the year, and in a sense it was — though the ‘event’ aspect often drowned out the music. Stadium shows are always more like vast communal gatherings than rock concerts, and this one was no exception. People danced en masse in remote comers and corridors where one could barely hear the music, and many others partied, picnicked, and otherwise ignored the show. This is partly attributable to the fact that sound tends to get lost in stadiums; with a mass of amps stageside and two sets of speakers in the middle of the field, there was a lot of bounce, echo, and im- precision. When fans started clapping along to one song, there was even a time-lapse effect, with the clapping from one side of the stadium coming at you about a second or two after the clapping from the other side, destroy- ing the band’s rhythm. Nonetheless, the music was often im- mensely enjoyable. The Dead opened the concert, playing such old favorites as “Bertha,” “Playing In The Band,” and “Ramblin’ Rose,” along with several songs from their new top ten album, “In The Dark” (Arista). Dylan joined the Dead for the last part of the show, and his set included obscure gems from his golden days: “Chimes Of Freedom,” “The Wicked Mes- senger,” and “Queen Jane Ap- proximately.” But with the Dead as a backing band, most of his set sounded more like the Grateful Dead than Bob Dylan, which benefited some songs (“Wicked Messenger”) and ruined others (imagine two Deads and a Dylan howling “Joey”). In theory it was an inspired cou- pling, but in practice they need a smaller venue to make it work. Per- haps the Dead can be persuaded to play, say, seven nights at a small Man- hattan club, while Dylan goes solo for a two-week stand at New York’s Town Hall. Now that’s something worth tie- dyeing a t-shirt for. Paul Iorio T he North Sea Jazz Festival CONGRESGEBOUW, THE HAGUE HOLLAND - Look, there are zillions of jazz festivals at this point, but Holland’s North Sea Jazz Festival is, beyond a doubt, the Big Daddy of them all. No festival is big- ger, no festival presents a more impres- sive line-up of talent, no festival covers the wide scope of jazz that the North Sea Jazz Festival manages to choke into the Hague’s masssive Congres- gebouw convention center every year. And, the wonder of it all is that this is a weekend festival-three measly days. To try to convey a sense of the breadth of the festival, here’s a list of some of the trumpet players who were on hand this year: Dizzy Gillespie, Lester Bowie, Kenny Wheeler, Randy Brecker, Clark Terry, Woody Shaw, Freddie Hubbard, Don Cherry, Jon Fad- dis, Wynton Marsalis, Jimmy Owens, Doc Cheatham, Wild Bill Davison, James Morrison, Ornette Coleman, Ruby Braff, Arturo Sandoval, Palle Mikkelborg, Miles Davis, Benny Carter and Roy Hargrove. That’s a par- tial list-in one building, on one weekend! Of course, it’s impossible to see all of these people. In fact, it’s impossible to see almost everybody who is on the North Sea Jazz Festival, since 12 stages go full-tilt simultaneously for about 10 hours each of the three days. So, without going into details , about the enormous difficulties of just getting around this thing, here is a quick wrap- up of what I heard, in the order, more or less, that I heard it. Friday: I began with a set of Monty Alexander’s Jamaican Jazz Jamboree, a band that combines jazz and calypso quite effectively (thanks, in great part, to the excellent steel drum playing of Len “Boogsie” Sharp). I then scurried upstairs for a taste of Armando Cairo, a young Dutch tenor saxophonist whose playing was more impressive than his writing (which, on this set, was fea- tured). Stuck around in the same room for a set of Benny Carter-the inim- itable swing master-and guest James Morrison, an adroit young Australian multi-instrumentalist who was best, here, on trombone. Then, whoosh, across the building for the Dexter Gor- don “Round Midnight” Band (Dexter, Bobby Hutcherson, Pierre Michelot, Billy Higgins, Cedar Walton). Ole Dex’s chops, though not yet at their sharpest, were pretty damned good, and his sound-that phenomenal big sound—was intact. Then way upstairs for some Dutch boredom-Tam Tam Fanfare, saxophones and hand drums- and Courtney Pine. Now Courtney Pine is a big deal in England-he’s young, he’s talented, he’s English and he’s black—and he’s getting himself into the Wynton Marsalis conundrum. The jazz press helped make him a media star, and now that he’s a media star the jazz press is quick to point out how overrated he is. In any case, he showed, to me, an impressive ability to play the tenor saxophone-updated Coltrane, swinging and adven- turesome. His young band may not be much, but Mr. Pine is one to keep an eye on. To bed. Saturday: 1. The Lonnie Brooks Blues Band. Sharp, ringing Chicago blues. 2. Rockin’ Dopsie and the Cajun Twisters. Goodtime-rolling Louisiana zydeco. 3. Arturo Sandoval. Scorching modem day Cu-bop. 4. Adalberto Alvarez y Su Son. Scorch- ing modem day Cuban salsa (look, there were four Cuban bands on this festival, four Cuban bands who, at the moment, are no more likely to play in American than Fidel Castro is to pitch for the Pittsburgh Pirates). 5. Oliver Lake Quartet. Silken modem New York (yeah!) jazz. 6. Willem Breuker Kollektief. Yeah, the excellent mad- cap Dutch band in a not-quite-tongue- in-cheek set of George Gershwin’s con- cert music. Excellent. 7. Herbie Steward. Herbie Steward? Yep, the fourth Four Brother was rescued from , obscurity and, on alto only, he swung, swang, swinged. 8. Jeannie & Jimmy Cheatham and the Sweet Baby Blues & Jazz Band. Los Angeles-based blues and jazz, natch, and quite entertaining. Nice to hear trumpeter Clora Bryant and clarinetist Jimmy Noone in the flesh (got to go to Europe to hear bands from L.A.). To bed. Sunday: I listened to the Dizzy Gil- lespie Big Band, which was smoooooooking!!! I listened to Polish tenor saxophonist Tomasz Szukalski, which was booooooooooring! I lis- tened to Chuck Berry, who was per- functory (but who was to improve-see next week’s Nice Festival review). I listened to Alice Coltrane & the Coltrane Legacy which was, well, not good. Alice has taken her and John’s two sons, Ravi and Oran, stuck saxophones in their hands, and sent them up on stage in front of her, Reg- gie Workman and Rashied Ali. They are not ready-not ready at all-to be professional musicians. I listened to Ornette Coleman & Prime Time, with Don Cherry guesting, and it was a good blend of Ornette’s old and new dreams- and hearing Prime Time play “Lonely Woman” was a treat. I then listened to a rip-snorting 17-year-old trumpeter from Dallas named Roy Hargrove sit- ting in with Frank Morgan. The kid has got a nice, gruff sound and a wide- open approach. He’ll be graduating high school next summer. Then, as if all of this wasn’t enough, I stumbled back to my hotel and found Wynton Marsalis, Arturo Sandoval and young Hargrove jamming in the lobby-in the lobby!—with Wynton’s band. I listened for two hours before I went to bed. The sun was already up. ONJAZZ EL DOCTOR — Tito Puente was recently made a doctor of music by SUNY/Old Westbury. Here, draping the good doctor, are (l - r) Prof. Basileo Serrano, pres L. Eudora Pet- tigrew and trustee Dr. John L.S. Hol- loman. B luebirds of happi- NESS-Another nail has been driven into the coffins of the turntables of jazz col- lectors. RCA has 16 spank- ing-new Bluebird reissues on the market and, yes, they are available only on CD. As usual with the RCA jazz program, the reissues are an odd as- sortment and represent a number of different approaches to the concept of reissuing albums. Two of the reissues stand out: be- cause they have been unavailable for many years, because they are excel- lent and important albums, and be- cause they both include alternate takes. They are Duke Ellington’s “And His Mother Called Him Bill,” and The Sextet of Orchestra U.S.A.’s “Theatre Music of Kurt Weill.” The former is an Ellington masterpiece, pure and simple. Recorded in 1967 as a memorial to composer Billy Strayhorn, the album drips with brilliance, and this reissue includes an unreleased ver- sion of “Lotus Blossom” and alter- nate takes of “Smada” and “My Lit- tle Brown Book.” The latter is one of the hardest-to-find albums featur- ing Eric Dolphy. Arranged and con- ducted by Mike Zwerin, Dolphy is featured on three numbers- “Alabama Song,” “Havana Song,” and “As You Make Your Bed”-but the disc also includes fine work from Thad Jones, Jerome Richardson, John Lewis and others. There are three alternates here but, alas, none from the numbers with Dolphy. The other discs just released are Art Blakey’s “The Theory of Art” (the 1957 LP “A Night in Tunisia” plus two unusual previously-unissued septet numbers); “A Song After Sun- down,” Stan Getz and his excellent mid- ’60s group (Jim Hall, Gary Bur- ton, Steve Swallow, Roy Haynes) with Arthur Fiedler and the Boston Pops; “Just a Mood,” Red Norvo; “Say When,” JJ. Johnson; “Time Was,” Bud Powell; “Swingin’ Till the Girls Come Home,” Lambert Hendricks and Bavan (culled from three albums); “Artist’s Choice,” Gary Burton (a Burton-picked com- pilation disc); “Clap Hands Here Comes Charlie,” Charlie Barnet (compilation); “Begin the Beguinc,” Artie Shaw (compilation); “Major Glenn Miller & The Army Air Force Band 1943-44;” a sampler; and three Benny Goodman discs: “After You’ve Gone-The Original Benny Goodman Trio and Quartet Sessions Vol. 1,” “Sing, Sing, Sing” (an B.G. Orchestra compilation), and “Together Again!,” a 1963 reunion of the original quartet (Teddy Wil- son, Lionel Hampton, Gene Krupa, of course). The sound on the ones I’ve listened to is just fine, particular- ly on the post 78-Era sides. And the discs are, for the most part, generous, with at least half of them clocking in at over an hour. PolyGram, which has been one of the labels spearheading the CD-only trend, has just put out four jazz CD reissues from the Verve catalogue, three with extra tracks. They are Stan Getz’s “Big Band Bossa Nova” (the one without alternate takes), Lester Young’s “The Presi- dent Plays” (withfive extra tracks, in- cluding a Lester Young vocal-!-on “It Takes Two to Tango”), Wes Montgomery’s “Tequila” (four extra tracks), and Getz and Lionel Hampton’s aptly-titled “Hamp and Getz’ ’ (with two unreleased sides). ONJAZZ W PATMETHENY P AT METHENY, ONE. THE SOVIET UNION. - “The place is a very high energy, intense place. And I mean, it’s a cliche, I think, to say this, but it’s really true: it’s much more like the States than anyplace else in Europe. The vibe is very similar to America. ’ ’ The place Pat Metheny refers to is the Soviet Union, where the Pat Metheny Group began its current world tour with 13 June dates. Pat says he went thinking, “Wow, what is this going to be?,” and came up with a few surprises. There was noth- ing John Le Carreish about the place, he says: you could go where you wanna go, do what you wanna do. He doesn’t think the phones were tapped, he doesn’t think he was fol- lowed anywhere, and he does think that all this glastnost business is for real. “The biggest surprise, though, may have been a few of the musicians that we met, most notably a young tenor player named Igor Budman. You know, we always like to go hang with musicians and play in clubs-we’ve always been known for that around Europe. Usually it’s fun, but it’s not usually all that exciting. Usually the players are not so good. When we played Poland the level of musicians was pretty low, so we ex- pected it to be something like that. We went into this club, and these guys were ripping, I mean tearing it upl But where are they getting it from? “The whole Voice of America thing is where they get their knowledge - Willis Conover. And everybody had tapes that are like 90% hiss - like sssssssssss- hhhhhhhhhhhhhh, and then, way in the background, you hear some music. Like 15th generation stuff. That was one of the other surprises- we went into these places and they would start playing our tunes. Guys that would know songs, changes and stuff, where the records are not avail- able there officially. ’ ’ One thing the Soviet audience is not, says Metheny, is very dis- criminating. When the posters went up with his name and “U.S.A.,” the concerts (some in arenas) sold out, bam. People knew it was an American pop-type group and that was good enough for them. Much of the audience, he says, didn’t know if they were going to be getting heavy metal or dixieland. But when the music started, he says, the 97% of the audience that didn’t walk out got right into it. “One thing that was nice was, after the concert, if there were 10,000 people there, 3,000 of them were waiting to get an autograph or just to take a picture or see you or some- thing. Which is really nice, because one thing in Europe which is true is that, especially in Northern Europe, you play a concert, and by the time it takes you to get off the stage, there’s not one person there — they’ve gone. But there everybody wanted to talk. And people would say, ‘I thought it was great, but what was the one thing you did - it was awful?’ I mean, they’re very frank. The bullshit level is very low - the tolerance for pretense. “And every night they’d bring us gifts. I have two flight cases, maybe a cubic yard, full of records, books, tapes, artwork, gifts, paintings that were done by hand. Every night after the gig, it was like people would just give us anything: they’d give us their children. ‘Here, you want my dog?’ It’s very embarrasing. Especially be- cause it’s a poor country and you feel it. People are always staring at your shoes and stuff.” But he says that, despite a couple of skeptics, he could sense that the people were, for the most part, ex- cited about glasnost, excited about the changes, and taking things like Pat Metheny’s appearance as further evidence that things are loosening up. “The sad part of it all is that, I made some great friends there, fantas- tic people. And, you know, when you meet somebody you say, ‘Hey, maybe I’m going to see you in the States some time,’ or, ~Maybe we’ll hook up in England or something.’ You start to say that and then you see the smile fade, ’cause they’re not going anywhere. That’s the one thing that totally pisses them off, and they hate their government for: that they’re prisoners, they can’t go. And they want to; not even to leave. I would say that 90% of the people that I put the question to, ‘If you could leave, would you leave?,’ would say, ‘No, this is my home, this is where I grew up, this is where I want to be. But I want to visit, I want to see things.’ And they can’t. And that is really heartbreaking. ’ ’ In Part Two (due in a week or so), Pat Metheny talks about his music. NATIONAL azz In Rio On, Rock In Rio Off, And Other Brazilian Matters By Christopher Pickard RIO DE JANEIRO-The Brazilian promoters Dueto have announced the line-up of 21 artists who will perform at the Third Free Jazz Festival, which is slated to take place September 2-7 in Rio de Janeiro and September 9-13 in Sao Paulo. In a very short time, the Free Jazz Festival has established itself as the most important in Latin America and mixes top international attractions with their Brazilian counterparts. The festival, which is a guaranteed sell-out, has helped introduce many of the international acts to a wider Brazilian audience thanks to the heavy media coverage the festival attracts. Last year’s festival helped establish David Sanborn, Larry Carlton, Stanley Jordan, Wynton Marsalis and Manhat- tan Transfer, with the resultant release and sales of their albums. The September festival will bring Sarah Vaughan, Philip Glass, Gil Evans, Chick Corea, Art Blakey, Lee Ritenour, King Sunny Ade, Spyro Gyra, Jim Hall and Michel Petrucciani to Brazil. They will share the bill with such Brazilian performers as Hermeto Pascoal, Doninguinhos, Laurindo Al- meida, Nivaldo Ornelas and Marcos Ariel. Glass, Corea, Evans, Blakey, Hall and Spyo’s Jay Beckenstein have also agreed to give a number of workshops for Brazilian music students. The record companies are now work- ing to suppport the festival, and a num- ber of releases will be scheduled before the event, which is also likely to stimu- late sales from the artists who per- formed in previous years. The event, even with Brazil’s cur- rent economic problems, continues to be viable thanks to the “Lei Samey,” a law which gives tax breaks to com- panies who support recognized cultural events. Among the main supporters of the festival are Free cigarettes and Pan Am... Despite the success of the giant Rock’n Rio festival in 1986, which had been planned as a yearly event, the promoters, Artplan, have had to moth- ball the second festival, slated for early 1988, because of the lack of a sponsor who is willing to invest the eight mil- lion dollars needed to realize the event. A number of major attractions have been rumored to be holding back from playing in Brazil—where, despite the crisis, record sales are holding firm-in the hope of playing Rock’n Rio. Most managers are now likely to turn to the Brazilian promoter Manuel Poladian, who has been quietly making a name for himself internationally with a series of well-organized Brazilian tours. 1986 saw visits from James Taylor and Miles Davis, and so far this year Poladian has toured the Cure and Echo and the Bunnymen, with Big Audio Dynamite due in August. Poladian also looks after most of the top Brazilian artists, and has just com- pleted a successful tour with Milton Nascimento, who was celebrating 20 years since the release of “Traves- sia”... Xuxa Meneghel, a model who fronts the top-rated children’s television series in Brazil, shipped one million units of her second album, “Xegundo Xou da Xuxa,” which her record com- pany, Som Livre, excepts to sell over 2.6 million units of by the end of the years. This would make her the big- gest-selling artist in Brazil for the second consecutive year. The album is now firmly planted at the top of the Brazilian charts and there is little chance it will be knocked off the top spot in the near future. The first CDs specifically aimed at the Brazilian market have started to ar- rive in the stores, having been imported for the occasion by PolyGram, EMI, WEA and RCA/Ariola. The releases are a mixture of top-selling Brazilian titles alongside sped ally -produced compilations. PolyGram, for example, is launching a package called “Per- sonalidade” which offers compilations of 18 Brazilian artists. The first six to hit the stores will feature Maria Bethania, Elis Regina, Gal Costa, Caetano Veloso, Chico Buarque and Gilberto Gil. The CD market in Brazil is es- timated to be worth around 400,000 units each year, but the figures are very basic as nobody knows, despite CDs being one of the few imports allowed by Brazil, just how many CDs are being illegally shipped to Brazil from Europe and the U.S.. The country’s first CD factory, to be run by Microservice, is expected to start operating in the next few months and should help lower prices in Brazil, where most CDs cost over US$30. ALL IN THE FAMILY - CBS record- ing artist Billy Joel recently completed a successful tour of Australia with a special presentation by CBS Australia of gold, platinum, and multi-platinum awards. Pictured at the presentation are the family of Denis Handlin, managing director CBS Records Australia and thefamily of Billy Joel. FULL HOUSE- In the eighth and final Countdown Music and Video Awards, EMI Records Australia/Capitol recording artists Crowded House picked up just awards for “Best Debut Act," “Best Debut Album," “Best Video," and “Best Songwriter" (Neil Finn). EMI Records Australia presented the group with an award representing triple platinum album sales of its debut album in Australia. Pictured (l-r) are: Rob Walker, head ofA&R and promotion for EMI Australia; Paul Hester, Finn and Nick Seymour of Crowded House; TV personality Ian ‘ ‘Molly’ ' Meldrum; and Brian Harris, general manager, EMI Australia. News From Japan TOKYO - According to a survey conducted by the Cash Box Tokyo of- fice, the total revenue reported by the 26 largest record and tape manufac- turers of Japan for the six months en- ding March 31, 1987 was 198,208,- 540,000 yen ($1,321,000,000). This is a 13% increase for the comparable months of last year and an increase of 10.7 over the past six months. Most manufacturers mentioned the growth came mainly from the new media such as CDs and Videos. CDs posted a 130.6% increase during the past six months, while analogue record sales dropped 67.8% compared to the same time last year. The Yamaha Music Foundtion will hold its 18th World Popular Song Fes- tival (WPSF) at the Budokanhall in Tokyo on Saturday, October 31, 1987. The foundation said this year’s festival should prove to be the most exciting ever as it marks the climax of the cont- memortive concerts for Yamaha’s cen- tennial year. Yamaha announced the finalists selected this year represent the finest “new talent” from around the world. WPSF gives many record com- panies an ideal forum to showcase and promote their new talent to the music world. Crown Records (president, Noboru , Saito) has signed with two U.S. jazz labels - Muse Records and Xanadu Records. First releases begin this j month. Joe Fields, president of Muse Records, was in Japan recently to meet with the executives of Crown records. He told Cash Box Muse offers tradi- 1 tional jazz and prides itself on its artis- tic excellence. Fields mentioned he was very pleased to be in partnership with Crown Records. He said,“We are very impressed with the sales and promotional capabilities of Crown Records. We believe our agreement will be benefit us both.” i Japan’s Top Ten Top Ten 45s 1. JAZZ ON JAZZ AT METHENY, TWO. THE MUSIC. - Pat Metheny's new album, "Still Life (Talking)," is the first album in several years from the Pat Metheny Group (the core of which remains Lyle Mays, key- boards; Steve Rodby, bass; and Paul Wertico, drums). For his Gef- fen debut last year, Pat Metheny turned in "Song X," the spectacular collaboration with Ornette Cole- man that turned some heads; rarely does a label like Geffen release a jazz record as startlingly adven- turous and avant-garde as "Song X." 'The reason 1 went with Geffen," says Pat Metheny, "was a portion of a conversation I had with David Geffen, during what 1 think Cash Box called 'the bidding war period' - hahaha. He just said, 'Look, the reason we want you is we want you to do what you do. We don't want you to do something else, because what you're doing is working.' "When 1 did 'Song X,' 1 hadn't signed the bottom line. Everything was cool - it took months, with lawyers and all that stuff, and everything was ready for me to sign it; they had already signed it. So we did the record and 1 went to Califor- nia with the tape and the contract and said, 'Okay, you guys, this is my first record. Listen to this, and if you don't want me to sign this. I'm not going to sign it. But 1 want you to know that this is what it is.' And they listened to it. They played it and they said, 'Wow, that's really far out. It's great, it's great. This is going to be something special, we're going to really do this.' And then they said, 'Well, you know, maybe you can do a Group record next." "Still Life (Talking)" is that record and its a continuation of the Pat Metheny Group's unique sound - a jazz-rock fusion that leans much closer to jazz and, on this record, is beginning to sound more and more Brazilian. Brazilian percussionist Armando Marcal is there, as are two vocalists - David Blamires and Mark Ledford - whose wordless vocalizing is closely related to the work of Milton Nascimento. "I'm kind of becoming an honorary Brazilian," says Pat. "1 spend almost all my time there and I've had a Brazilian girlfriend for about a year or so. It's been real good for me, because 1 feel very at home there and I've kind of been adopted, almost, as a local cat. "A funny thing, though. If you go to Brazil now, you don't hear anybody playing like we play on this album - they're all trying to sound like they're from L.A.. You hear Gaetano Veloso's band or Ivan Lins and they're playing rock beats. Milton too. And I just don't under- stand it. I feel almost like we should deal with it because they're not. To me, the music that Milton in par- ticular came up with throughout the '70s is just infinitely expandable. 'The thing of having singers is directly related to that. Although it does have a practical side as well: as we're getting more and more into these synthesizer things, having natural elements in the music is be- coming more and more important." Pat Metheny and Milton Nas- cimento have been talking serious- ly about collaborating on an album - in fact the second Geffen release was almost that collaboration. But Milton has just signed to CBS in Brazil and both CBS/Brazil and Geffen were anxious for solo al- bums from their new artists (a Group album, in Metheny's case), so that project is temporarily on hold. However, it's likely that Metheny's next album will be another one of his side projects: he's sifting through hours of live tour tapes featuring his trio with Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins - one of those projects that Metheny turns to every few years which has numerous jazz critics pronouncing, "Gee, 1 didn't know he could play like that." "To tell you the truth," says Metheny, "whenever somebody says, 'Well, 1 didn't know you could play jazz,' 1 just assume they probably never really heard me play. The way 1 see it is, how could they miss it? Because if there's one thing about the way 1 play is that it's obviously rhythmically and har- monically a descendant of Wes Montgomery. And if somebody can't identify that instantly, then there's nothing to say." So Pat Metheny - Geffen or not - will bounce along his merry way. The current Group tour will go through the end of the year and then - who knows? - the tapes with Haden and Higgins are there (as is the possibility of a tour), the col- laboration with Milton Nascimento is still in the works, the collabora- tion with Ornette Coleman is some- thing both men want to pursue fur- ther, and film scores and other projects beckon. All of it - and here's the key - will sound like Pat Metheny. "I'm sensitive to this subject," says Pat, "because it bugs me when I see guys and they've got their syn- thesizer band and they play just electric stuff, and then they play only acoustic. To me, regardless of whether Tm playing with Ornette or whether I'm playing on a film score. I'm playing the same guitar, the same amps, etc., etc.. So it's a conceptual thing more than a physi- cal thing. Because none of it is like a shift in gears, it's just a different way of playing. And 1 like playing a lot of different ways." Look for The Fairer Sax (about, naturally, a female saxophone quartet), part six of Women In Jazz, and Michel Petruc- ciani Live at the Village Vanguard (Sept. 3), Sun Ra: A Joyful Noise and David Murray Live at the Village Vanguard (Sept. 10), Courtney Pine and the New Jazz and Joe Turner (a one-hour concert film from 1980) (Sept. 17), and Art Pepper: Notes From a Jazz Survivor and Ernie Andrews: Blues for Central Avenue (Sept. 24). CRESCENT CITY SOUNDS- Jazztown is the name of a 13-part radio series on contemporary New Orleans jazz, set to air over public radio stations from October through December. A project of the Louisiana Jazz Federation, alor^ with stations WWNO and WWOz, Jazztown will be hosted by Ellis Marsalis and will feature inter- views, commentary and digitally- recorded live music. The worthwhile project will spotlight Alvin Batiste, the Improvisational Arts Quintet (led by Kidd Jordan), the New Orleans Saxophone Quartet, Earl Turbinton, Ellis Mar- salis, Fred Kemp/Smokey Johnson Quintet, the Young Tuxedo Brass Band/the Rebirth Jazz Band, Ger- maine Bazzle, Alvin "Red" Tyler and James Rivers, the Chester Zar- dis Band/the Pladde Adams Band, Tony Dagradi and Astral Project, Steve Masakowski and The Dirty Dozen Brass Band. GANELIN GONE-ALIN- Vyacheslav Ganelin, the leader of the Ganelin Trio (thanks to Leo Records, perhaps the best-known Soviet jazz group in the West), has applied for, ana received, permis- sion to emigrate from the Soviet Union to Israel. He will arrive in Is- rael early in September and will begin planning his new jazz career in the West. Leo Records still has some Ganelin Trio albums yet to release (including the band's first CD), and they have just put out "Con Amore,*^' Ganelin's first solo album. What this means for the fu- ture of the Trio, I do not know. EUROJAZZ-Stop the presses- the names of the six young European groups (all members under 30 years old) who have been nominated in the International Jazz Federation's Sixth European Jazz Competition have just been an- nounced. In no particular order they are Catalypso (Austria), Pageone (Denmark), the Toon Roos Quartet (Holland), Bad Circuits (Holland), the Jani Malmi Quartet (Finland) and Sprinx (West Ger- many). The alternates, in case of withdrawal, are the Legrand- Huber-Guettler Trio (West Ger- many), the Modem String Quartet (West Germany), and French Con- nection (Switzerland). The jurors are Pawel Brodowski, Lajos Dudas, Mitchell Feldman, Luca Cerchiari, Steve Lake and Bemd Hoffman. MORE FESTIVALIA-The Eleventh Russian River Jazz Fes- tival will take place September 12 & 13 at Midway Beach near Guer- neville, California. On the slate are Nancy Wilson, Wayne Shorter, Tony Williams, the Timeless All- Satrs, Jan Garbarek, Gary Bur- ton/Ralph Towner, Richie Cole/Hank Crawford/Frank Mor- gan and many others. The Fourth Richmond Jazz Fes- tival will run from October 3-10 in Richmond, Virginia and will fea- ture Max Roach, the DirW Dozen Brass Band, the MJQ, Ellis Mar- salis, Roberta Flake, Kevin Eubanks and many others. And the Zurich International Jazz Festival will get Swiss cheers October 29-November 1 as it rolls out the David Miuray Big Band, the Willem Breuker Kollektief, the Ornette Coleman Quartet, a John Coltrane memorial band (McCoy Tyner, Elvin Jones, Reggie Workman, Sonny Fortune and Freddie Hubbard) and a whole lot more. LESTER CREEPS IN - Lester Bowie (r) and Jack Dejohnette caught hanging out N.Y.'s Beacon Theatre, where the trumpeter sat in with the drummer and Special Edition. (L-r) Billy Higgins, Alan Broadbent, Ernie Watts, Charlie Haden.H ADEN-'There was a period in Los Angeles that's completely unique to L.A., like no other city. And that was around the '30s and '40s and came from the movie in- dustry-there was a real romantic flourish there. In architecture, in writing, in all the art forms. And the composers-Dimitri Tiomkin, Max Steiner, Franx Waxman, Vic- i tor Young-all these great com- posers that were writing romantic music for the films, the black and white films with John Garfield and Humphrey Bogart and Alan Ladd and Gregory Peck." Charlie Haden, an L.A. resident since 1979, is serenely eating a Caesar's salad on a trip to New York and talking about the motivation behind Quartet West, the band that ! he formed this year and which released an excellent self-titled album on Verve. "It's just a real special feeling, and there was a writer who was writing about that particular period, Raymond Chandler, and he's one of my favorite novelists. And so I wrote this piece and dedicated it to him and titled it 'Bay City,' which is how he referred to Santa Monica- which is where I live-in his novels. So part of the album is about that feeling, and part of it is my respect for beauty and reverence for listen- ' ing. There are some free lines that I wrote, there's a minor blues, there's a Charlie Parker tune, there's my favorite ballads, there's a hillbilly folk song that I wrote for my mom and dad, there's a Pat Metheny tune, an Ornette Coleman tune, a Duke Ellington tune. So there's a little bit of everything that I like to do, and I'm finding that it's attract- ing much more of a mass audience than I've ever had before as a leader." Quartet West is an interesting and unusual blend of players, one of those blends that just works. Tenor saxophonist Ernie Watts, pianist Alan Broadbent, drummer I Billy Higgins, and Haden don't necessarily look compatible on paper, but they make for a rich and harmonious quartet-a successful melding of its parts, tied together with Haden's own romantic vision of Los Angeles. "One of my loves in the music world is to get special people whose music I feel close to together and make music with them. I've done it so much, and so 1 did it again here. I called Ernie and Alan and Billy and said, 'Let's play a gig, man.' I found out when everybody was going to be in town, we played a gig at At My Place in Santa Monica, and it sold out and the music was tremen- dous. So I said, 'Let's make a record.'" Charlie Haden is himself a blend of unusual musical influences and experiences. He came into the world singing hillbilly music with the Haden Family Band (his parents were a popular radio attrac- tion in midwest country music circles), played bebop bass in L.A. until moving out into free jazz ter- ritory with Ornette Coleman in the late '50s, and has recorded and per- formed in diverse settings (with Pat Metheny, with Egberto Gismonti and Jan Garbarek, with Hampton Hawes, etc.) for some 30 years. This year, Charlie Haden hasn't been suffering from a lack of what to do. He's head of jazz studies at the California Institute of the Arts, he's part of the original Ornette Coleman Quartet (as is Billy Hig- gins) which reconvened this year for a marvelous album ("In All Lan- guages," Caravan of Dreams) and which is going to tour Europe in Oc- tober, and he's currently on the road with his Liberation Music Or- chestra (they'll be at New York's Cathedral of St. John the Divine on Sept. 12), now in it's 18th year of sporadic touring and recording. All of these things are important to him, he says, but Quartet West is, if he can help it, for real-not just a one- shot recording band. 'The working that we've done so far has been Los Angeles, San Fran- cisco, and the Vanguard in New York. We just played on my 50th birthday and the place was sold out-it was fantastic. We played the tunes from the record, everybody recognized the tunes, the next day we went to San Francisco to play the Great American Music Hall and the same thing happened. The guys want to keep the band together, and 1 want to play in Detroit and Chicago and Washington, D.C. and Boston and come back in the Van- guard. "And the more we play, the bet- ter the music gets and the more I'm finding out about the musical per- sonalities and the characters that are in the group, because they're really starting to play and to flourish, on free tunes even. We're even playing 'Lonely Woman' and we're stretching out." Charlie Haden is, in a word, thrilled at the positive response Quartet West has received in a short period of time. "It isn't like 1 sat down and said, '1 want to do this so more people will hear it,"' he says, "but that's what's happening." SOUNDS Sc VISIONS CD SPOTLIGHT I 0,0 o o maniacs 10,000 MANIACS = In My Tribe - Elektra 60738-2 - Producer: Peter Asher 10,000 Maniacs second album for the Elektra label is possibly one of the most brilliant and sophisti- cated pop albums ever released. Produced by veteran Peter Asher and recorded using full digital technology, "In My Tribe" features some of the most breathtaking mo- ments ever recorded. Asher has brought a slick, but not overbear- ing, style to the Maniacs latest ef- fort - enabling them to fully utilize their talents. Lead vocalist and songwriter Natalie Merchant's haunting vocals stir with unbeliev- able power and conviction. The first single, an unlikely cover of Cat Stevens' 1971 classic "Peace Train," is exceptional. Merchant contributed 11 of the 12 songs in- cluded on the LP, some co-written with other members of the band - each breathtaking and wrung with genuine emotion. Guests on the LP include Michael Stipe of REM (on the stirring "A Campfire Song"), and the lushly-arranged "Verdi Cries" features work from musicians Don Grolnick and Den- nis Karmazyn. A must own... MICHAEL JACKSON Bad - Epic EK 40600 - Producers: Michael Jackson-Quincy Jones The most anticipated album of the year! The full digital "Bad" was released simultaneously by Columbia in compact disc forma- tion. Jackson delivers a power- house package of pop, funk and melodic ballads, guaranteed to burn up the charts for months to come. The LP, an excellent follow- i up to the groundbreaking | "Thriller," features Jackson at his . finest. The gloved one once again teams with the amazing Quincy ! Jones at the helm, together the two present a slickly produced, perfect- ' ly polished product. Exceptional ' moments include "Leave Me ' Alone," "Liberian Girl," "Smooth Criminal" and the album's musical 1 centerpiece "The Man In The Mir- ror." Not to be missed is Jackson's pairing with Stevie Wonder on the fiery "Just Good Friends," possibly the finest duet Michael has ever recorded. Also included on the project is "Another Part Of Me," a tune featured in the Jackson film "Captain EO" - showing in- definitely at the Walt Disney parks.
