JAZZ O N JAZZ W HAT GIVES? - Let's talk about CDs. Specifically, let's talk about this weird thing happening that reminds me of that gas station business of whether the^re charg- ing you a surcharge for paying with a credit card or whether they're giving you a discount on cash. Example: Steve Lacy's "Momentum" (RCA Novus). In the press release for "Momentum" - a wonderful record, if you ask me - Lacy says, "It was designed for a CD, so we're talking about an hour of music. The extra time allows the band to stretch out more." Good news that - Lacy's got a great sextet and they could stretch out all day as far as I'm concerned. But, rather than put out a short double LP and a single CD (something that, for ex- ample, Impulse! has done with the new Henry Butler album), they've hacked two cuts off the LP: 'The Gaze" (11:10) and "Utah" (6:58). Seems to me that rather than giving the CD buyer extra cuts, they're sell- ing the LP buyer a condensed ver- sion of the album. The CD buyer isn't getting something extra, the LP buyer is getting something less. Example: Mose Allison's "Ever Since The World Ended" (Blue Note). The CD of this delightful album boasts two extra tracks: the sixth song, "Indian Summer" (3:52), and the last song, 'Tumblin' Tumbleweeds" (3:46), bringing the CD length up to a modest 45:43. Now is there a good reason why those two tracks weren't just put on the LP, which, if things haven't taken a serious turn for the worse recently, could have easily accom- modated 45 minutes? Example: Sonny Rollins' "G- Man" (Milestone), another terrific album. The CD has an extra track, 'Tenor Madness" (12:10). With a bit of juggling, however, "Tenor Madness" could have been in- cluded on the LP, giving the LP a Side A of about 21 minutes and a Side B of about 23 minutes. That would fit, right? Example: "Big Joe Turner: The Rhythm and Blues Years" (Atlan- tic), an essential collection, is of- fered as a double LP or a single CD. Trouble is, the CD is short four tracks, one of those cases of the LP buyer getting more than the CD buyer and the CD collector, who is a completist, being forced to avoid the CD or acquire both the LP and CD. So people are getting "extra track" crazy. It's okay, in my opinion, to add some extra tracks to a CD, but not okay, in the same opinion, to give the LP buyer a hard time by forcing him to purchase a shoddy product. In other words, truly extra tracks - like alternate takes, like an extra track that doesn't really break up the album's momentum and, no matter what. won't fit on the LP but is too short and too insignificant to support a double LP - are fine, but record producers - and, particularly, ar- tists - should make sure that their buying public is being offered their best possible product. Where pos- sible, I think, LPs and CDs should be kept in sync, even if it means ad- ding a second LP to the package. Anybody disagree? SONY JAZZ MASTERPIECES - Just kidding, just kidding, that's Columbia Jazz Masterpieces. In any case, that series keeps plowing steadily along, with their fifth release just out, six digitally- remastered albums (and CDs with no extra tracks) that deserve the at- tention of all and sundry. They are: Miles Davis's classic 1958 "Miles- tones," Duke Ellington's wonder- ful 1951-52 "Uptown," "Benny Goodman, Volume II: Clarinet A La King" (1939-41 tracks), 'The Essen- tial Count Basie, Volume II" (bril- liant 1939-40 sides), and a pair of compilations, 'The Bebop Era" and 'The 1930s - The Singers." PASSING ON - Harold Vick, a hard-edged post-bop tenor saxophonist with a long list of credits, died November 13 of a heart attack in New York at the age of 59. And Walter looss Sr., a veteran jazz bassist who put in time with Dizzy Gillespie, Billie Holiday and others, died November 15 of a heart attack in New York at the age of 73. CATCH THE WAVENDON - The Wavendon AllMusic Awards (see photo above), the brainchild of Cleo Laine and John Dankworth (an offshoot of their Wavendon All- Music Plan, a non-profit school for up-and-coming musicians), were given out in London recently and, among those cited, were Gil Evans, Tristan Fry, Django Bates and Michael Tilson Thomas. Gil Evans, on the precipice of his 75th birthday, seems to be raking in the honors (and gigs) recently. THEIR BUDDY - The Buddy Rich Band is about to hit the road for their first gigs since the death of Buddy Rich. Steve Marcus, Buddy's longtime tenorman, is at the helm and Danny Dilmperio is in the hot seat. They hit New York's Blue Note, November 27-29, with Anita O'Day. LASNOST - With oF Gorbachev hanging out in Washington this week, I thought I'd ojffer some comments by a couple of musicians for whom glasnost has some mean- ing. They are Grover Wasliington Jr. (him you know) and Igor But- man (him you don't). When I interviewed Pat Metheny this summer, shortly after his return from a tour of the U.S.S.R., he was going on about this terrific saxophonist he heard in the Soviet Union: Igor Butman. Better than most European musicians, said Pat, a real find. Well, lo and behold, I got a call a couple of weeks after talking to Pat from somebody who said that Igor Butman was going to be playing a concert in Buffalo, New York with Grover Washington (as part of the week-long Chautauqua Conference on U.S.-Soviet Relations). Grover, you see, had heard Igor during an '86 trip to the Soviet Union and he, too, was impressed; and, in the meantime, Igor went ahead and married an American woman and, shortly after Pat left the U.S.S.R., emigrated to the States, where he is currently a student - on full scholar- ship “ at the Berklee School of Music. Grover: "Igor's a tremendous young man. I had a chance to meet him in Leningrad and we had a chance to first play together in Riga. He's a very good musician, and he has the will to learn. He's a good player, irregardless of whether he comes from Leningrad or Chicago. 'They get the chance to hear a lot of music in the Soviet Union, but they don't have the variety of music that each artist has compiled over his career. Out of, say, 40 or 50 al- bums that John Coltrane recorded, the state might make one or two available. So the player who wants to learn will probably have to go to the black market and if they have to pay three or four times the price for a tenth generation tape or a used record, they will do that. Because the creative process is the creative process, no matter where you live. And you will find what you're look- ing for if you're really serious. "When we got back from the Soviet Union, folks asked me, 'How was it?' And you really can't ex- plain it. Because it's the feeling of the people that live there, it's the constant tension that you feel. I would very much like to go back there." Igon "I play straight-ahead jazz, mostly. I played it in Russia, where it's hard to find. I had good young musicians - bass player, my brother on drums, and a piano player - but, because we haven't enough equip- ment, I couldn't play another kind of music, which requires that. I never thought about other kinds of music until I came here. "I began to play jazz when I went to musical college. I played clarinet, I was supposed to go study classical clarinet. But then I came to the college and I met my teacher, and he said that I can play saxophone. And then I started lis- tening to jazz. "There are some musicians in Russia who could play here on a high level, but only about three or four percent. We haven't, in our of- fical store, records. Maybe we have one record of John Coltrane, and one Charlie Parker, and one Miles Davis, and one Benny Goodman. But every jazz musician listens to the Voice of America. "Here, I'm scared to go to the record store, because if I decide to buy one record, I buy eight or nine records. I went with my wife and I said, T want this record, I want that record. I need this, I need that.' She said, 'Maybe another time.' But my most exciting moment when I came here was in the supermarket. In the supermarket and then in the department store and then in the musical store. 'Tt only took me about a month to get permission to leave; now is a good time for everything in Russia. "Now I have a full scholarship at the Berklee School of Music. I played with Gary Burton in Russia and he helped me to go to Berklee with a full scholarship. Now all my musicians want to leave the Soviet Union and come here. Because I'm here, I'm the leader of the band, and they miss me. "Yes, I'm worried about being able to become a professional musician here. But I want to be a professional musician, and I didn't think that I could do another job. I will work hard to try to find a job as a musician. And not only straight- ahead, all kinds of music. Because I think now musicians must play all kinds of music." NEW FACES TO WATCH Peter Moffitt By Lee Jeske Jazz pianists traditionally have to suffer such indignities as horribly out-of-tune pianos. Peter Moffitt, whose debut album, "Zoe's Song" was recently released on RCA/Novus, won't have to worry about this as his career progresses. For one, he frequently plays electric keyboards. For two, he's a profes- sional piano tuner and he always car- ries his timing handle with him. In fact, tuning more or less got him his record deal. 'Tuning was something I sort of was forced to do by the necessity of having to pay the bills, so it developed into a career. While I was tuning. I'd also practice afterwards and reap the rewards of tuning. It's like test-driving the piano. And I al- ways knew that if I played after I tuned, someday somebody would hear me. And it happened. "While I was playing at a studio in White Plains, Bob James stuck his head in and said, 'Is that your stuff?' I was doing improvs that were really com- positions, ongoing pieces that I'd work on a little bit every time I tuned . He said, 'Give me a tape.' And about five tapes later he took me to his publisher, who then got me a record deal in a couple of tries." The first record, not surprisingly, was produced by Bob James, and his influence is heard on the album. But so are other influences. Peter lists McCoy Tyner, Keith Jarrett, Bill Evans, Royd Kramer, King Sunny Ade, Yousou N'dour, Philip Glass and Steve Reich as inspirations, and he has been a part of The Ordinaires, an eclectic New York group that can spin out things ranging from Thelonious Monk to Mer^ith Monk. But "Zoe's Song" has a definitie pop spin on it. 'T had been partial to the kinds of sounds that Bob James was into," says Moffitt, "in coming out of the funk-fusion '70s. And that whole kind of music seemed to sort of die PETER MOFFirr and shrink. I'm also into Richard Tee, Tm into gospel playing. I'm into Ray Charles, a lot of stuff." And on "Zoe's Song" one hears pretty melodies and pretty rhythms and such things as ballaphones, flutes, cellos, steel drums, bongos and African talking drums go by. One also hears pots and pans. Rhythmic pots and pans. Now Peter Moffitt is putting together a band. "I had not r^ly put together a working imit before this, but seeing as how the album got such a good response out of the tex, I immediate- ly started putting a small band together. Before that, I thought I'd just be a studio artist, which seemed plausible, but now it seems imthink- able not to support the record. 'T would like to tour as energetical- ly as possible. I think, as far as studio playing where you're really trying to clean everything up and make it as perfect as possible, it doesn't convey the energy that a live performance does." Of course, the emergency timing handle will be at the ready. "Guitar players take responsibility for it, why not pianists? I love the whole craft - putting in pin blocks, new strings, all that stuff. But my only tuning now is for a few favors here and there. I love the craft, but it's so time consuming and it's not my main talent." His main talent, one gathers, is dis- played on "Zoe's Song." In order: Pete Seeger, Oscar Brand, Steve Chapin and Tom Chapin joined forces for a rousing "Circle," Tom Chapin bumbled through "Taxi" (twice forgetting the lyrics), the Smothers Brothers broke things up with their familiar schtick on "Six String Orchestra," Graham Nash delivered a lovely version of "Sandy," Richie Havens tackled "WOLD," Pete Seeger - one of Chapin's biggest influences - led a sing-along on his own "If I Had A Hammer," Paul Simon sang a lilting (Continued on page 31) EAST COASTINGS F orward into the PAST - Some life when each of my three fave new records leaves me with the quesy feeling that, geez, music isn't going anywhere but backwards. I mean, if rock 'n' roll's not a dead art form, it's certainly standing still, feeding off its own swiftly decaying corpus. At least this week. From Glasgow, Scotland come The Soup Dragons, and I love them. Sire has just issued Hang Ten, a collection that combines an EP with some singles and clocks in at a whoppingly short 27 minutes. "No Soup Dragons single has failed to reach either Numl^r One or Num- ber Two on the [U.K.] indie charts," reads the press release, and while that's no small accomplishment, it should be tempered by the fact that The Soup Dragons do absolutely nothing new. They play the same power-mower pop the Buzzcocks had going 10 years ago. Oh, they sound a bit more like the Beach Boys with buzzsaws than the Buz- zcocks ever did, and sometimes they even sound more like the Vibrators than Buzzcocks, but the idea's still the SAME: music that captures all the energy ofpunk with none of its rage. The songs are relentlessly hooky, with rubber- band basslines and one guitar sawing while the other chimes out tense solo lines. The danger here is nostalgia over- coming all else - you know, sort of a Stray Cats with the Sex Pistols as inspiration instead of Gene Vin- cent. Fear not. The Soup Dragons play as though they stumbled over this stuff one day and were stunned to find, gee, you can play aggressive guitar rock and still be poppy; there's the illusion of invention. And the songs keep me too busy wondering what'd happen if you combined Martha and the Vandel- las with white noise (answer: you'd get the Velvet Undergound) to bother working up much anxiety about influences. "Man About Town With Chairs" is one minute and 50 seconds of amphetamine guitar hooks, with a suuusshing noise and some muffled words. It's absurdly simple, and only topped by the single piano note that runs through most of "Head Gone Astray." One little note plinking away while guitars shift around it every which way, and it brings everything into focus, like some minimalist mantra that unlocks the secrets to the pop universe. Sounds like a pretty great record, so what's the problem? Well, last week another pretty great compila- tion by another bunch of Brit nostal- gics arrives, and I begin to sense there's a conspiracy afoot. Felt's Gold Mine Trash (PVC) is like the long rumored but never released David Bowie Sings the Tom Ver- laine Songbook. The (short) record collects singles, album cuts, and un- released demos from '81 -'85, and everything on it explores the ter- ritory mapped out by Television on Adventure. Heck, most of it never gets past the territory mapped out by "Days." It's all ethereal, spider- web guitar lines criss-crossing over atmospheric drones in a thorough- ly delightful, sometimes beautiful, mannner. And it's all been done before with more reckless passion. Verlaine's worth worshipping be- cause his solos head for the outer limits as often as the gut, but the solos on Gold Mine Trash are just the same hooks played over and over. Circularly hypnotic, which is often rewarding, but music to drink cough syrup by. So to get away from this replay- ing of 1977 punk I turn to the Less Than Zero soundtrack. Bad move. The album is irresistible, but it's a no cure for the nostalgia blues. Poison does Kiss, Bangles do Simon and Garfunkel, Slayer does Iron Butterfly, The Black Flames do The Chi-Lites, Aerosmith does Huey "Piano" Smith, and Roy Or- bison does Roy Orbison. It works so well because every one of these performers draw their inspiration from the music of the Original Ar- tists they cover. The record's a paradigm for the way pop works these days: retro or recombination or recontextualization. The only in- novation comes in dance/black music, and fittingly the only shock- ingly new material on Less Than Zero comes from L.L. Cool J and Public Enemy. Sad days for modernism in popular music? Triumph of the old- guard? Nah, I just should have lis- tened to the Screaming Blue Mes- siahs or Age of Chance records, that's all. MR. MONY MONY! - That's Tommy James himself in the center. His songs have been high on the charts, the Billy Idol and Tiffany versions, that is. International Creative Management has signed James for worldwide representation. Tommy's recorded new original material, and a summer concert tour is possible. Pictured toasting the future of rock as we knew it (r to 1): Steven Levine, ICM; James; Troy Blakely, ICM. HOT HOUSE MIRACLES - Tina B has a new 12" single out, "Miracles Explode"(Criminal), produced by Arthur Baker. The house side, remixed by Junior Vasquez, is hot, hot, hot. Rhythmi- cally insistent with nice piano and a hook big enough to hang a record on, which is just what Tina and Ar- thur B. do. Tina B.'s breathy vocals give "Miracles" a, um, sexy feel. This should do well in the clubs. Joe Levy Cash Box December 19, 1987

ON JAZZ S INATRA ~ Frank Sinatra, who will turn 72 this Saturday (the 12th), is an American icon. There's no way to just look at Frank Sinatra as a singer of songs anymore, he's too big for that. The very name "Frank Sinatra" holds too many associations: Bobby-Soxers, the Rat Pack, Fmm Here to Eternity, the Mafia, "My Way," Vegas at its most glitzy and revolting, odd displays of generosity and loy^ty, piggish bAavior, His Way, and on and on and on. "Frank Sinatra, singer" almost gets buried. Yet, between 1953 and 1961, Frank Sinatra waxed a seri^ of albums that rOTiain among the ^eat masterpiece this country has produced. The Frank Sinatra who recorded for Capitol Records in those years - recorded, main- ly, Great American Songs arranged by Nelson Riddle - was a man who per- fectly matched his time, who perfectly captured the sounds of post-World War II, pre-Vietnam War America. Those records formed the soundtrack of the lives of the pre-baby boomers, those who were already adults when rock rolled m. Earlier Sinatra -- the Hariy James, Tommy Dorsey Sinatra, the Columbia Sinatra - was an artist in devdopmeiit. Later Sinatra - the Reprise Siiratra - was a man, for the m<»t part, swimming against the musical tide. Capitol Sinatra is the Sinatra that will last. So the fact that Capitol Recorcb is reis- suing these albums on CD is cause for serious rejoicing. Because these great al- bums have never sounded better and, more importantly, because American Capitol Records has, to put it rtuldly, abused the^ albums for too long, fre- quently chopping than into Httle bits and pieces (turning 16-song concept al- bums into 10-song midlin®). A few years ago, English Capitol - spedficaly, a man named Alan Dell, digitally- remastered these albums and put them out, on vinyl, whole (and in a wonderful 20-record boxed set). Tbe new Capitol Ctb feature the fuE albums (with one glaring exception), padded with some extra tracks here and there, and good, lengthy liner not® by Pete Welding. The music is, for the most part, brilliant - confident, buoyant, heartfelt singing backed by wonderfully subtle, com- plementary arrangements. The upbeat stuff is coAy and optimistic - this was tire Eisenhower Era after all. The ballad work is haunting in its loneliness and heartbreak. Nancy Sinatra once told me that Frank Sinatra was the loneli«t man she ever met. You can hear that here. One is always trying to find "the real Sinatra." I think the real Sinatra is cap- tured by some of these ballad perfor- mances, sublime interpretive sing^g. There were 16 "concept" albums put out by Sinatra on Capitol - some of the first pop albums to treat a collection of songs as something to be blended together to fit a mood or a theme. There were plenty of other Capitol albums too - collections of singles and movie soundtracks. But it's the concept al- bums that are the focus of this reissue program. Eleven of them are now avail- able on CD - four having come out last February, seven (two of them on a single CD) just out. Voyle Gilmor and, later, Dave Cavanaugh produced them. In chronological order, they are: "Songs For Young Lovers/Swing Easy." Originally 10-mch albums, here they are both on one CD (their original 12-inch releases were separate, with extra songs padding each out). Riddle arrangements for two mid-sized en- sembles. "In The Wee Small Hours of the Morning." Believe it or not, this carries the slogan "Special Abridged Compact Disc Version of the Album"!!! 15 songs are here, "Last Night When We Were Young" has been hacked off! Ballads. Riddle. Stimning emotional depth and maturity. But abridged??? "Songs for Swingin' Lovers." All 15 songs, including "It Happened in Monterey" and "I've Got You Under My Skin." Snappy. Riddle. Excellent! "Qose To You And More." A small, lovely album of ballads, arranged by Riddle for a string quartet, rhythm sec- tion and soloists, this has the fuB 12 songs originally issued plus three in- ferior extra tracks from the same ses- sions. "The Sinatra Christmas Album." Originally "A JoEy Christmas." Riddle and Gordon Jenkins arrangements, with two extra tracks: "White Christmas" and two versions of "The Qiristmas Waltz." "Come Fly With Me." Ring-A-Ding- Dtng. Billy May's breezy charts, ^ traveling songs. Includes three extra songs that don't quite fit, though they're also traveling songs: "Chicago," "South of the Border," and "I Love Paris" (ar- ranged by Riddle). "Frank Sinatra Sin^ for Only The Londy." Sinatra and Riddle's master- piece. Billie Holiday's the only other singer who rould sing ballads with this much feeling. Two songs from the same sessions - "Sleep Warm" (so-so) and a beautiful "Where or When" - are added to the ori^al 12, but they are an anti- climax, coming as they do after the original album-closer, "One For My Baby," the ultimate performance of the ultimate saloon song. "Come Dance With Me." The most chipper Sinatra album of them all, thante to BiHy Ma/s most chipper ar- rangements. Four inferior songs from the same sessions are added to the original dozen, induding two awful duels with Keely Smith. "Sinatra's Swingin' Session And More." Bang, bang Riddle charts. Three songs from the same s^sions are added, and they're okay, but I can see why they were left off originally. "Point of No Return." The Capitol swan song, reuniting Sinatra with his pre-Capitol arranger Axel Stordahl. This CD, oddly, doses with four 1953 Stordahl /Sinatra Capitol collaborations that pre-date the Riddle albums. A love- ly album all around, with a nice passing- of-time feeling to it, a feeling that would reemerge on "September of My Years," perhaps Sinatra's b^t Reprise album. Still to come, along with various com- pilations and soundtracks (and since the extra tracks induded on many of th^e CDs come from the previously-issued compilations, they'll have to be reor- ganized), are "A Swinging Affair" (Rid- dle), "VAere Are You" (Jenkins), "No One Cares" 0enkms), "Nice 'n' Easy" (Riddle), and "Come Swing W^th Me" (May). All 15 are wonderful, all 15 pin- point a time and a place and an attitude with remarkable clarity, all 15 are the work of an incredible American artist. REISSUING ONE FOR THE NIP- R - RCA, under its Bluebird ban- x, has recently added to its grow- g CD-only reissue series with an triguing (and, at times, confusing) tch of reissues - a wide-ranging p into various vaults and talogues. One of the interesting ings they've done is start some- ing called "Series 70," pulling in :ms from the now out-of-print -ista Novus catalogue (the Novus me, of course, is being used by IA; Steve Backer was the brains hind both Novuses). So here, ith an idea of what's there and laat's not there, is a tally (in no par- :ular order) of the 14 new CDs. ear with me on this): "Air Lore," Air. One of the finest jums of the past 20 years, and the eatest expression of the whole ea behind "in the tradition." No tra tracks, but none necessary. 72 release, originally on Arista. "Nexus One," John Klemmer. ilf of a double album, originally out l Arista in 1979, in which the tenor xophonist (with only drums and iss) salutes John Coltrane. “Creative Orchestra Music 976)," Anthony Braxton. One of axton's best efforts, originally out i Arista, featuring a large, all-star isemble. “There Comes a Time," Gil fans Orchestra. Gil Evans has ken this 1975 album and com- etely retooled it, taking out some icks, adding some solos, turning into another album. An impor- nt album, but this can't really be lied a reissue - it's more like a consideration. "Pops: The 1940's Small Band des," Louis Armstrong. Just hat it says - a selection of 20 1946- recordings by the greatest of them all, some of them (but not all) issued on the recent Bluebird Armstrong double LP. “The Joint is Jumpin'," Fats Waller. A good CD sampler (23 tracks) from the great Waller's mas- sive RCA catalogue. 1929-41 recordings (solo piano and small group) featuring all the hits in one form or other. "Jazz Workshop," George Rus- sell Smalltet. Important 1956 recording of Russell's small group including Bill Evans. Extra takes of 'The Ballad of Hix Blewitt" and "Concerto for Billy the Kid" have been added. “The Birdland Dreamband," Maynard Ferguson. Most (not all) of two '56 LPs featuring a roaring Ferguson ensemble playing charts by some of the best big band ar- rangers of the time (Paich, Wilkins, Cohn, Holman, Albam, etc.). “Natural Rhythm," A1 Cohn/Freddie Green. Originally two '55 LPs (Cohn's “Natural Seven" and Green's "Mr. Rhythm") which featured almost identical swing septets, used the same ar- rangers, and had much the same feeling. 22 tracks, but, again, not everything from the LPs (a ques- tionable practice, if you ask me). "Hot Mallets Volume 1," Lionel Hampton. 21 1937-39 sides from some of the most swinging sessions in jazz history. All-star (Coleman Hawkins, Benny Carter, Chu Berry, Charlie Christian, Dizzy Gillespie, Jo Jones, Harry James, Herschel Evans, etc., etc., etc.!!!) small band groupings, volcanic swing. The first of two CDs (but they won't be complete - all of these sides were on a marvelous six- record boxed set a few years back). "From A to Z And Beyond," A1 Cohn/Zoot Sims. All 12 tunes, and four alternate tracks, from a '56 LP from these two mucho simpatico tenormen. "The Legendary Duets," Ran Blake/Jeanne Lee. A real collectors item, originally issued in '61 as 'The Newest Sound Around," this reis- sue adds four previously unissued tracks, but removes "Summertime" because "the artists were dissatis- fied with it." (Another highly ques- tionable practice!!) 'The Music of Ornette Coleman: Forms and Sounds." Another high- ly-prized collectors item, this '67 album appeared for about two minutes on RCA Red Seal before disappearing. Ornette's chamber music played by the Philadelphia Woodwind Quintet (with Ornette on trumpet) and the Chamber Sym- phony of Philadelphia String Quartet. 'Time Being," Buddy Rich Big Band. A good title for this sampler from Buddy's smoking 1971-72 band. Three tracks from "A Dif- ferent Drummer," three from "Stick It," four from "Rich in London." TALENT ON STAGE L adysmith Black Mam- bazo/Queen Ida CARNEGIE HALL, N.Y.C. - When I first heard Ladysmith Black Mam- bazo a few years ago - thanks to some records that Shanachie put out here - I was bowled over. The har- monies, the blend of voices (seven bas- ses), just knocked me out. Now, at that time, if you had told me that this Zulu choir would be packing Car- negie Hall for a concert, well, I would have told you that Santa Claus really exists and Dove Bars can cure cancer. But that was in the pre-Paul Simon days. Now Ladysmith Black Mam- bazo is a constant presence on the New York concert scene: Since their appearance with Simon at Radio City earlier this year they've played S.O.B.'s, the Ritz, and a free Central Park concerts. Their admirers, naturally, have increased with each appearance - how could they not? Those voices, that delightful choreography and natural stage presence, the unique, soulful voice of lead singer Joseph Shabalala - hell, you'd have to be tone-deaf and blind not to be swept away by this group. So Carnegie Hall was packed to the rafters on this night - the cul- mination, incredibly, of a nearly-30 city tour for the group - and Ladys- mith delivered a delightful set, ably abetted by their onstage interprete, Denzyl Feigelson. They performed items familiar from their earlier New York appearances - things like "Un- omathemba," "Hello My Baby," "Yibo Labo," and "How Long" from their "Shaka Zulu" album - and they waved their arms like birds, kicked their legs like Zulu Rockettes, and just enveloped the audience with musical warmth. As a kicker, they performed the last part of the concert dressed in Zulu dress - animal skins and furs (the garb they're wearing on their Shanachie albums) - and they brought Paul Simon on for "Homeless" and "Amazing Grace." The rise of Ladysmith Black Mam- bazo proves something that some of us like to believe, but which doesn't get proved too often - that, at times, all you have to do to get the general public to recognize genuine artistic quality is to present it to them. If a Zulu choir can pack Carnegie Hall (and a long U.S. concert tour), cer- tainly other worthwhile kinds of music can do it. Having a benefactor like Paul Simon doesn't hurt, but that's the point - pop stars who pay lip service to various forms of music should shut their lips and try to figure out ways to give boosts to deserving artists and music. Opening the show was Queen Ida ind her Bon Temps Zydeco Band, a ively, San Francisco-based zydeco outfit. This was a brilliantly con- reived double bill, and it worked - the accordions and rubboards and perky cajun rhythms complemented the Ladysmiths perfectly. (Paul Simon, of course, recognized these connections on "Graceland," which featured Rockin' Dopsie on the cajun-based "That Was Your Mother." It would've been nice if Simon and Queen Ida's band had teamed up for that one, but it didn't happen.) Queen Ida and company were allowed a full hour, and the hour went by in a flash. Lee Jeske X /Jerry Lee Lewis THE UNIVERSAL AMPHI- THEATRE, LOS ANGELES - It was an unusual, but ultimately winning, double bill at Los Angeles' Universal Amphitheatre a few nights back when L.A.'s own X shared the stage with the legendary Mr. Jerry Lee Lewis. Considering the obvious musical diversities between the two acts, the show seemed an unusual pairing - yet once one saw both Lewis and X perform, it was evident that they were viewing two different generations of very similar rockers. Both X and Lewis, in his heyday, per- form heartfelt music that encompas- ses countless genres and styles. Jerry Lee Lewis took the stage with the stamina and power one expected (...and hoped for), unleashing his un- dying talents on the unsuspecting crowd. Joining him onstage was Brian Setzer on guitar; this merging of generations proved successful as well, the ex-Stray Cats frontman complimented Lewis brilliantly. In his set, the killer performed powerful renditions of a variety timeless clas- sics, including Chuck Berry's "Sweet Little Sixteen," The Big Bopper's "Chantilly Lace" (which Lewis him- self recorded in 1972), and a surpris- ingly effective, bluesy reading of "Somewhere Over The Rainbow." Throughout the performance, Lewis charmed and amused the crowd with his onstage chatter and anec- dotes, allowing one a rare insight to this legendary rocker. Lewis closed his set with his signature songs "Great Balls Of Fire" and "Whole Lotta Shakin' Going On." Instantly, the entire crowd rose to their feet, praising one of the true kings of rock and roll. After a brief intermission, X took the stage (unveiling a very pregnant Exene Cervenka) receiving an in- credible homecoming welcome from the crowd. The band quickly dis- played their talents with forceful ren- ditions of "Left & Right," "Burning House Of Love," "Around My Heart," "I'm Lost" and "True Love." With this show, it appears as though Los Angeles has finally stopped mourning the loss of guitarist Billy Zoom (who amicably departed the ranks a couple of years back) - a stigma hanging over the band for quite a while. The addition of replacement Tony Gilkyson (for- mally of Lone Justice) proved benefi- cial; Gilkyson contributes a heartfelt attitude towards the band, com- plimenting their sound with his flaw- less guitar talents. The band then brought out Jonny Ray Bartel, who contributed stand up bass during an all-too brief Knit- ters segment. "The Knitters" is a moniker for the band; an outlet for them to perform a bevy of country covers and originals. Included in the set was the John Doe/Dave Alvin composition "The Call Of The Wreckin' Ball" (from the Knitters' sole album. Poor Little Critter In The Road, available on Slash), and Exene's cutting ode to Ft. Lauder- dale, Horida, "Skin Deep Town." Without missing a beat, X im- mediately broke into a driving rendi- tion of Jerry Lee Lewis' "Breathless" (recorded by the band on their 1983 More Fun In The New World LP), fol- lowed by the recent composition "Anyone Can Fill Your Shoes." Before closing out the show, the band treated the audience to a selection of their earliest work (from their two Slash albums): "Johny Hit And Run Paulene," 'The World's A Mess; It's In My Kiss," their cover of The Doors' "Soul Kitchen" and the ap- parent anthem, "Los Angeles." It is amazing to witness the evolu- tion X has undergone, both musical- ly and in their acceptance by the mas- ses. A refreshing sight because this is a band who has not prostituted them- selves musically in any way at any point of their career, rather they have waited for the audience to come to them. Evolution at it's finest... )CK LABEL ROLLS ON SST: Rock as a Reason By Kevin Coogan DS ANGELES - "We don't need >mpromise our aesthetics to keep business alive - they work hand ind in fact." Not what you might Kt to hear from the head of a rd company these days, unless of rse that company were SST >rds. om the start Greg Ginn and ck Dukowski have always done gs differently. As a young teen i was designing and manufac- ng Ham radio components, iving three patents by the age of rteen. Soon after, he met owski. After discovering they ed similar interests in music, the went on to form Black Flag, the ers of the American hardcore e and one of the most influencial is of the decade. In 1978, almost years later, the band decided it ted to release a single. Realizing no record label was going to h their product, SST Records was ted. The name incidentally, was n from Ginn's electronics com- y. For a while after that the label essentially "a means to an end," is, a method to get their music to the public. In 1980, after Ginn the Minutemen perform (only r second gig!) he asked if they ild be interested in joining up. 2 r that year the Minutemen ild record The Punch Line, SST's long playing record. 1981 and ! would see the addition of the t Puppets and Husker Du to the 2r repectively, thus forming the 1 base which SST has built upon ds day. /Ve like to divide the line very rply between the people that :e the music and create the music, what we do businesswise," af- ed Ginn, referring to the fact that artists have 100% creative con- Meat Puppets' Cris Kirkwood inues, "It's always comes down hat we want to do . . it's enabled ) become a band, a real band with ething to say and an angle on life people can hang onto, you know, ty - rock as a reason." Mike t, bass player extaordinaire with Minutemen and now fIREHOSE es, "I get to do whatever I want tey're so willing to back you up, /d go into debt with you." For- itely, SST has had no trouble with ing in the black. In the past year e they have consolidated their ribution efforts internationally, 2ased their staff from a dozen to 2 to 30 employees, and have seen r annual billings increase well seven figures. Not bad for a ch of musicians who are trying to ape the face of modem music. 2ing an independent has enabled to be idealistic and to turn a it. "If you need to turn 100,000 s to show a negligible profit, then 're gonna think real hard about what kind of group you're working with." Independent distribution has been one of the keys to SST's low overhead. Not being tied to one dis- tributor allows SST to sell to many companies who openly compete for the market. Dukowski continues, "No single person has us over a bar- rel, which minimizes financial pres- sure ... it's very key in operating with groups that deal in under 100,000 units, the independent distributor knows that market very well." Being as independent as they are has allowed the people behind SST to make their own rules. Ten years ago there weren't "opportunities avail- able for doing the kinds of music that wouldn't sell a lot right off," says Ginn. "We had to learn how to deal with music where there really isn't already a pre-set market for it." One of the areas where Ginn and Dukowski had to "learn by doing" is booking. Their experience in this area began during the early days of Black Hag when they set up their own tours. "We got good at doing a lot of things in those areas just be- cause we didn't know any better." The hard work has paid off in the form of The Global Booking Agency, the company formed by Dukowski and Ginn which coordinates tours for the majority of the label's artists. It is apparent that creativity is as im- portant an attribute in dealing with the daily operations of the business as it is in dealing with the artists. Ginn explains, we "constantly try a certain amount of new things . . . and if you find things that work, then a lot of times you can apply them in a lot of different situations and that's where, hopefully, the label can con- tinue to be real creative . . . and al- ways look for new ways to do things in terms of promotion and every- thing else." Another area in which SST differs from other record companies is in their artist contract philosophy. Everything is on an on-going, per record basis. If you want to record - great. If not - that's fine too. Also, SST has never dropped a band from the label, no matter what the record sales might have been. "We like to be able to sell a few thousand records and view it as a positive experience . . . with us there's a feeling we can do whatever we want," explains Ginn. In addition to being the year in which SST realized its most impres- sive growth, 1987 saw - for the first time - the simultaneous releasing of compact discs for the label's major artists. In 1988, SST will initiate this treatment for all acts. For retailers and the rock-public alike, possibly the most exciting news is the re- release of SST's back catalog on disc. Classic recordings from the likes of Husker Du, Gone, Minutemen, Das Damen, Meat Puppets, Swa, Descen- dents, and Sonic Youth are available to a whole new following of music fans. Also, must-have compilations like Black Flag's "The 1st Four Years," and the various artists samplers, "The Blasting Concept, Volumes I, II, and III," are or will be available. Some other SST releases worth noting are those of avant-garde ar- tists Fred Firth, Henry Kaiser and El- liot Sharp, plus the efforts of new labelmates. Always August, These Immortal Souls, Run Westy Run, Blast, and Brian Ritchie. For more information concerning new releases or to find out when a group will be burning through your town, contact Mike Whittaker at (213) 835-8977 or write SST, P.O. Box 1, Lawndale, CA. 90260. NEWS he Year In Jazz: Forward To The Past Lee Jeske EW YORK - It has become onable for jazz mavens to wring hands and complain about hing new under the sun." The ens have a point, although both New York Times and The Village : jumped on what they saw as a trend this year - a small group of ig musicians in Brooklyn who attempting to broaden (not then, broaden) the music by ling something of an ever- ening clique. These are icians who grew up on funk and 'n' roll and who have the con- ice, and the freedom, to mix in l 1 parts Charlie Parker and equal ; Maceo Parker. They may turn me minute playing with Art ey and the Jazz Messengers, her minute playing with Sting, another minute playing with Dus bands led by each other. r are serious, they are talented, they've got the right idea: use t you know, bring to jazz what 're comfortable with. Alto phonist Steve Coleman is the :ho of the group, and the circle is -widening. They're not doing hing new, really, but they're not ig around stirring the old soup, ;r. As usual, their music is cur- .y being documented by small >pean labels. •herwise, the main jazz trend this has been labels sending musical le pigs into their vaults looking tuff to reissue on compact disc, it was an explosion last year has me a full-scale Armageddon this . Obscure collectors items that xly thought would ever see the : of a major label reissue (Ran e and Jeanne Lee's "The Newest \d Around" on RCA, for ex- le) are popping up - digitally istered and with alternate takes, ess. And increasingly these 5s are showing up on compact only. PolyGram, a leader in jazz >ues, has practically scrapped 1 reissues, RCA and Blue Note most of their reissues out this on CD only. Last year, you dn't get an American Sonny k album for love or money. This ; you can get three Blue Note ly Clark CDs. Not only that, but 1 Note released an album of k's compositions by something id The Sonny Clark Memorial irtet (spearheaded by pianist me Horvitz and altoist John d). ae jazz story for 1987 was, in the >rd business, the story of CDs, not just for reissues of things that e previously been available on zz fans who have been holding who have put their CD-player purchases on hold for another year, were not able to enjoy the new releases by Carmen McRae, McCoy Tyner, Phil Woods and Art Blakey; were not able to begin assembling "The Complete Dinah Washington on Mercury" (some of which never showed up on LPs at all); were not able to secure the full amount of music recorded for the new albums by Art Farmer, Hilton Ruiz, George Adams/Don Pullen and Sonny Rol- lins; were not able to hear some five hours of remarkable previously-un- released Duke Ellington sessions (from the new LMR label); were not able to pick up the first dozen or so reissues from the CTI catalogue (which CBS made available on CD only); were not able to enjoy Lester Young singing "It Takes Two to Tango." Other CD news since last year in- cludes the introduction of Columbia Jazz Masterpieces, the first jazz CD transfers from Columbia's massive catalogue (also being made available on LP and cassette); the improbable sound of King Oliver in digital stereo, thanks to a remarkable process developed by Australian Robert Parker, and thanks to Mobile Fidelity Sound Labs, which is making the "Jazz Classics in Digital Stereo" CDs (recorded for England's BBC) available stateside; and the in- troduction of mid-line CDs. The flood of multi-album boxed sets continued, and this extended into the CD business as well. Poly- Gram issued "The Complete Keynote Collection" on 21 LPs late last year, and this year followed it up with ten CD sets called 'The Essen- tial Keynote Collection." They also put out "The Complete Sarah Vaughan on Mercury Vol. 4," in mul- tiple CD and LP sets, and started the CD-only Dinah Washington program. Atlantic Jazz issued "At- lantic Jazz," a history of jazz on the label, on multiple LPs and CDs. Fan- tasy issued the 22-LP "Complete Riverside Recordings of Thelonious Monk," reissued the five-LP "River- side History of Classic Jazz," and is- sued, on CD, the 12-disc "Complete Riverside Recordings of Bill Evans." Columbia put out 'Trank Sinatra, The Voice, The Columbia Years: 1953- 52" on LP and CD sets, and the Smithsonian updated its seven-LP "Smithsonian Collection of Classic Jazz." And, to prove that the LP wasn't dead. Fantasy not only put out 20 Original Jazz Classic LPs, but pressed them on red vinyl. Other news flashes from the past 12 months in jazz: PolyGram Special Imports, which steadfastly brought in such impor- tant and adventurous European labels as Black Saint and Soul Note (consistent "Label of the Year" win- ners in the down beat Critics Poll), Owl, JMT, Sound Aspects, Minor Music and Red Records, was on its way to being dismantled at year's end, due to the promotion - to another part of the company - of PSI director Paul Del Campo. PolyGram Jazz - where this stuff belongs - is set to pick up some of this material (and Black Saint/Soul Note has one hefty catalogue) but not all of it by a long shot. This can be a very serious blow to creators and fans of contemporary (call it avant-garde, if you'd like) jazz. Time will tell. Ornette Coleman reconvened the Ornette Coleman Quartet that came east from California 28 years ago and set the jazz world on its ear. Coleman, Don Cherry, Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins not only recorded together (for Caravan of Dreams, a new Texas label that seems to have invigorated the sometimes quiet recording career of Ornette), but began live performances for the first time in 25 years. "I did it be- cause so many people think I'm play- ing different music with Prime Time," said Ornette. Dexter Gordon returned from his ill-health-induced retirement with a bang. He not only starred in Round Midnight, Bertrand Tavernier's intel- ligent film about the expatriate jazz life, but was nominated for the Best Actor Oscar for his efforts. He also returned to active concertizing - per- forming with the New York Philhar- monic, and touring Europe (and doing select American dates) with an all-star quintet. Round Midnight seemed to signal an opening of other media doors to jazz. Director Clint Eastwood - a longtime jazz buff - has just wrapped up shooting on Bird, the long over- due screen biography of Charlie Parker; Cinemax taped Sarah Vaughan and a slew of trumpet players for Sass & Brass; New York's WNET aired 18 weeks of jazz films under the heading Jazz Tonight; PBS taped a spectacular Wolf Trap con- cert honoring Dizzy Gillespie's 70th birthday for Great Performances and aired Celebrating a Jazz Master: Thelonious Sphere Monk and Miles Ahead: The Music of Miles Davis; jazz videos were released at a healthy rate (including Trumpet Kings and The Coltrane Legacy, two fine videos culled from David Chertok's film col- lection). Other artistic doors opened to jazz musicians, with Anthony Davis' full- length opera, X, having a successful New York run; Miles Davis and Mar- cus Miller collaborating on the soundtrack to Siesta; Benny Golson penning the music for an off-Broad- way play; Henry Threadgill receiv- ing a two-night showcase as part of the Broolyn Academy of Music's prestigious"Next Wave Fes- tival,"and Gil Evans scoring the music for a couple of movies and col- laborating (on record and in concert) with rock star Sting. And the jazz literature kept on coming, with, among other things, new biographies or autobiographies of Duke Ellington, Charlie Parker, T- Bone Walker, Larry Adler, Buck Clayton, Alberta Hunter, Dinah Washington and Leonard Feather. In the record biz: RCA, as promised, began issuing new jazz albums under the Novus banner, along with the reissues under the Bluebird name. PolyGram reactivated the Verve and Emarcy imprints for contem- porary recording, and started a "Live at Vine Street" series, recording vocalists at the L. A. club. Fantasy's already enormous catalogue swelled even further when it acquired Pablo Records from Nor- man Granz. Nesuhi Ertegun returned to the recording studios for the first time in years, producing the new MJQ record (their first for Atlantic in ages) and overseeing Atlantic's overdue CD-reissue program. Herb Wong resigned as president of Black Hawk Records, slowing that label's flow of product (like a flood in the summer of '86) to a trickle. Word as year's end was the the label had been sold. Enigma, the rock label, began a fusion imprint called Intima, and Is- land unveiled its "New Directions" imprint, which gave us, amongst other things, the U.S. debut of England's young saxophone sensa- tion, Courtney Pine. After 30 years on Columbia, Miles Davis released his first album on Warner Bros., "Tutu," sending Columbia burrowing into its vaults for unreleased Miles Davis sessions. Elektra announced that it was reviving Elektra/Musician, the jazz label dormant since Bruce Lundvall left Elektra for Manhattan/Blue Note. Gazell was formed to distribute the records of the Swedish/Danish Storyville label stateside. And a number of artists who have been minor label stalwarts for years found themselves on major labels: like Tim Berne and Jane Ira Bloom on Columbia, Steve Lacy on RCA, and the World Saxophone Quartet on Nonesuch. The jazz world lost Woody Her- man, Buddy Rich, Jaco Pastorius, John Hammond, Slam Stewart, Turk Murphy, Howard McGhee, Dick Wellstood, Bob Parent, Freddie Green, Eddie Durham, Maxine Sul- livan, Wilbur Little, Victor Feldman, Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis, Sippie Wal- lace, Theorgeir Stubo, Alfred Lion and Bola Sete during the past 12 months - irreplaceable losses, all. As this year made abundantly clear, however, the work of these in- dividuals will live on - as jazz con- tinues to turn to its past, continues to reissue and reevealuate its heritage. Cash Box December 26, 1987
